title: Data Modeling in MongoDB (with Designing Your Schema, Best Practices for Data Modeling, Schema Design Patterns and Schema Design Anti-Patterns)
subcategory: Data modeling principles, embedding vs referencing, design patterns, anti-patterns
core_concepts: flexible/polymorphic schema; schema validation optional; core principle: data accessed together should be stored together; four-step process: identify workload, map relationships, apply design patterns, create indexes; embed vs reference decision criteria; data duplication trade-offs; single-document atomicity; patterns: computed values, group data (bucket/outlier), polymorphic, document/schema versioning, archive, single collection; tree structures; anti-patterns: unbounded arrays, too many collections, unnecessary indexes, bloated documents, too many $lookup; 16 MB document limit as the hard ceiling on embedding
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (core): 'A core principle of data modeling in MongoDB is that data that's accessed together should be stored together. You should structure your data model based on your application's data access patterns.' Embed when 'You have a has-a or contains relationship', 'Your application queries pieces of information together', 'data that's often updated together'; reference when 'The child side of the relationship has high cardinality', 'Your embedded data grows without bounds', 'Your data is written at different times in a write-heavy workload', 'your data can exist by itself without a parent'. 'Duplicating data can remove the need to perform joins ... However, frequently updating duplicate data can cause heavy workloads.' MANDATORY semantics: 'a write operation is atomic on the level of a single document'; 'the availability of distributed transactions should not be a replacement for effective schema design.' Anti-patterns: 'if you do not limit the number of elements in an array, your documents might exceed the 16MB BSON document size limit. An unbounded array can strain application resources and decrease index performance' -> subset pattern ('best for ... data that is not frequently updated') or referencing ('best for ... large or frequently updated datasets'); bloated documents: 'if documents are too large, the working set might not fit into RAM'; unnecessary indexes: 'Creating indexes for every field in a collection can lead to bloated collections and negatively impact write performance.' Bucket: 'Time series collections apply the bucket pattern automatically, and are suitable for most applications that involve bucketing time series data.' Versioning: 'adds a schemaVersion field to tell the application how it should query each document.'
practical_examples: Book/reviews: unbounded reviews array -> subset (3 embedded reviews + reviews collection) or references (reviews: ['review1','review2']) joined with db.books.aggregate([{ $lookup: { from: 'reviews', localField: 'reviews', foreignField: 'review_id', as: 'reviewDetails' } }]); bloated document split into mainBookInfo and additionalBookDetails with $lookup + $mergeObjects + $replaceRoot; bucket pattern _id '123_1698349623', count field, db.trades.updateOne({ _id: /^123_/, count: { $lt: 10 } }, { $push: { history: {...} }, $inc: { count: 1 }, $setOnInsert: { _id: '123_1698939791', customerId: 123 } }, { upsert: true }); db.courses.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]) then db.courses.hideIndex('building_1') before db.courses.dropIndexes([...]); tree patterns: parent references, child references, array of ancestors, materialized paths, nested sets.
why_it_matters: This is the official document-model counter-doctrine to relational normalization: co-locate and duplicate by access pattern, but within explicit bounds (16 MB, working set in RAM, bounded arrays) and with named anti-patterns. A framework must present embedding as a bounded default, not an absolute, and note the direct conflict with Oracle's 3NF-for-OLTP statement.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual (version selector 9.0 Current); multiple sub-pages fetched directly.
notes: Pages fetched: Data Modeling (this URL); Designing Your Schema https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/schema-design-process/; Best Practices (served when requesting /data-modeling/concepts/embedding-vs-references/); Schema Design Patterns https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/; Bucket Pattern https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/group-data/bucket-pattern/; Document and Schema Versioning https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-patterns/data-versioning/; Model Tree Structures https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/applications/data-models-tree-structures/; Anti-Patterns https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-antipatterns/ plus unbounded-arrays, bloated-documents and unnecessary-indexes sub-pages. The current manual's pattern page does not list attribute, extended reference, approximation or preallocation patterns (older blog taxonomy); no per-page dates (footer © 2026).

title: Schema Validation (with Specify JSON Schema Validation, Specify Validation Level, Documents, MongoDB Limits and Thresholds, Release Notes for MongoDB 9.0)
subcategory: Integrity ($jsonSchema validation), document structure, field naming, hard limits, version currency
core_concepts: schema validation for established applications; rejects invalid inserts/updates by default; $jsonSchema (JSON Schema draft 4): required, bsonType, minimum/maximum, title/description; validationLevel strict (default) / moderate / constraint (new in 9.0, cannot be bypassed); validationAction error / errorAndLog (warn via separate page); document = BSON field/value pairs; _id reserved, unique, immutable, not array/regex; ObjectId default; field names: no null character; 5.0 relaxed $ and .; unique within document; field order significant; limits: 16 MiB document, 100 nesting levels, 64 indexes/collection, 32 fields/compound index, 255-byte namespace (235 sharded), 60 s transaction default; MongoDB 9.0.0 released Sept 28, 2026
engineering_principles: 'MongoDB uses a flexible schema model ... After you establish an application schema, use schema validation to prevent unintended schema changes and data type errors.' 'Schema validation is most useful for an established application with a defined data structure.' 'By default, MongoDB rejects any insert or update operation that would produce an invalid document.' Levels: strict 'applies the same validation rules to all document inserts and updates'; moderate exempts existing non-conforming documents; constraint (9.0) 'guarantees that every document in the collection satisfies the rules ... You cannot bypass document validation' and requires validationAction error or errorAndLog. MANDATORY limits: 'The maximum BSON document size is 16 mebibytes'; 'no more than 100 levels of nesting'; 'The field name _id is reserved for use as a primary key; its value must be unique in the collection, is immutable, and may be of any type other than an array or regex'; 'Field names cannot contain the null character'; 'Each field name must be unique within the document'; 'A single collection can have no more than 64 indexes'; 'no more than 32 fields in a compound index'. Cannot validate admin/local/config or system collections.
practical_examples: db.createCollection('students', { validator: { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: 'object', title: 'Student Object Validation', required: ['address','major','name','year'], properties: { name: { bsonType: 'string', description: "'name' must be a string and is required" }, year: { bsonType: 'int', minimum: 2017, maximum: 3017 }, gpa: { bsonType: ['double'] } } } } }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', validator: {...}, validationLevel: 'moderate' }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', prepareConstraintValidationLevel: true }); db.runCommand({ collMod: 'movies', validationLevel: 'constraint', validationAction: 'error' }); example document { _id: ObjectId(...), name: { first: 'Alan', last: 'Turing' }, contribs: [...], views: Long(1250000) }.
why_it_matters: Defines how integrity is (optionally) enforced in a document database and the 9.0 'constraint' level that makes schema rules as binding as relational constraints; the limits page supplies the hard numbers (16 MiB, 64 indexes, 100 levels) that bound every MongoDB schema decision and the naming rules that replace relational identifier rules.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual pages (9.0 Current) and official 9.0 release notes; all fetched directly.
notes: Pages fetched: Specify JSON Schema Validation https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/schema-validation/specify-json-schema/; Specify Validation Level https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/schema-validation/specify-validation-level/; Documents https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/document/; Limits and Thresholds https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits/; Release Notes 9.0 https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/9.0/ (9.0.0 released Sept 28, 2026; server now validates all ingested BSON by default). The 'warn' validationAction is on a separate page not fetched.

title: The ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline and Indexing Strategies (MongoDB)
core_concepts: compound index key order: Equality first, then Sort, then Range (ESR); ERS when range is very selective; equality fields keep remaining keys sorted; sort fields before range avoid in-memory sorts; $ne, $nin, $regex are range operators; $in equality under 201 elements with sort, range at 201+; map application queries before indexing; indexes have a write/storage cost; drop unused indexes; MongoDB generally uses one index per query (except $or)
engineering_principles: 'In most cases, applying the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) Guideline to arrange the index keys creates a more efficient compound index.' 'Ensure that equality fields always come first. Placing equality fields first keeps the remaining index fields in sorted order.' 'If avoiding in-memory sorts is critical, place sort fields before range fields (ESR)'; 'If your range predicate in the query is very selective, then put it before sort fields (ERS)'. 'To improve query efficiency, limit the range bounds and use equality matches to reduce the number of documents to scan.' Strategy (RECOMMENDED): 'Before building indexes, map out your application's queries and the fields they access. Indexes have a performance cost, but are worth it for frequent queries on large data sets'; 'Drop indexes that are no longer used'; 'MongoDB only uses one index to fulfill most queries. However, each clause of an $or query may use a different index.' Caveat: 'The $in behavior change at 201 array elements is not guaranteed to stay the same for all MongoDB versions.'
practical_examples: db.movies.find({ directors: 'David Lynch', runtime: { $lt: 130 } }, { title: 1, year: 1, runtime: 1 }).sort({ year: 1 }) -> optimal index { directors: 1, year: 1, runtime: 1 } (directors = equality, year = sort, runtime = range).
why_it_matters: The ESR rule is MongoDB's equivalent of SQL Server's 'SARGable key columns first, cover the rest' and Oracle's selectivity guidance; it is the one index-ordering heuristic stated as a named rule by a vendor and transfers conceptually to composite B-tree indexes in relational engines.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual (9.0 Current), Indexes > Strategies section.
notes: Indexing Strategies overview fetched at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/applications/indexes/. Covered-query, selectivity and RAM-fit details live on sub-pages not fetched. | Also catalogued as PERF-28 in catalog_11_performance.json

title: Transactions (MongoDB) with Production Considerations, Choose a Shard Key, Model Monetary Data and Backup Methods for a Self-Managed Deployment
subcategory: Transactions and their limits, sharding/shard key selection, monetary data types, backup
core_concepts: multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets/sharded clusters; not on standalone; single-document atomicity + embedding reduce the need for transactions; transactions not a substitute for schema design; 60-second default lifetime; no 16 MB total limit but each oplog entry <= 16 MB; 5 ms lock wait; write conflicts abort; one open transaction per session; 9.0 cap on concurrent transactions (10000); read concern snapshot + w:majority for cross-shard consistency; w:1 can roll back on failover; shard key: high cardinality, low frequency skew, avoid monotonic (or use hashed); choose key covering common queries; reshardCollection since 5.0; _id immutable; monetary data: Decimal128 preferred; double unsuitable; scale-factor long and string alternatives; backup: Cloud/Ops Manager (PITR), filesystem snapshots (journal same volume; sharded clusters need balancer off), mongodump for small deployments
engineering_principles: 'The MongoDB document model supports embedding related data within a single document, which reduces the need for multi-document transactions'; 'for many scenarios, modeling your data appropriately will minimize the need for distributed transactions'; 'a distributed transaction incurs a greater performance cost over single document writes, and the availability of distributed transactions should not be a replacement for effective schema design.' MANDATORY limits: 'MongoDB standalone deployments do not support transactions'; 'a transaction must have a runtime of less than one minute' (transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds default 60); 'each oplog entry still must be within the BSON document size limit of 16MB'; 'transactions wait up to 5 milliseconds to acquire locks'; 'You can have at most one open transaction at a time for a session'; cannot write to capped or system.* collections. Shard key (RECOMMENDED): 'Where possible, choose a shard key with high cardinality'; 'A shard key on a value that increases or decreases monotonically is more likely to distribute inserts to a single chunk ... consider using Hashed Sharding'; 'When the queries do not contain the shard key, the queries are broadcast to all shards'. Money: 'binary-based floating-point arithmetic ... is unable to represent exact decimal fractions ... unsuitable for monetary arithmetic'; 'Using the decimal type for modeling monetary data is preferred over the Scale Factor method.' Backup: mongodump/mongorestore are 'tools for backing up and restoring small MongoDB deployments'; snapshots require 'journaling enabled and the journal must reside on the same logical volume'; only Cloud/Ops Manager 'offers point-in-time recovery' and guaranteed sharded-cluster consistency.
practical_examples: db.gasprices.insertOne({ date: ISODate(), price: Decimal128('2.099'), station: 'Quikstop', grade: 'regular' }); migration db.clothes.updateMany({ price: { $type: 'long' } }, { $mul: { price: Decimal128('0.01') } }); transaction read/write concern: readConcern 'snapshot' with writeConcern { w: 'majority' }; reshardCollection / refineCollectionShardKey commands; backup comparison table: Cloud/Ops Manager RPO/RTO low, PITR yes; snapshots and mongodump PITR no, require write lock on sharded clusters.
why_it_matters: Encodes the document-model position that schema design (embedding) comes before transactions, with the hard transaction limits that make long multi-document units of work impractical; shard key rules are MongoDB's analogue of partitioning-key design; Decimal128 completes the cross-vendor 'exact decimal for money' rule; and the backup page makes the 'dump tools are not enough' point parallel to Oracle and SQL Server.
authority_rationale: Official MongoDB Database Manual pages (9.0 Current), all fetched directly; limits cross-checked against the Limits and Thresholds page.
notes: Pages fetched: Production Considerations https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions-production-consideration/; Choose a Shard Key https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-choose-a-shard-key/; Model Monetary Data https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/model-monetary-data/; Backup Methods https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/backups/. The shard key page does not state a shard-key size limit; the 1000-document transaction recommendation was not found on the 9.0 pages and should not be asserted. | Also catalogued as TXN-09 in catalog_12_transactions.json

title: PERF03-BP01 Use a purpose-built data store that best supports your data access and storage requirements (AWS Well-Architected Framework)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (AWS Well-Architected Framework, Performance Efficiency pillar)
core_concepts: purpose-built data stores; data characteristics inventory (type, volume, durability, ACID, access pattern, latency, throughput, IOPS, retention); OLTP vs OLAP as a selection axis; relational vs key-value vs document vs in-memory vs graph vs time-series vs wide-column vs ledger; modern data architecture (lake + warehouse + purpose-built stores); anti-pattern: one data store for everything
engineering_principles: Select the store from documented data characteristics rather than team familiarity; break away from one-size-fits-all storage. Risk level if not followed: High. Relational (RDS/Aurora/Redshift) for ACID, referential integrity and complex joins; DynamoDB for high-throughput read-as-is transactional access; Redshift or S3+Athena for analytical queries; NoSQL implies denormalizing into a single document/collection instead of joining; relational stores have storage upper bounds and may need sharding; caching (ElastiCache/DAX) and read replicas for read-heavy workloads; benchmark in non-production.
practical_examples: Table mapping store types to AWS services (S3 object, Kinesis/MSK streaming, EBS block, Aurora/RDS/Redshift relational, DynamoDB key-value, DocumentDB document, ElastiCache/MemoryDB in-memory, Neptune graph, Timestream time series, Keyspaces wide column, QLDB ledger). Decision-question table: data structure, referential integrity, ACID, growth, read/write ratio, OLTP vs OLAP priority, durability (Aurora 3-AZ replication, S3 11 nines), licensing, operations, BI tooling compatibility.
why_it_matters: Frames schema design as downstream of store selection: normalization and foreign keys belong to relational OLTP, denormalized aggregates to NoSQL, columnar star schemas to Redshift. The OLTP-vs-OLAP question is the vendor's own definitional separator.
authority_rationale: Official AWS Well-Architected Framework best-practice page with a formal BP identifier and risk rating.
applies_to: OLTP; OLAP; data_warehouse; data_lake; streaming; general
notes: Label: RECOMMENDED (WAF best practice; vendor rates non-compliance risk High). Page shows no publication date. Links to Aurora, Redshift, DynamoDB best-practice docs as related resources.

title: Data Analytics Lens - AWS Well-Architected Framework (incl. 'Modern data architecture' scenario)
core_concepts: modern data architecture (formerly lake house); data lake + data warehouse + purpose-built data stores with unified governance; inside-out, outside-in, around-the-perimeter data movement; Well-Architected pillars applied to analytics workloads; customer-proven best practices
engineering_principles: Modern data architecture 'integrates a data lake, a data warehouse, and other purpose-built data stores while enabling unified governance and seamless data movement.' Avoid ad hoc copying between stores; classify movement as inside-out (lake subset to OpenSearch/Neptune), outside-in (operational store such as DynamoDB exported to the lake), or around-the-perimeter (store-to-store, e.g., relational to NoSQL for dashboards). Lens covers only analytics-specific deltas from the core framework and tells readers to still apply the full framework.
practical_examples: Gaming company keeps game state in DynamoDB and exports to the lake for analytics (outside-in); enterprise copies customer profiles from relational DB to NoSQL for reporting dashboards (around the perimeter); knowledge graph built in Neptune from lake data (inside-out). Lens is installable in the AWS Well-Architected Tool Lens Catalog.
why_it_matters: Supplies AWS's official definitions of data lake vs data warehouse vs purpose-built store and the governing 'lake house'/modern-data-architecture pattern that a schema-design framework must map onto (raw/open-format lake storage vs modeled warehouse schemas).
authority_rationale: AWS-official Well-Architected lens with a stated publication date and document-revision history.

title: SaaS Lens - AWS Well-Architected Framework: Silo, Pool, and Bridge Models (with Tenant Isolation and Data Partitioning pages)
core_concepts: silo model (dedicated per-tenant resources, e.g., separate database); pool model (shared resources, classic multi-tenancy); bridge model (mixed silo/pool per microservice); tenant isolation as a foundational, non-optional concern; data partitioning (separate database vs comingled shared construct); noisy neighbor, regulatory profile, cost and agility trade-offs
engineering_principles: Silo: tenants get dedicated resources but still share identity, onboarding and operations (what distinguishes SaaS from managed hosting). Pool: tenants share compute/storage/messaging for economies of scale, manageability and agility. Bridge: choose silo or pool per microservice based on the regulatory profile of its data, noisy-neighbor attributes, access patterns and cost profile. Tenant isolation 'is one of the foundational topics that every SaaS provider must address'; crossing a tenant boundary 'would represent a significant and potentially unrecoverable event'; isolation mechanisms are 'not universal' and depend on domain, compliance, deployment model and AWS services.
practical_examples: Per-tenant database as a silo example; shared web tier with per-tenant application tier and storage as a bridge example (from search summary of the lens); Data Partitioning page frames the design question as separate database vs shared construct. SaaS SUS 1 best practice asks how silo/bridge/pool deployment models align tenant consumption with resource utilization.
why_it_matters: Defines the vocabulary (silo/pool/bridge) that governs whether a schema carries a tenant identifier/partition key (pool) or relies on physical separation (silo), and makes isolation itself MANDATORY while leaving the storage mechanism contextual.
authority_rationale: AWS-official Well-Architected lens, available in the Well-Architected Tool Lens Catalog; dated publication.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/saas-lens/saas-lens.html (landing, publication date April 4, 2023), https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/saas-lens/tenant-isolation.html, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/saas-lens/data-partitioning.html (both short intro pages). Labels: tenant isolation MANDATORY; silo/pool/bridge choice OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL. | Also catalogued as TEN-01 in catalog_14_tenancy_audit_temporal.json

title: SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies: Isolating Resources in a Multi-Tenant Environment (AWS whitepaper) and Multi-tenant SaaS Storage Strategies (AWS whitepaper)
core_concepts: silo, pool and bridge isolation models; deployment-time vs runtime isolation; IAM-based isolation easier in silo, harder in pool; cost attribution easier in silo; pool storage model scoped by a partitioning key; bridge storage model with per-tenant tables in a shared database (historical definition)
engineering_principles: Per WebSearch summaries of the indexed sub-pages: bridge applies silo or pool 'wherever each fits'; 'Attributing consumption to a specific tenant is much easier in silo, while pooled attribution is more challenging'; 'IAM works well for expressing silo isolation policies, but it becomes more involved in the pool model' so the SaaS application must enforce tenant scoping; the storage whitepaper's pool model 'uses a partition key to scope access to shared tables' and bridge 'typically uses separate per-tenant tables in a shared database'; 'Pool requires a partitioning key that scopes and controls access to tenant data.'

title: NoSQL design for DynamoDB (with 'Best practices for designing and using partition keys effectively')
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide)
core_concepts: access-pattern-first modeling; data size, data shape, data velocity; keep related data together (locality of reference); as few tables as possible; use sort order; distribute queries / avoid hot partitions; global secondary indexes; partition throughput limits (3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU per partition); write sharding
engineering_principles: 'The first step in designing your DynamoDB application is to identify the specific query patterns that the system must satisfy'; do not start the schema 'until you know the questions it will need to answer.' In RDBMS 'you design for flexibility... normalization is important'; in DynamoDB 'you design your schema specifically to make the most common and important queries as fast and as inexpensive as possible.' Maintain as few tables as possible (exceptions: high-volume time series or very different access patterns); group related items via key/sort design; 'design data keys to distribute traffic evenly across partitions as much as possible, avoiding hot spots'; use GSIs for alternate queries. Design 'for uniform activity across all partition keys'; each partition delivers at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second; factor item size into throughput math.
practical_examples: Single table with inverted indexes building hierarchical structures; 20 KB item consuming 5 RCU per strongly consistent read, so one item supports about 600 reads/s before partition limits; write-sharding and data-upload distribution sub-pages; NoSQL Workbench for data modeling.
why_it_matters: The clearest vendor statement that NoSQL schema design inverts relational practice (queries drive schema; normalization is replaced by locality and key design) and that partition-key design is a schema decision with hard throughput consequences.
authority_rationale: Official AWS service developer guide best-practices chapter.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html (partition limits, uniform activity). Labels: RECOMMENDED; partition limits are hard product limits (MANDATORY constraints). No date shown.

title: Data Modeling foundations in DynamoDB (single table vs multiple table design)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide)
core_concepts: single-table design; item collections (same partition key co-located); multiple-table design; RCU cost of multi-entity reads; backup/encryption granularity trade-offs; multi-tenant per-tenant encryption keys; DynamoDB Streams fan-out cost; GraphQL and typed SDK mapper friction
engineering_principles: Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one table using item collections to optimize access patterns, performance and cost. Advantages: one query for two sub-4 KB items costs 0.5 RCU vs 1 RCU for two queries; fewer IAM policies, alarms and CMK rotations; capacity 'averaged across all entities' giving smoother, more predictable consumption. Disadvantages: steep learning curve; 'Backups are all or nothing'; 'Table encryption is shared across all items... client side encryption would be required' for per-tenant keys; all changes flow to Streams; Infrequent Access class less effective when mixing historical and operational data; harder with GraphQL resolvers and DynamoDBMapper/Enhanced Client. Multiple-table design is 'simpler to design', allows per-table backups/encryption/storage class and per-table change streams, at the cost of client-side joins and more alarms/IAM management. Use single table when access patterns frequently query multiple entity types together; multi-table is 'good and sufficient' when they do not.
practical_examples: Forum/Thread tables as a multi-table example; UserID item collection with sort key distinguishing entity types as a single-table example; recommendation to keep non-mission-critical data in a separate table for backup granularity.
why_it_matters: Gives the authoritative pros/cons for the most debated NoSQL schema choice and ties it to multi-tenancy (per-tenant encryption keys favor multi-table/silo), cost (RCU and storage class) and operations.
authority_rationale: Official AWS DynamoDB developer guide.
notes: Label: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL (vendor presents both as valid; general guidance in CLOUD-06 defaults to as few tables as possible). Search-surfaced but unfetched related pages: bp-table-design.html, bp-modeling-nosql.html, bp-time-series.html; AWS PG 'Modernizing your application by migrating from an RDBMS to Amazon DynamoDB' HTML welcome page returned 404.

title: Amazon Redshift best practices for designing tables (with 'Choose the best distribution style' and 'Choose the best sort key')
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (Amazon Redshift Database Developer Guide)
core_concepts: sort key (AUTO, timestamp leading column, range/equality filter column, join column); distribution style (AUTO, KEY, EVEN, ALL); fact/dimension collocation on a common DISTKEY; compression encodings chosen by COPY; primary/foreign key constraints as optimizer hints; smallest column size; date/time data types; automatic table optimization; zone maps / block skipping
engineering_principles: Table design decisions 'heavily influence overall query performance' and storage. Distribution goal: 'minimize the impact of the redistribution step by locating the data where it needs to be before the query is run.' Steps: distribute the fact table and one dimension on their common columns (a fact table 'can have only one distribution key'); choose the largest dimension by filtered dataset size; choose a high-cardinality column in the filtered result set; use ALL distribution for dimensions that cannot be collocated (at the cost of storage and load time); or specify AUTO. Sort keys: AUTO, or timestamp leading column if recent data is queried most, the range/equality filter column (enables block skipping via per-block min/max), or the join column as both sort and distribution key to enable sort-merge joins. Also: let COPY choose compression, define PK/FK constraints, use smallest column sizes and date/time types.
practical_examples: Sales table distributed on date column yields even distribution unless seasonal, but range-restricted date predicates skew work onto few slices; designating dimension PK and fact FK as DISTKEY for collocated joins.
why_it_matters: Defines warehouse schema design as physical-layout design (distribution + sort + encoding) on top of a star schema; directly comparable to Synapse hash/replicated/round-robin and BigQuery partition/cluster guidance.
authority_rationale: Official AWS Redshift developer guide.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c_best-practices-best-dist-key.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c_best-practices-sort-key.html. Pages carry a banner that Python UDF support ends after June 30, 2026 (blog dated June 30, 2025), indicating current maintenance. Labels: RECOMMENDED; AUTO is the default recommendation when automatic table optimization is used. Compression and constraint sub-pages were listed but not fetched.

title: Best practices for Amazon RDS (with Best practices with Amazon Aurora)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (Amazon RDS User Guide / Aurora User Guide)
core_concepts: SLA-required operational guidelines; working set in RAM; MySQL/MariaDB table size (16 TiB file limit; >100 GB tables degrade) and table count (<10,000); InnoDB as required storage engine; PostgreSQL autovacuum must not be disabled; bulk-load parameter tuning; DNS TTL < 30 s and failover testing; AWS database drivers for fast failover; parameter group testing
engineering_principles: 'The Amazon RDS Service Level Agreement requires that you follow these guidelines': monitor memory/CPU/replica lag/storage, scale before capacity limits, enable automated backups in low-write windows, keep DNS TTL under 30 seconds, test failover. Allocate RAM so the working set 'resides almost completely in memory' (watch ReadIOPS / BufferCacheHitRatio). MySQL/MariaDB: partition large tables well under the 16 TiB file limit; very large tables (>100 GB) hurt reads, writes and especially DDL; 'We recommend having fewer than 10,000 tables total'; InnoDB is the recommended and supported engine (MyISAM breaks PITR). PostgreSQL: autovacuum 'is required by PostgreSQL... critical to good performance'; 'we strongly recommend that you do not turn off autovacuum.' Aurora: clusters over 40 TB should not use db.t2/t3/t4g; prefer AWS drivers (single-digit-second failover); test parameter-group changes on a test cluster first.
practical_examples: Query to find the ten largest tables/indexes via information_schema; dead-tuple query against pg_stat_all_tables; bulk-load recipe (disable backups and Multi-AZ, raise maintenance_work_mem/max_wal_size/checkpoint_timeout, disable synchronous_commit and autovacuum, use pg_dump -Fc / pg_restore -j, then revert); SQL Server Multi-AZ guidance to avoid simple recovery/offline/read-only modes.
why_it_matters: Sets the relational OLTP operating envelope that schema designs must respect on AWS (table count, table size, partitioning for size, index memory footprint) and marks which practices are SLA-conditioned.
authority_rationale: Official AWS RDS and Aurora user guides.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.BestPractices.html (operational guidelines, RAM, drivers, parameter groups). Labels: operational guidelines MANDATORY (SLA wording); table-count/size and autovacuum RECOMMENDED (autovacuum 'strongly'). Neither page shows a date. title: Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework (overview; with Reliability principle 'Perform testing for recovery from data loss')

engineering_principles: Overview lists pillars and five core principles; it contains no database-specific recommendations (stateless architecture mentions 'shared storage or cached services'; financial-services perspective notes data residency affects failover region). The reliability principle on data loss: judge recovery tests by data integrity, RTO and RPO; schedule backups to meet RPO (e.g., 'at least every 15 minutes' for a 15-minute RPO); run automated consistency checks after each backup and restore into non-production regularly; use Cloud SQL automated backups, Spanner backups, Cloud Storage; PITR for Cloud SQL and incremental backups for large datasets; alert in Cloud Monitoring when backup intervals exceed RPO; replicate backups across regions; combine with active-active or cross-region replication; 'a data restoration test must include testing of the entire application stack.'

title: Schema design best practices - Spanner (Choose a primary key to prevent hotspots)
core_concepts: hotspotting; no monotonically increasing/decreasing first key part on high-write tables; UUID v4 (not v1) primary keys; bit-reversed sequences; hash-prefix logical sharding; DESC timestamp key parts; interleaved (parent-child) tables; no non-interleaved index on high-write monotonic columns
engineering_principles: Best practice 1: 'Do not choose a column whose value monotonically increases or decreases as the first key part for a high write rate table' (reversing sort order does not help). Remedies: put a high-cardinality column such as UserId first; use UUID v4 via NEW_UUID()/gen_random_uuid() and avoid v1 UUIDs whose high-order bits are timestamps; bit-reverse sequential integers; add a shard column computed as hash of key columns modulo N with N roughly equal to expected node count and kept static. Best practice 2: add DESC to timestamp key parts when reading most-recent-first. Interleave child tables under parents to co-locate rows when a parent is unlikely to produce thousands of events per second. Best practice 3: 'Don't create a non-interleaved index on a high write rate column'; use interleaved indexes or the same sharding techniques because index tables inherit hotspot risk.
practical_examples: Generated shard column using FARM_FINGERPRINT; swapping (Timestamp, UserId) to (UserId, Timestamp); interleaved event history read with LIMIT in reverse chronological order.
why_it_matters: Shows that even a fully relational, ACID database at horizontal scale requires NoSQL-style key-distribution thinking; sequential surrogate keys that are standard in single-node OLTP become an anti-pattern.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud Spanner product documentation.
notes: Fetched at docs.cloud.google.com after 301 from cloud.google.com. Labels: RECOMMENDED (phrased 'do not'/'don't'). Conflict with traditional RDBMS practice (auto-increment PKs) is explicit in the source. | Also catalogued as PERF-47 in catalog_11_performance.json

title: Use nested and repeated fields - BigQuery (with 'Schema and data transfer overview' denormalization/partitioning guidance)
core_concepts: denormalization for read performance; nested STRUCT and repeated ARRAY fields; hierarchical one-to-many relationships inline; star/snowflake schemas supported but not native; when denormalization does not help; partition and cluster migrated tables
engineering_principles: 'Denormalization is a common strategy for increasing read performance' for relational datasets; BigQuery's way to denormalize is nested and repeated fields, which preserve relationships inline and reduce joins; 'It's best to use this strategy when the relationships are hierarchical'; storage savings from normalization matter less than performance. Caveat: 'In some circumstances, denormalizing your data and using nested and repeated fields doesn't result in increased performance' because 'star schemas are typically optimized schemas for analytics.' Migration overview: BigQuery 'supports both star and snowflake schemas, but its native schema representation is neither'; nested/repeated is 'an excellent evolutionary choice'; 'transfer the schema without any changes during initial iterations'; 'consider creating partitioned tables even if your schema is not modified'; cluster on frequently filtered columns.
practical_examples: Transaction record with an ARRAY of line-item STRUCTs; dot-syntax queries over STRUCT; UNNEST to flatten arrays; recommended AVRO/ORC/Parquet transfer formats.
why_it_matters: Documents the one official conflict with star-schema primacy: Google offers nested/repeated denormalization as a native alternative while conceding star schemas remain optimized, so a schema framework must treat nested fields as a hierarchical-case tool rather than a universal replacement.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud BigQuery documentation.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/migration/schema-data-overview. Neither page exposed a date. The commonly cited '10 GB dimension table' threshold was NOT present on either fetched page (it appears only in the partitioned-tables page as a clustering-vs-partitioning rule, see CLOUD-13). Labels: RECOMMENDED with explicit exception (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL for existing star schemas).

title: Introduction to partitioned tables - BigQuery
core_concepts: integer-range, time-unit column, and ingestion-time partitioning; partition pruning and cost estimation; partitioning vs clustering decision; partitions under ~10 GB favor clustering; single partitioning column, top-level non-repeated; partitioned tables over date-sharded tables; granularity selection (hourly/daily/monthly/yearly)
engineering_principles: Partition to scan only part of a table, estimate cost before running (dry run), and use partition-level features (expiration, per-partition load/delete). 'BigQuery does not support partitioning by multiple columns'; the column must be top-level and not REPEATED; existing tables cannot be converted in place. Prefer clustering when you need more granularity, filter on several columns, have high cardinality, do not need strict cost estimates, when partitions would hold roughly under 10 GB each, when too many partitions would result, or when most partitions change every few minutes; partitioning and clustering can be combined. 'Partitioned tables perform better' than date-sharded tables. Hourly partitioning only for high-volume data over short ranges (typically under six months); monthly/yearly for small daily volumes over wide ranges or when updates touch many dates (e.g., >500), adding clustering on the partition column.
practical_examples: customer_id integer-range partitions with interval 10 (out-of-range rows go to __UNPARTITIONED__, NULLs to __NULL__); _PARTITIONTIME / _PARTITIONDATE pseudocolumns; partition boundaries in UTC.
why_it_matters: BigQuery's equivalent of Redshift sort/distribution keys and Synapse partitions: physical schema choices that determine bytes scanned and therefore cost, with explicit small-partition anti-guidance shared by Fabric (Liquid Clustering) and Synapse (too many partitions slow queries).
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud BigQuery documentation.
notes: Fetched at docs.cloud.google.com after 301. The page did not state a numeric partition-count limit (links to quotas). Labels: RECOMMENDED; single-column/top-level constraints are hard limits (MANDATORY). | Also catalogued as PERF-50 in catalog_11_performance.json

title: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL best practices
core_concepts: SLA-conditioned operational guidelines; many smaller instances over one large instance; shard when CPU/memory maxed; table count under 10,000; memory under 90%; standard VACUUM over VACUUM FULL; autovacuum tuning; connection pooling and exponential backoff; short transactions; backups vs PITR vs exports; Private IP, pgAudit
engineering_principles: 'Read and follow the operational guidelines to ensure that your instances are covered by the Cloud SQL SLA.' 'When possible, using many smaller Cloud SQL instances is better than one large instance.' If an instance is at maximum CPU or memory, 'you must shard your database across multiple instances.' 'Keep your instance's table count to fewer than 10,000.' Keep memory usage under 90%; keep 20% free disk and alert at 80%; use connection pooling with exponential backoff; keep transactions small and short; prefer standard VACUUM that runs alongside production; tune autovacuum and monitor transaction-ID consumption. Backups cannot restore a single database/table and die with the instance; 'A point-in-time recovery always creates a new instance'; exports survive deletion and can target one table. Security: prefer Private IP, avoid 0.0.0.0/0, use pgAudit, set search_path to pg_catalog for privileged users.
practical_examples: 80% disk-utilization alert; sizing storage for transaction-log retention; testing application behavior during failover and maintenance windows; read replicas to offload reads.
why_it_matters: Mirrors AWS RDS almost exactly (10,000-table ceiling, autovacuum, shard-at-ceiling) and therefore establishes a cross-vendor consensus on relational OLTP scale boundaries that schema designs must stay within.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud SQL product documentation.
notes: Fetched at docs.cloud.google.com after 301; no date exposed. Labels: SLA guidelines MANDATORY; 'must shard' at ceiling MANDATORY (source wording); table count, instance splitting, pooling RECOMMENDED.

title: Lakehouse: Key concepts (Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse; with 'Architecture and functions in a data mesh')
core_concepts: borderless Lakehouse (storage decoupled from compute, open formats on Cloud Storage); Lakehouse runtime catalog as single source of truth for metadata; Iceberg tables (open-engine vs BigQuery-managed), native BigQuery tables, external tables; medallion bronze/silver/gold; BigQuery often serves the gold layer; data mesh: data as a product, domains, self-service platform, central governance
engineering_principles: 'A borderless Lakehouse architecture lets you unify data analytics across distributed environments and open-format storage systems on Google Cloud'; it 'decouples storage from compute'; the runtime catalog is 'a centralized, serverless metadata service that acts as the single source of truth.' Medallion is 'A common design pattern in a data lakehouse': bronze ingests raw data 'typically in open formats, such as Apache Iceberg on Cloud Storage', silver cleanses/standardizes, gold delivers curated aggregated tables; 'BigQuery is often used to serve the gold layer.' Table types: open-engine Iceberg tables (BigQuery read; write in Preview), BigQuery Iceberg tables ('only BigQuery can write to them directly'), native BigQuery tables, external tables ('BigQuery can only read them'). Data mesh: 'an architectural and organizational framework which treats data as a product'; products exposed as tables, views, files, topics or streams; embed governance in every step; fund the platform as a product; plan coexistence with existing lakes/warehouses.
practical_examples: Four-part table naming Project.Catalog.Namespace.Table and multi-bucket catalog storage (recommended) per search summary; BigQuery authorized views as data-product interfaces in the data-mesh reference.
why_it_matters: Supplies Google's official lake/lakehouse vocabulary and confirms the cross-vendor medallion pattern with an open ACID table format (Iceberg here, Delta in Fabric), positioning the warehouse (BigQuery) as the gold serving layer rather than the primary store.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud documentation.
notes: Also fetched: https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/data-mesh (no lake/warehouse/lakehouse distinctions on that page). WebSearch summary (unfetched page https://docs.cloud.google.com/lakehouse/docs/lakehouse-basics) says BigLake was renamed effective April 20, 2026 and the metastore became the 'Lakehouse runtime catalog'; APIs/CLI/IAM still use the BigLake name. Labels: medallion and BigQuery-for-gold OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL ('common', 'often used'); multi-bucket catalog RECOMMENDED.

title: Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) - Azure Architecture Center (with 'Online Analytical Processing' companion page)
organization_author: Microsoft (Azure Architecture Center, Data Architecture Guide)
core_concepts: OLTP definition and transactional data; atomicity/consistency (ACID), pessimistic locking; OLTP trait table: highly normalized, schema-on-write, strong consistency, heavy writes, MBs to a few TBs; offload history to data mart/warehouse; HTAP; OLAP definition and trait table: star/snowflake/cube, read-only, hundreds of GB to PBs; semantic models (tabular, multidimensional); MPP OLAP in Microsoft Fabric
engineering_principles: OLTP 'record[s] business interactions as they occur'; transactions must be atomic and consistent; traits: 'Highly normalized', 'Schema on write, enforced', 'Strong consistency, ACID guarantees', 'Heavy writes, moderate reads', 'Small (MBs) to large (a few TBs)'. Normalization 'breaks up the data into smaller, less redundant chunks' enabling independent transaction processing. Challenges: aggregate analytics are 'very resource-intensive for an OLTP system'; highly normalized data makes reporting queries complex; keep a relevant time window in OLTP and offload history to a data mart or warehouse. OLAP 'organizes large business databases to perform complex calculations and trend analysis... without disrupting transactional systems'; 'optimized for heavy-read and low-write tasks'; traits: 'Schema on write, strongly enforced', 'Uses transactions: No', 'Updateable: No, typically requires recomputing cube', 'Data shape: Cube, star, or snowflake schema', 'Scale: Large, hundreds of gigabytes (GBs) to multiple petabytes (PBs)'; 'OLAP systems typically use a star or snowflake schema instead of traditional normalization.' HTAP via updateable nonclustered columnstore indexes 'eliminates the need for multiple copies of your data and separate OLTP and OLAP systems.'
practical_examples: Azure OLTP stores: SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on VM, Azure Database for MySQL/PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB; selection questions include multitenancy (elastic pools, Cosmos DB isolation models), ACID for nonrelational data (Cosmos DB transactional batch within a logical partition), row-level security, distributed/elastic transactions. OLAP stores: Fabric, SQL Server/SQL Database with columnstore indexes, Analysis Services; capability matrix (MPP only in Fabric).
why_it_matters: The only vendor-published side-by-side trait tables for OLTP and OLAP; they anchor the definitional section of a schema-design framework (normalized schema-on-write vs star/snowflake read-only) and name HTAP as the exception.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure Architecture Center pages with named principal authors and ms.date/updated_at metadata.
notes: OLTP page: ms.date 2026-02-06, updated_at 2026-08-28, authors Charles Allard and Amber Sitko. Also fetched OLAP page: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/data-guide/relational-data/online-analytical-processing (ms.date 2025-04-11, updated_at 2026-08-28, author amattas). The data-guide root and old data-warehousing URL redirect to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/databases/database-get-started (ms.date 2026-03-05, updated 2026-10-23). Labels: offload history RECOMMENDED; HTAP OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.

title: Understand Data Models - Azure Architecture Center (with 'Big Data Architectures')
core_concepts: polyglot persistence; store models: relational (OLTP), document, column-family, key-value, graph, time series, object, search, vector, analytics/OLAP/MPP; five-step model-selection method; heuristics table and re-evaluation signals; anti-patterns (shared DB across microservices, search index as primary store); data lake vs data warehouse vs lakehouse; lambda vs kappa architectures; Kimball-style analytical store
engineering_principles: 'A single data store rarely satisfies all access patterns efficiently. Most production systems adopt polyglot persistence.' Method: identify access patterns, map to models, shortlist services, apply criteria (consistency, latency, scale, governance, cost), 'Combine models only where access patterns or life cycles clearly diverge.' Relational stores 'organize data into normalized tables by using schema-on-write'; 'Horizontal scale generally requires sharding or partitioning, and normalization can increase join cost.' Heuristics: strict multi-entity transactions -> relational; evolving JSON aggregates -> document; low-latency key lookups -> key-value; wide sparse telemetry -> column family/time series; deep traversal -> graph; massive historical scans -> analytics/OLAP. Avoid premature fragmentation and the listed anti-patterns. Big data guide: data lake stores raw data in original format without predefined schema; data warehouse stores structured/semi-structured data for BI; lakehouse 'combines the best elements of data lakes and data warehouses' using open formats (Parquet, ORC); lambda = immutable batch layer + low-latency speed layer; kappa = single stream path with replay.
practical_examples: Comparative trait tables for document/column-family/key-value/graph (normalization, schema approach, atomicity scope, locking) and for time series/object/search; Azure service tables per model (SQL Database, Cosmos DB for NoSQL, Managed Cassandra, Managed Redis, Data Explorer/Eventhouse, Data Lake Storage, AI Search, Fabric); re-evaluation signals such as 'Increasing ad-hoc joins on a document store -> Introduce relational read model'.
why_it_matters: Azure's canonical model-selection guide and definitional source for lake/warehouse/lakehouse; its normalized-vs-denormalized per-model table is directly usable in a schema-design framework.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure Architecture Center guidance with ms.date/updated_at metadata.

title: Architectural Approaches for Storage and Data in Multitenant Solutions - Azure Architecture Center
organization_author: Microsoft (Azure Architecture Center, Azure Patterns & Practices; principal author John Downs)
core_concepts: key considerations: scale, performance predictability (noisy neighbor), data isolation, complexity, operations, cost; patterns: deployment stamps, shared multitenant database, sharding, dedicated database per tenant, geode; relational anti-patterns: table-based isolation, column-level tenant customization, manual schema changes, version dependencies; row-level security trade-offs; tenant-level encryption (Always Encrypted, CMK); resource pooling (elastic pools, Cosmos DB database throughput); schema version tracking per tenant
engineering_principles: 'There's no single solution that works for every scenario.' Isolate or group tenants when they need their own encryption keys, individual backup/restore policies or different geographies. 'the higher the density of tenants... the lower the cost... However, shared infrastructure increases the likelihood of problems like the noisy neighbor problem.' Create deployment stamps even when using multitenant or sharded databases. Shared database: highest density/lowest cost but scale limits, noisy neighbors, metering difficulty and 'tenant-level schema customization is difficult.' Sharding scales to large tenant counts but complicates per-tenant config and customer-managed keys. Database per tenant: 'It's important to use automated deployment approaches.' Anti-patterns: avoid per-tenant tables ('use a single set of multitenant tables with a tenant identifier column' or separate databases); avoid per-tenant columns (use a dedicated custom-data table); avoid manual schema changes (automate and 'Track the schema version that you use for each tenant'); avoid app dependence on one schema version ('backwards-compatible with at least one previous schema version, and sequence destructive schema changes across multiple versions'). RLS requires propagating tenant identity on every query; 'Many multitenant solutions don't use row-level security because of those complexities.'
practical_examples: Cosmos DB: separate containers, databases or accounts per tenant; database-level throughput sharing not suitable when per-container guarantees are required; Azure SQL: separate tables in shared DBs, or separate databases/servers; blob path or container-per-tenant isolation with Valet Key pattern; restoring one tenant from a shared database requires restoring to a separate resource and selectively recovering data.
why_it_matters: The most concrete official guidance on how multitenancy shapes relational schema (tenant-ID column, no per-tenant tables/columns, schema versioning) and on the isolation/cost trade-off; maps one-to-one onto AWS silo/pool/bridge.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, authored by Azure Patterns & Practices; current (updated 2026-11-07).
notes: ms.date 2026-08-21; updated_at 2026-11-07. Labels: anti-patterns RECOMMENDED (avoid); automation for DB-per-tenant RECOMMENDED; pattern choice OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL. Conflict noted vs retired AWS storage whitepaper's bridge-as-per-tenant-tables definition (CLOUD-04). | Also catalogued as SEC-34 in catalog_09_security_privacy.json | Also catalogued as TEN-04 in catalog_14_tenancy_audit_temporal.json

title: Multitenant SaaS Patterns - Azure SQL Database (tenancy models) with Architecture Best Practices for Azure SQL Database (Well-Architected service guide)
organization_author: Microsoft (Azure SQL Database documentation; Azure Well-Architected Framework)
core_concepts: tenancy model = how tenant data maps to storage; standalone single-tenant app + database; database-per-tenant with elastic pools; single multitenant database; sharded multitenant databases with catalog/shard map; hybrid sharded model; tenant identifier as leading PK element; row-level security; WAF pillars for Azure SQL: Business Critical/Hyperscale, zone redundancy, failover groups, backup immutability, Always Encrypted, ledger tables, Entra-only auth, elastic pools, automatic tuning
engineering_principles: 'A tenancy model determines how each tenant's data is mapped to storage... Switching to a different model later is sometimes costly.' Standalone: greatest isolation, most expensive (no pools across resource groups). Database-per-tenant: strong isolation, per-tenant schema customization is 'straightforward', elastic pools are 'cheaper than requiring each database to be large enough to accommodate the usage peaks', management scales to 'well over 100,000 databases'. Multitenant database 'necessarily sacrifices tenant isolation'; schema 'must have one or more tenant identifier columns'; RLS can scope queries to one tenant; no built-in per-tenant resource monitoring (noisy-neighbor risk). Sharded multitenant: 'all the data for any one tenant is contained in one shard'; a catalog maps tenants to databases; the split/merge tool 'requires that the schema includes the sharding key'; 'The tenant identifier is the leading element in the primary key of all sharded tables.' Hybrid: every database carries the tenant ID so tenants can move between shared and dedicated databases. WAF guide: Business Critical for highest reliability, Hyperscale for strict RTO/RPO via storage snapshots, zone redundancy, failover groups, PITR plus backup immutability, retry/backoff, isolated connection pools, sharding for fault isolation; TLS 1.2+, Always Encrypted (+ secure enclaves), ledger tables, Private Link, Entra-only authentication; elastic pools, serverless, Hyperscale and reserved capacity for cost; vCore model, read-scale-out replicas, automatic tuning and query store for performance.
practical_examples: Comparison table: scale Medium (1-100s) / High (1-100,000s) / Unlimited (1-1,000,000s); isolation High / High / Low; cost per tenant High (sized for peaks) / Low (pools) / Lowest; development complexity Low / Low / Medium. Example of 1,000 tenant databases x 20 indexes = 20,000 indexes managed by automatic indexing; free-trial tenants pooled in a shared DB and Premium tenants moved to dedicated DBs.
why_it_matters: Specifies the schema consequences of each tenancy model for a relational OLTP store (tenant-ID column, tenant-ID-leading primary keys for sharding) and pairs them with pillar-level reliability/security/cost controls for the same engine.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure SQL documentation and Well-Architected service guide, both with ms.date/updated_at metadata.
notes: Tenancy page: ms.date 2025-08-21, updated_at 2026-08-27, author William Assaf. Also fetched: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/service-guides/azure-sql-database (ms.date 2026-08-19, updated_at 2026-10-16). Labels: tenant-ID-leading PK MANDATORY when using the split/merge tool; tenancy-model choice OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL; WAF items RECOMMENDED. | Also catalogued as TEN-03 in catalog_14_tenancy_audit_temporal.json

title: Partitioning and horizontal scaling - Azure Cosmos DB (with 'Data Modeling - Azure Cosmos DB')
organization_author: Microsoft (Azure Cosmos DB documentation; author Mark Brown)
core_concepts: logical vs physical partitions; partition key immutability; 20 GB per logical partition; 10,000 RU/s and 50 GB per physical partition; high cardinality and even RU/storage distribution; partition key anti-patterns (/id for general workloads, low-cardinality fields, non-query-aligned high-cardinality keys); synthetic and hierarchical partition keys; global secondary indexes; embed vs reference (denormalize vs normalize); unbounded arrays anti-pattern; weak references (no foreign keys); multi-document transactions within a logical partition; item type discriminator in shared containers; flatten for Fabric mirroring (1,000-column limit)
engineering_principles: 'Once you select your partition key, you can't change it in place.' For all containers the key should be immutable, string-typed, high-cardinality, spread RU consumption and storage evenly, and be at most 2048 bytes; 'Hot partitions cause inefficient use of provisioned throughput, which can result in rate limiting and higher costs.' Read-heavy containers over 30,000 RU/s or 100 GB need a key that minimizes cross-partition queries (2-3 RU overhead per physical partition). Modeling: 'treat your entities as self-contained items'; embed for contained, one-to-few, infrequently changing, bounded, read-together data ('denormalized data models provide better read performance'); reference for one-to-many, many-to-many, frequently changing or unbounded data ('normalizing provides better write performance'); no foreign-key enforcement; precomputed aggregates are safe because Cosmos DB supports multi-document transactions in a logical partition; add a type field when mixing item types in one container; for Fabric mirroring prefer flat models and avoid excessive nesting; 'you must find the right balance for your transactional and analytical workloads.'
practical_examples: Partition-strategy table (regular key CustomerId, synthetic CustomerId+OrderDate, hierarchical CustomerId/OrderId, GSI on OrderId) with pros/cons; blog post with unbounded comments array split into post + comment items partitioned by postId; stock portfolio referencing stock documents instead of embedding volatile prices; author/book many-to-many via reference arrays; Change Feed used to normalize a 1,000+-property container into Customers/Orders/Items for analytics.
why_it_matters: Cosmos DB's rules (immutable high-cardinality partition key, embed-vs-reference by boundedness and volatility, hot-partition cost) are the Azure counterpart of DynamoDB's access-pattern-first and locality principles, establishing a cross-vendor NoSQL schema consensus.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB documentation with ms.date/updated_at metadata.
notes: Fetched URL resolves to canonical https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning (ms.date 2026-02-02, updated_at 2026-10-05). Also fetched: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/modeling-data (canonical /azure/cosmos-db/modeling-data; ms.date 2026-07-31). Labels: partition limits MANDATORY (product limits); key-selection 'should' list and embed/reference rules RECOMMENDED; Fabric flattening OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.

title: Implement Medallion Lakehouse Architecture in Fabric (with 'Dimensional Modeling - Microsoft Fabric' and 'Designing tables - Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool')
organization_author: Microsoft (Microsoft Fabric documentation; Azure Synapse Analytics documentation)
core_concepts: medallion architecture (bronze raw, silver enriched, gold curated) as the recommended Fabric design; OneLake as the single logical data lake; Delta Lake as default ACID storage format; deployment patterns (all lakehouses vs lakehouse + warehouse gold); one workspace per layer; file sizes 128 MB-1 GB; V-order; VACUUM retention; Liquid Clustering over partitioning for silver/gold; materialized lake views; data mesh domains; star schema as recommended Fabric Warehouse design (Kimball); Synapse distribution: hash for facts, replicated for small dimensions, round-robin for staging; clustered columnstore default; unenforced PK/unique; no FKs
engineering_principles: Medallion 'is the recommended design approach for Fabric'; bronze: 'Store everything exactly as it arrives. No changes are allowed'; silver: fix errors, standardize, deduplicate; gold: organize for reports. 'The silver and gold layers should contain Delta tables'; 'Fabric standardizes storage file format with Delta Lake'; 'we recommend that you create each lakehouse in its own, separate workspace'; target file sizes 'between 128 MB and 1 GB'; 'In the bronze layer, partitioning is acceptable but discouraged for new implementations. For silver and gold layers, use Liquid Clustering instead of partitioning'; limit Delta history retention to control cost (seven-day default minimum); plan and control access per layer. Fabric Warehouse: star schema 'is a recommended design approach'; 'considered a prerequisite for enterprise Power BI semantic models'; fewer joins and more useful indexes; build the warehouse iteratively; capture slowly changing dimensions via ETL when history matters. Synapse dedicated SQL pool: fact tables hash-distributed with clustered columnstore (joins on the same distribution column avoid data movement), small dimensions replicated, staging round-robin; 'too many partitions can slow query performance'; PRIMARY KEY only NONCLUSTERED NOT ENFORCED, UNIQUE only NOT ENFORCED, foreign keys unsupported, surrogate keys via IDENTITY.
practical_examples: E-commerce example: bronze raw JSON sales, CSV inventory, CRM SQL export; silver standardizes dates/currency, removes test transactions, matches customers; gold builds daily sales, customer lifetime value and inventory forecast tables. Shortcuts instead of copying from ADLS Gen2/S3/Google into bronze; MERGE with partition filters; WideWorldImportersDW wwi.DimCity / wwi.FactOrder naming; CTAS loads into round-robin staging then INSERT...SELECT into production.
why_it_matters: Microsoft's current lakehouse + warehouse schema doctrine: raw immutable bronze, Delta ACID tables, star schema for the serving warehouse, and MPP distribution/columnstore rules that parallel Redshift; also documents a vendor conflict in partitioning posture (discouraged in Fabric lakehouse vs encouraged in BigQuery).
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse documentation with ms.date/updated_at metadata.
notes: Medallion page: ms.date 2026-02-12, updated_at 2026-08-26. Also fetched: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/data-warehouse/dimensional-modeling-overview (ms.date 2025-04-06, updated_at 2026-07-06) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/synapse-analytics/sql-data-warehouse/sql-data-warehouse-tables-overview (ms.date 2025-01-22, updated_at 2026-05-03; banner recommends Fabric Data Warehouse for new workloads). Labels: medallion, Delta, star schema, separate workspaces RECOMMENDED; Liquid Clustering over partitioning RECOMMENDED; Synapse constraint behavior is a hard product constraint (MANDATORY). Conflict vs BigQuery nested/repeated denormalization (CLOUD-12) noted.

title: Medallion lakehouse architecture
core_concepts: Medallion as a data design pattern denoting data quality layers (multi-hop architecture); Bronze: raw, unvalidated, append-only source of truth; store fields as string/VARIANT/binary; Silver: validated, deduplicated, schema-enforced, non-aggregated representation of each record; Gold: aggregated, business-aligned, query-optimized datasets, dimensional modeling; Recommended best practice but not a requirement; Streaming vs triggered vs batch ingestion cost/latency trade-offs
engineering_principles: Medallion is a layering/quality pattern, not a data model: 'a series of data layers that denote the quality of data stored in the lakehouse' and 'a data design pattern used to organize data logically'. Bronze keeps raw data for reprocessing and audit and is 'not for access by analysts and data scientists'; Databricks recommends storing most Bronze fields as string, VARIANT or binary to survive schema change (schema-on-read at ingestion). Silver applies schema enforcement, null handling, deduplication, late-data handling, type casting and joins, and 'Databricks does not recommend writing to silver tables directly from ingestion'. Gold is modeled 'using a dimensional model' with relationships and measures; large histories stay in Silver. Label: RECOMMENDED (not mandatory).
practical_examples: Three-level namespace example ops.bronze / ops.silver / ops.gold; spark.readStream from Bronze into Silver; Gold materialized view weekly_bookings pre-aggregating bookings and revenue; table of ingestion modes (continuous incremental = higher cost/lower latency; triggered incremental = lower cost/higher latency; batch = lowest cost/highest latency).
why_it_matters: Establishes that lakehouse 'layers' are orthogonal to schema design: a framework must choose a data model per layer (Databricks' own blogs put 3NF/Data Vault in Silver and star schemas in Gold). Also documents the deliberate deferral of schema-on-write from ingestion (Bronze) to Silver, which contradicts classic warehouse staging practice.
authority_rationale: Official vendor product documentation, dated, maintained by Databricks.
notes: Page never names Kimball, star schema or Data Vault. Model-to-layer mapping comes from the Databricks blog 'Data Warehousing Modeling Techniques...' (LAKE-05). Unity Catalog best practices (https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/best-practices, Oct 30, 2026, verified) adds: catalogs are 'the primary unit of data isolation', organize by division/project/environment, one metastore per region, managed tables recommended; it does not prescribe medallion layers as catalogs vs schemas. | Also catalogued as DWM-17 in catalog_06_warehouse_modeling.json

title: Constraints on Databricks
subcategory: Enforced vs informational constraints on Delta tables
core_concepts: NOT NULL and CHECK constraints are enforced; violating transaction fails; PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE are informational only (not enforced); Constraints require Delta Lake; PK/FK tied to Unity Catalog (GA DBR 15.2+), UNIQUE in Public Preview (DBR 18.2+); Existing rows verified when a constraint is added; CHECK expressions limited to deterministic Spark SQL functions; Adding constraints upgrades the table writer protocol
engineering_principles: 'Primary key, foreign key, and unique constraints are informational only and aren't enforced.' NOT NULL and CHECK: 'When a constraint is violated, the transaction fails with an error.' A foreign key must reference a PK or UNIQUE in another table; PK must be added before dependent FKs; CTAS does not accept constraint clauses; NOT NULL inside structs requires the parent struct NOT NULL and is not allowed inside arrays/maps; informational keys 'might improve performance through' query optimizations. Label: MANDATORY semantics (platform behaviour).
practical_examples: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE main.default.people_demo (id INT NOT NULL, ...); ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ssn SET NOT NULL; ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT dateWithinRange CHECK (birthDate > '1900-01-01'); CREATE TABLE T(pk1 INTEGER NOT NULL, pk2 INTEGER NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT t_pk PRIMARY KEY(pk1, pk2)); FOREIGN KEY(fk1, fk2) REFERENCES main.default.T; CONSTRAINT u_uq_email UNIQUE(email).
why_it_matters: Critical for any schema framework that assumes integrity enforcement: on Databricks only NOT NULL and CHECK will reject bad writes; uniqueness and referential integrity must be guaranteed by pipeline logic (MERGE keys, dedup, dbt tests). Keys remain valuable as metadata for BI tools and optimizer hints.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with explicit, dated enforcement semantics.
notes: The docs page does not mention the RELY keyword; the Databricks 2025 blog (LAKE-06) describes RELY as an optimizer hint. Corroborated by the 2022 blog 'Data Modeling Best Practices & Implementation on a Modern Lakehouse' (verified): 'Databricks does not support enforcement of the PK/FK relationship.'

title: Use liquid clustering for tables
subcategory: Liquid clustering vs partitioning vs Z-ORDER
core_concepts: Liquid clustering replaces table partitioning and ZORDER; Recommended for all new tables including streaming tables and materialized views; Clustering keys can be changed without rewriting data; up to four keys; Automatic liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY AUTO) chooses keys from query history; Hierarchical clustering for low-cardinality priority keys (DBR 17.1+); Incremental OPTIMIZE and predictive optimization maintenance
engineering_principles: 'Liquid clustering is a data layout optimization technique that replaces table partitioning and ZORDER'; 'Databricks recommends liquid clustering for all new tables'; 'Clustering is not compatible with partitioning or ZORDER'; 'Clustering columns are flexible and simple to alter, whereas partitioning is rigid and difficult to alter'. Use for high-cardinality filter columns, skewed data, fast-growing tables, concurrent writes, changing access patterns. Keys must have statistics (first 32 columns by default). Label: RECOMMENDED.
practical_examples: REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY for migration (DBR 18.1+); CLUSTER BY (cols) then CLUSTER BY AUTO for hints; OPTIMIZE ... FULL to recluster after key changes; clustering-on-write thresholds (e.g., 64 MB for one key on UC managed tables, 1 GB for four keys); run OPTIMIZE every 1-2 hours for frequently updated tables or rely on predictive optimization.
why_it_matters: Physical schema design on the lakehouse no longer fixes partition columns at CREATE time; a framework should model clustering keys as a mutable property driven by query patterns. Supersedes the 2022 Databricks blog advice to Z-ORDER on primary/foreign keys.
authority_rationale: Official, recently updated vendor documentation.
notes: CONFLICT (temporal): Databricks blog 'Data Modeling Best Practices & Implementation on a Modern Lakehouse' (Oct 20, 2022, verified) says partition 'sparingly' and 'Use Z-order on your Primary Keys and foreign keys'; the 2026 docs state liquid clustering replaces and is incompatible with ZORDER. Treat Z-order guidance as legacy.

title: Row filters and column masks (Unity Catalog)
subcategory: Row-level security and column masking in Unity Catalog
core_concepts: Row filter = SQL UDF returning BOOLEAN evaluated per row at query time; Column mask = SQL UDF returning original or masked value; one mask per column; ABAC (tag-based) policies at catalog/schema level recommended for scale; Policies cannot be applied to views; dynamic views are the alternative; Type mismatch between column and UDF parameter can silently return wrong rows unless ANSI mode is on; Limitations: no time travel, no clones, no path-based access on policy-protected tables
engineering_principles: Row filters and column masks 'restrict the rows and column values a user can see at query time'; 'Rows where the function returns FALSE are excluded from query results'; 'Each column can have one mask'; 'You cannot apply row filters or column masks to a view'. Databricks recommends ABAC policies attached by governed tags (table owners cannot override) and ANSI mode so failed casts raise errors. Performance guidance: simple CASE-based UDFs, few arguments, SQL over Python UDFs. Label: RECOMMENDED (ABAC, ANSI); MANDATORY (limitations).
practical_examples: ALTER TABLE employees SET ROW FILTER salary_filter ON (department); ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK; worked bug where CREATE FUNCTION salary_filter(dept INT) on a STRING column with ANSI off casts to NULL and returns all four rows, fixed by declaring dept STRING.
why_it_matters: Governance policies are schema-coupled: the data types of filtered/masked columns must exactly match policy signatures, and protected tables lose time travel and cloning. Schema designers must plan policy columns (region, tenant, department) and types deliberately.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation, updated Nov 6, 2026.
notes: Related verified pages: 'What is Unity Catalog?' (https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/, Sep 11, 2026) — three-level namespace catalog.schema.object, automatic lineage, audit log system table, managed vs external tables; 'Unity Catalog best practices' (Oct 30, 2026) — privileges 'are inherited downward', lineage does not cross region boundaries.

title: Data Warehousing Modeling Techniques and Their Implementation on the Databricks Lakehouse Platform
organization_author: Databricks blog — Soham Bhatt and Deepak Sekar
subcategory: Mapping Kimball / Inmon 3NF / Data Vault onto medallion layers
core_concepts: Bronze = source structures as-is plus metadata (CDC, audit, reprocessing); Silver = matched/merged/conformed data in 3NF-like or Data Vault models; Gold = denormalized, read-optimized Kimball star schemas or Inmon-style marts; Star schema described as the gold standard for the presentation layer; Lakehouse supports many modeling styles; DV and dimensional both have a place; Fully denormalized Gold tables acceptable for data-science feature engineering
engineering_principles: Data Vault 'typically fits well in the Silver layer'; Silver 'has more 3rd-Normal Form like data models' loaded with 'just-enough' ELT; Gold holds Kimball star schemas, 'pretty much the gold standard for the presentation layer', or Inmon-style marts; the lakehouse 'can support many different data modeling styles'. Label: RECOMMENDED (vendor guidance, not enforced).
practical_examples: Auto Loader converting landed files to Delta in staging; Delta recommended for Bronze so CDC updates can be written; Unity Catalog for discovery/governance/lineage; DV hubs/satellites feeding dimensions and links feeding facts in Gold.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest official statement that medallion layers are populated by classic data models rather than replacing them — a direct bridge between lakehouse architecture and Kimball/Inmon/Data Vault schema design.
authority_rationale: Official vendor engineering blog by Databricks solution architects; prescriptive but not product documentation.
notes: Companion verified Databricks blogs: 'Prescriptive Guidance for Implementing a Data Vault Model on the Databricks Lakehouse Platform' (Jun 24, 2022; hubs/links/satellites, raw vs business vault, PIT/bridge tables, hash-of-business-key PKs, Z-order join keys, smaller optimize.maxFileSize); 'Data Modeling Best Practices & Implementation on a Modern Lakehouse' (Oct 20, 2022; IDENTITY surrogate keys, informational PK/FK, NOT NULL/CHECK, partition sparingly); 'Loading a Data Warehouse Data Model in Real Time with the Databricks Lakehouse' (Nov 7, 2022; SCD Type 2 via APPLY CHANGES INTO, CHECK constraint valid_product_id, conformed dimensions). CONFLICT: DV blog recommends hash keys while Snowflake performance guidance (LAKE-14) prefers numeric surrogate keys. | Also catalogued as DWM-18 in catalog_06_warehouse_modeling.json

title: Databricks Lakehouse Data Modeling: Myths, Truths, and Best Practices
organization_author: Databricks blog — Shannon Barrow and Kyle Hale
subcategory: Dimensional modeling, constraints, medallion as guideline
core_concepts: Relational principles (ACID, schema enforcement, SQL) are fundamental to the lakehouse; PK/FK supported since DBR 11.3, GA 15.2; informational, with RELY optimizer hint; CHECK and NOT NULL for column-level data quality; DQX and Lakehouse Monitoring for more; Star and snowflake schemas translate exceptionally well to Delta tables; SCDs implementable with Delta time travel; identity columns for surrogate keys; Medallion is a guideline, not a rigid requirement; multi-statement transactions in preview
engineering_principles: Eight myths rebutted: relational modeling is supported ('Relational principles are fundamental to the Lakehouse'); PK/FK exist 'for query performance, but are not enforced'; column-level quality via CHECK/NOT NULL; semantic modeling via Unity Catalog Metric Views; dimensional models belong on Databricks; no separate BI engine needed (Photon, DBSQL); 'Medallion is a guideline, not a rigid requirement'; multi-statement transactions (Private Preview) add multi-table atomicity. Best practices: define keys now, liquid clustering on frequently joined columns, catalog.schema.table organization, materialized views for pre-aggregated facts. Label: RECOMMENDED.
