practical_examples: Organizing dimensional models with the Unity Catalog three-level namespace; applying (automatic) liquid clustering to join columns; identity columns as surrogate keys; materialized views for aggregated fact tables.
why_it_matters: Most recent official Databricks position on schema design: it explicitly endorses Kimball-style star/snowflake schemas and keys-as-metadata, and explicitly denies that medallion is a mandatory or model-defining structure.
authority_rationale: Official vendor blog, recent (Dec 2025), authored by Databricks staff; marketing framing, no benchmarks.
notes: Does not mention 'one big table' or 'denormalize everything'. Metric Views and multi-statement transactions were preview features at publication; current status not verified.

title: Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics
organization_author: Michael Armbrust, Ali Ghodsi, Reynold Xin, Matei Zaharia (Databricks, UC Berkeley, Stanford) — CIDR 2021
subcategory: Foundational research paper defining the Lakehouse
core_concepts: Lakehouse = low-cost, directly accessible storage plus ACID, versioning, auditing, indexing, caching, query optimization; Four problems of two-tier lake+warehouse: reliability, staleness, limited advanced analytics, TCO; Transactional metadata layer (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) over open formats; Metadata layer as natural home for schema enforcement, constraints, access control, audit; Data layout optimization (Z-order), caching, auxiliary statistics for SQL performance; Trade-off: direct access gives up some data independence
engineering_principles: 'We define a Lakehouse as a data management system based on low-cost and directly-accessible storage that also provides traditional analytical DBMS management and performance features such as ACID transactions, data versioning, auditing, indexing, caching, and query optimization.' Two-tier architectures mean 'data may be stored with different schemas in the lake and the warehouse (e.g., denormalized in one)' and data 'is first ETLed into lakes, and then again ELTed into warehouses'. Metadata layers 'are a natural place to implement data quality enforcement features' (Delta schema enforcement and constraints API) and governance. Caveat: lakehouses 'give up some aspects of data independence, which has been a cornerstone of relational DBMS design.'
practical_examples: Delta Lake rejecting or quarantining records that violate expectations (e.g., country limited to a list of values); TPC-DS results for a Parquet-based lakehouse vs cloud warehouses; Delta converting a Parquet directory into a table 'with zero copies' by adding a transaction log.
why_it_matters: Supplies the theoretical justification for applying warehouse-grade schema enforcement and constraints to open-format lake storage, and candidly notes the relational trade-off (loss of data independence) that a schema framework must account for.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed foundational paper at CIDR 2021 by the Delta Lake/Spark authors; official conference PDF.
notes: PDF fetched (707 KB) and text extracted locally with pdftotext; quotes taken from the extracted text. Paper does not discuss star/snowflake schema design beyond the denormalization remark. | Also catalogued as LIT-36 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores
organization_author: Michael Armbrust et al. (Databricks, CWI, UC Berkeley, Stanford) — PVLDB 13(12), 2020
subcategory: ACID transactions, schema enforcement/evolution, time travel on object stores
core_concepts: Object stores lack atomic multi-object updates and isolation; metadata operations are expensive; Write-ahead transaction log stored in the object store; Parquet data objects; optimistic concurrency; Serializable writes, snapshot-isolated reads; transactions scoped to a single table; Time travel (AS OF timestamp / VERSION AS OF), UPSERT/DELETE/MERGE, exactly-once streaming; Schema enforcement on write and transactional schema evolution; Z-ordering plus min/max statistics for data skipping; audit logging
engineering_principles: 'multi-object updates are not atomic, there is no isolation between queries'; Delta maintains 'information about which objects are part of a Delta table in an ACID manner, using a write-ahead log'; 'all transactions that perform writes are serializable' while reads 'achieve snapshot isolation'; 'Delta Lake currently only supports transactions within one table'; write rate limited 'to several transactions per second' (not OLTP). 'Delta clients ensure that newly written data follows the table's schema. These simple checks have caught many user errors appending data with the wrong schema'. MERGE/DELETE support GDPR deletes and late/erroneous records.
practical_examples: MERGE INTO mytable target USING mytable TIMESTAMP AS OF <old_date> source ON source.userId = target.userId WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * to undo a bad overwrite; schema changes performed transactionally with older Parquet objects reused for column additions; BI workloads run directly on Delta tables (Tableau) without a separate warehouse load.
why_it_matters: Explains why ACID, schema-on-write enforcement, SCD-style updates and time travel are feasible on a data lake — the preconditions for applying warehouse schema design to the lakehouse — while stating limits (single-table transactions, low write TPS) that rule Delta out as an OLTP store.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed VLDB 2020 paper by the system's authors; official PVLDB PDF (DOI 10.14778/3415478.3415560).
notes: PDF fetched (418 KB) and text extracted locally. Current operational detail verified in Databricks docs: 'Update Delta Lake table schema' (Sep 11, 2026) — schema evolution must be enabled per write (INSERT/MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION, mergeSchema), session-wide autoMerge 'not recommended for production', new columns appended at end, 'Schema updates conflict with all concurrent write operations'; 'Work with Delta Lake table history' (Nov 6, 2026) — logRetentionDuration 30 days, deletedFileRetentionDuration 7 days, 'Don't use table history as a long-term backup solution'; delta.io batch docs (n.d.) — extra DataFrame columns or type mismatch raise an exception, column names case-insensitive. | Also catalogued as LIT-35 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: Constraints overview (Snowflake)
subcategory: Enforced vs not-enforced constraints; hybrid tables; RELY
core_concepts: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY not enforced on standard tables; NOT NULL and CHECK constraints are enforced; CHECK supported on standard, hybrid and Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables; Hybrid tables: PRIMARY KEY required and enforced; FK/UNIQUE/NOT NULL/CHECK enforced; RELY property enables join elimination; set only if data is known to comply; Unenforced constraints retained for DDL migration, BI tool discovery and documentation
engineering_principles: Verbatim: 'Snowflake doesn't enforce PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, and FOREIGN KEY constraints on standard tables.' 'NOT NULL and CHECK constraints are enforced.' 'Standard tables, hybrid tables, and Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables support CHECK constraints.' Rationale: 'Checking these constraints on very large, distributed, columnar tables would slow down data loading and DML operations.' 'Even though they aren't enforced, these constraints are still useful as metadata and documentation'. 'If you set the RELY property on a constraint, the optimizer can use it for join elimination' and 'Set RELY only if you've ensured that the data complies with the constraint.' Hybrid tables cannot set NOT ENFORCED on PK/FK/UNIQUE. Label: MANDATORY semantics; RELY OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: Migrating DDL with key definitions intact; BI and data-modeling tools reading PK/FK to infer relationships; RELY on PK/UNIQUE as prerequisite for join elimination; hybrid tables for transactional workloads needing enforced keys.
why_it_matters: Defines exactly which integrity rules a Snowflake analytical schema can rely on (NOT NULL, CHECK) versus which must be guaranteed by pipelines and tests (PK, UNIQUE, FK). Hybrid tables are the only OLTP-style exception.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation; key sentences re-verified verbatim in a second fetch.
notes: No last-updated date on page (© 2026 footer). CHECK support on standard tables differs from Snowflake's historical documentation; the date it was introduced was not found. Corroborated by Snowflake performance guide (LAKE-14): 'Snowflake supports foreign key constraints for SQL compatibility but does not enforce them.'

title: Clustering Keys & Clustered Tables (Snowflake)
subcategory: Micro-partitions, clustering keys, cardinality and cost guidance
core_concepts: Clustering key = designated columns/expressions that co-locate data in micro-partitions; Intended for multi-terabyte tables with many micro-partitions, not all tables; Max 3-4 columns per key; order from lowest to highest cardinality; use expressions to reduce cardinality; Prioritize selective filter columns, then join keys; Most cost-effective for tables queried frequently and updated infrequently; Automatic reclustering consumes credits and recreates micro-partitions
engineering_principles: 'a subset of columns in a table (or expressions on a table) that are explicitly designated to co-locate the data'; typically 'multiple terabytes (TB) of data'; 'Clustering keys are not intended for all tables due to the costs'; 'Snowflake recommends a maximum of 3 or 4 columns (or expressions) per key'; 'ordering the columns from lowest cardinality to highest cardinality'; very low cardinality (Boolean) yields minimal pruning and very high cardinality is 'not a good candidate... directly' (cast timestamp to date instead); 'clustering is generally most cost-effective for tables that are queried frequently and do not change frequently'; batch DML for clustered tables; test representative queries first. Label: RECOMMENDED / OPTIONAL-CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: Clustering a large fact table on a date expression plus a join key; monitoring with SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_DEPTH and SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION; grouping DML into large infrequent batches to limit reclustering cost.
why_it_matters: Replaces classic DW partitioning/indexing decisions: Snowflake schemas need no partitions or indexes, and a clustering key is an opt-in, cost-bearing optimization for very large tables. Directly informs which columns (and types) belong in fact tables.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Related verified Snowflake docs: 'Micro-partitions & Data Clustering' — 'Each micro-partition contains between 50 MB and 500 MB of uncompressed data', automatic on all tables, no user definition needed; 'Numeric data types' — default NUMBER(38,0), INT/BIGINT are synonyms, 'Precision ... doesn't affect storage' but scale does, FLOAT is 64-bit IEEE 754 (~15 digits), DECFLOAT for exact variable-scale; 'Semi-structured data types' — VARIANT max 128 MB uncompressed; 'Considerations for semi-structured data stored in VARIANT' — automatic columnar sub-column extraction, elements with a single JSON null or mixed types are not extracted, flatten dates/timestamps, numbers-in-strings and arrays into relational columns, default 200 extracted elements per partition. | Also catalogued as PERF-51 in catalog_11_performance.json

title: Understanding & using Time Travel (Snowflake)
core_concepts: Default retention 1 day for all accounts; Enterprise+ permanent objects 0-90 days; Transient/temporary objects limited to 0 or 1 day; AT | BEFORE (TIMESTAMP, OFFSET, STATEMENT) and UNDROP; Retention clock starts at each change; Time Travel cannot be deactivated account-wide; After retention, data moves to Fail-safe (7 days, Snowflake-only recovery); DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS and MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS
engineering_principles: 'The standard retention period is 1 day (24 hours) and is automatically enabled for all Snowflake accounts'; Enterprise permanent objects 'from 0 up to 90 days'; 'Time Travel cannot be deactivated for an account'; 'End of Time Travel = time of the change + data retention period'; afterwards 'the data is moved into Snowflake Fail-safe'. Fail-safe (separate page) 'provides a (non-configurable) 7-day period during which historical data may be recoverable by Snowflake' and 'is not provided as a means for accessing historical data after the Time Travel retention period has ended'. Label: MANDATORY platform behaviour; retention length OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: SELECT ... AT(OFFSET => -3600); CREATE TABLE ... CLONE ... BEFORE(STATEMENT => ...); UNDROP TABLE; setting DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS per table; using transient tables for staging to avoid Fail-safe storage.
why_it_matters: Determines whether a schema needs explicit history/SCD tables: Time Travel is a short recovery window (max 90 days) and Fail-safe is not user-accessible, so durable history must be modeled (SCD2, snapshots). Also drives the permanent vs transient table-type decision for staging schemas.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Fail-safe facts from the verified page https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-failsafe (n.d.). Zero-copy cloning verified at https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/object-clone (n.d.): clones 'share the same underlying storage as the source table', grants not copied without COPY GRANTS, clustering key kept but Automatic Clustering suspended, policies cannot be cloned individually, Time Travel cloning fails if any child object lacks retention. Parallel Databricks guidance: 'Don't use table history as a long-term backup solution for data archival.'

title: Decision guide for dynamic tables (Snowflake)
subcategory: Dynamic Tables vs Streams and Tasks vs Materialized Views
core_concepts: Dynamic tables recommended for new multi-table declarative SQL pipelines (joins, aggregations, bronze/silver/gold); Streams and tasks preferred for procedural logic, MERGE/complex upserts, external calls, CRON scheduling; Materialized views for single-table read acceleration with transparent query rewrite; Dynamic tables are read-only and represent current state, not history (no SCD Type 2); Minimum target lag 1 minute; definition changes trigger full reinitialization; SEQ/UUID_STRING/RANDOM unsupported in incremental refresh
engineering_principles: 'This is the recommended approach for new multi-table SQL pipelines in Snowflake'; 'Streams and tasks give you full control over the pipeline logic'; 'Use materialized views when your goal is read performance, not building a data pipeline'; 'Dynamic tables are read-only'; 'Dynamic tables represent the current state of the data, not a historical record'. A dynamic table 'replaces four objects and MERGE logic with a single SELECT definition'. Label: RECOMMENDED (dynamic tables for new pipelines); constraints MANDATORY.
practical_examples: Comparison table across scenarios (multi-step bronze/silver/gold pipeline, incremental processing, MERGE upserts, external function calls, always-current data); contrast of landing table + stream + MERGE task versus one dynamic table definition.
why_it_matters: Shapes how a Snowflake schema's derived layers are materialized: declarative dynamic tables for Silver/Gold transformations, but SCD2 history and complex MERGE logic still require streams + tasks (or an external tool like dbt snapshots). Shows medallion vocabulary adopted in Snowflake docs as a pipeline pattern.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Related verified pages: 'Dynamic tables' overview (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/dynamic-tables-about) — 'A dynamic table materializes the results of a SELECT query and keeps them up to date', TARGET_LAG and DOWNSTREAM, refresh modes INCREMENTAL/FULL/AUTO/ADAPTIVE/CUSTOM_INCREMENTAL, not for freshness under 60 seconds; 'Introduction to Streams' (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/streams-intro) — offset-based CDC with METADATA$ACTION, METADATA$ISUPDATE, METADATA$ROW_ID; standard/append-only/insert-only; 'Querying a stream alone does not advance its offset'; staleness tied to retention with MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS.

title: Design Patterns for Building Multi-Tenant Applications on Snowflake (white paper)
subcategory: MTT (multi-tenant table) vs OPT (object per tenant) vs APT (account per tenant)
core_concepts: MTT: shared tables stamped with tenant_id; scales to millions of tenants; requires same data shape; OPT: separate tables/schemas/databases/warehouses per tenant in one account; tens to hundreds of tenants; APT: one Snowflake account per tenant; tens to low hundreds; strongest isolation; requires OPT too; Hybrids common (e.g., MTT storage with dedicated compute); MTT security via entitlements table + secure views on CURRENT_ROLE/CURRENT_USER; Cluster transaction tables by tenant_id and date; numeric tenant_id
engineering_principles: 'MTT consolidates tenants within a shared table or warehouse'; 'OPT isolates tenants into separate tables, schemas, databases, and warehouses'; 'APT isolates tenants into separate Snowflake accounts'. MTT 'supports apps with millions of tenants' but 'an app's data model has to have the same general shape across all tenants'; OPT 'is a great fit if each tenant has a different data model' and 'typically scales well from tens to hundreds of tenants'; APT chosen for 'strong security reason' and 'can become unwieldy when managing thousands of tenant accounts'. 'Snowflake recommends starting with the MTT pattern.' Optimization: 'Tenants should have a unique numeric identifier (that is, a tenant_id)'; 'Cluster all transaction tables by tenant_id and a meaningful date field, at minimum.' 'Databases and schemas are largely logical constructs; they don't physically separate data.' Label: RECOMMENDED (start with MTT); pattern choice OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: Serving database with secure views joining base tables to an entitlements table on tenant_id; secure views by CURRENT_USER (one DB user per tenant) vs CURRENT_ROLE (fine-grained); schema separation of secure views from base/entitlement tables; automation for creating tenants in OPT/APT; flowcharts for storage/security and compute/security evaluation; Table 1/Table 2 comparing scalability, security burden and drawbacks (MTT: sharding, MERGE/auto-clustering challenges, per-tenant cost attribution; OPT/APT: object sprawl, lost compute pooling).
why_it_matters: Official Snowflake guidance on the schema-level multi-tenancy decision (tenant_id column + clustering + row-level security vs object/account isolation), including scale thresholds for each pattern — directly applicable to multi-tenant analytical schema design.
authority_rationale: Official vendor white paper, but undated in text (2021 per URL path and PDF metadata) and predating row access policies as the primary row-level-security mechanism.
notes: PDF (5.6 MB) fetched and text extracted locally; author names not printed. Modern row-level/column-level security verified in Snowflake docs (all n.d., Enterprise Edition): 'Understanding row access policies' — schema-level policy evaluated 'using the role of the policy owner', evaluated before masking policies, 'do not currently prevent rows from being inserted'; 'Understanding Dynamic Data Masking' — query-time column masking, 'write a policy once and have it apply to thousands of columns'; 'Tag-based masking policies' — policy set on a tag auto-protects matching columns including new ones, directly assigned policy takes precedence; 'Overview of Access Control' — DAC + RBAC, 'Unless allowed by a grant, access is denied', custom role hierarchy under SYSADMIN, no super-user role.

title: Performance guide (Snowflake Well Architected Framework)
organization_author: Snowflake Inc. — Well Architected Framework Team
subcategory: Star schema, Data Vault keys, denormalization, data types for joins
core_concepts: Star schema works well with Snowflake (right-deep join plans, join elimination on outer-joined dimensions); Numeric data types strongly recommended for equality-join key columns; Data Vault 2.0: prefer numeric surrogate keys over MD5 hash keys (clustering uses first five bytes of VARCHAR); No universal ideal degree of denormalization; test extensively; Very wide tables (hundreds of columns) increase compile time; avoid burying filter/join attributes in VARIANT; FK constraints not enforced; RELY on PK/UNIQUE is prerequisite for join elimination
engineering_principles: Star schema 'works well with Snowflake, favoring right-deep query execution plans'; cluster large fact tables on 'frequently used filters, join keys' plus a temporal attribute; 'Use of numerical data types for key columns involved in equality joins is strongly recommended for optimal performance'; for DV2 hash keys 'Snowflake only considers the first five bytes for clustering, ignoring the rest'; 'While a normalized schema ensures data integrity, it often necessitates multiple joins, adding computational overhead'; 'There's no universal guideline or ideal degree of denormalization; each data model and dataset is unique'; 'Avoid combining scalar attributes frequently used for filtering and joins into a single VARIANT or VARCHAR'; DATE and TIMESTAMP_NTZ perform well, TIMESTAMP_TZ/LTZ hurt pruning; collation 'never for join keys'; 'Snowflake supports foreign key constraints for SQL compatibility but does not enforce them'; 'The RELY property ... is a prerequisite for Snowflake's Join Elimination.' Label: RECOMMENDED; denormalization degree OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: Placing the largest fact table on the probe side of joins; keeping a non-timezone timestamp column for filtering and a separate timezone column for display; using INNER JOIN where referential integrity is pipeline-enforced so the optimizer can push equality filters; limited materializations with Dynamic Tables for slow multi-table DV joins.
why_it_matters: The most concrete official Snowflake statement on analytical schema design: it endorses star schemas with numeric surrogate keys, cautions against hash keys and over-wide tables, and refuses to prescribe a denormalization level — a direct, nuanced counterpoint to 'always denormalize/OBT' advice.
authority_rationale: Official Snowflake developer guide by the vendor's Well Architected team, but undated and only the first ~100k of ~158k characters were read.
notes: Supporting verified Snowflake sources: 'Overview of semantic views' (docs, n.d.) — 'We recommend starting with a simple star schema'; blog 'Support Multiple Data Modeling Approaches with Snowflake' (Graziano & Cuba, Apr 25, 2022, originally 2019) — 'Snowflake supports multiple data modeling approaches equally', no need to 'pre-plan partitioning or distribution keys, or build indexes'; blog 'Tips for Optimizing the Data Vault Architecture on Snowflake' (Graziano & Hoyle, Feb 3, 2020) — integer keys fastest, hash keys slower but 'very fast', may need a larger warehouse. CONFLICT: dbt style guide (LAKE-16) says 'Keys should be string data types'; Databricks DV blog recommends hash-of-business-key PKs.

title: How we structure our dbt projects (staging / intermediate / marts)
subcategory: Staging, intermediate and marts layers; materialization; denormalization stance
core_concepts: Arc from source-conformed to business-conformed data in modular layers; Staging: 1-to-1 with source tables, views, rename/cast/categorize only, no joins or aggregations, stg_[source]__[entity]s; Intermediate: int_[entity]s_[verb]s, ephemeral or hidden views, single purpose (re-grain, isolate complexity, combine 4-6 inputs); Marts: entity-grained, wide and denormalized, grouped by department, view -> table -> incremental ladder; 'Narrow the DAG, widen the tables'; multiple inputs but not multiple outputs; Denormalize heavily without the Semantic Layer; stay normalized with it
engineering_principles: 'a cohesive arc moving data from source-conformed to business-conformed'. Staging: 'our staging models should have a 1-to-1 relationship to our source tables'; 'joins are almost always a bad idea here'; materialized as views. Intermediate: 'should generally not be exposed in the main production schema'. Marts: 'Marts are entity-grained'; 'always start with a view... build it into a table, and finally... configure it as an incremental model'; 'Unlike in a traditional Kimball star schema though, in modern data warehousing — where storage is cheap and compute is expensive — we'll happily borrow and add any and all data from other concepts'; 'In a project without the Semantic Layer we recommend you denormalize heavily... if you're using the Semantic Layer, we want to stay as normalized as possible to allow MetricFlow the most flexibility.' Label: RECOMMENDED; denormalization OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
practical_examples: Jaffle Shop project tree (models/staging/stg_orders.sql, models/marts/orders.sql, __sources.yml); staging CTE pattern source -> renamed with id AS order_id and cents_to_dollars macro; int_orders_summed_to_customer; orders mart rolling up order_items; folder-per-source-system in staging and folder-per-department in marts.
why_it_matters: The de facto standard for transformation-layer schema organization in cloud warehouses; it codifies naming, grain, materialization and the 'wide marts' stance that departs from Kimball, while keeping dimensional outputs possible. Its Semantic Layer caveat shows denormalization is a tooling decision, not a universal rule.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a widely adopted tool vendor (dbt Labs); opinionated practice guidance rather than a standard.
notes: Layer pages verified separately: Staging (https://docs.getdbt.com/best-practices/how-we-structure/2-staging, Jul 7, 2026), Intermediate (https://docs.getdbt.com/best-practices/how-we-structure/3-intermediate, Aug 19, 2026), Marts (https://docs.getdbt.com/best-practices/how-we-structure/4-marts, Jul 7, 2026). ELT framing from dbt Labs blog 'ETL vs ELT: What's the difference?' (Daniel Poppy, Mar 15, 2023, https://getdbt.com/blog/etl-vs-elt, verified): 'With ETL, data is transformed before loading, while in ELT, data is transformed after loading into the data warehouse'; ELT 'has gained popularity in cloud-native environments'; hybrids acceptable. Best-practices landing page (https://docs.getdbt.com/best-practices, n.d.) lists the guide families.

title: How we style our dbt models (dbt style guide)
subcategory: Model and column naming for analytical schemas
core_concepts: snake_case for schema, table and column names; plural model names; underscores not dots; Every model has a primary key named <object>_id; keys as string data types; Booleans is_/has_; timestamps <event>_at in UTC; dates <event>_date; past-tense events; Decimal currency for price/revenue (suffix _in_cents otherwise); Business terminology over source terminology; no abbreviations; avoid reserved words; Column ordering: ids, strings, numerics, booleans, dates, timestamps; version suffix _v1/_v2
engineering_principles: 'Models should be pluralized'; 'Schema, table and column names should be in snake_case'; 'Each model should have a primary key'; 'The primary key of a model should be named <object>_id'; 'Keys should be string data types'; 'Consistency is key! Use the same field names across models where possible'; 'Booleans should be prefixed with is_ or has_'; 'Timestamp columns should be named <event>_at ... and should be in UTC'; 'Use names based on the business terminology, rather than the source terminology'; 'Do not use abbreviations or aliases. Emphasize readability over brevity.' Label: RECOMMENDED (style).
practical_examples: Staging model example grouping columns by type with comment banners (ids: id AS order_id, store_id AS location_id; numerics: (order_total / 100.0)::float; dates: date(order_date) AS ordered_date; timestamps: ordered_at); customers_v1 / customers_v2 naming.
why_it_matters: Supplies platform-agnostic naming rules for a schema framework (keys, booleans, temporal columns, currency units, business vocabulary). Its 'keys as strings' rule conflicts with Snowflake/Databricks performance guidance favouring numeric keys and must be reconciled per platform.
authority_rationale: Official tool-vendor style guide, widely adopted; opinion-based conventions.
notes: Page does not itself define stg_/int_/fct_/dim_ prefixes; those appear in the structure guide (stg_, int_) and the dbt developer blog 'Building a Kimball dimensional model with dbt' (Jonathan Neo, Apr 20, 2023, https://docs.getdbt.com/blog/kimball-dimensional-model, verified) which uses dim_/fct_ with singular dimension names (dim_product) — a minor intra-dbt naming conflict with the plural rule. CONFLICT: 'Keys should be string data types' vs Snowflake performance guide 'numerical data types for key columns ... strongly recommended'. | Also catalogued as DES-21 in catalog_10_core_design.json

title: Model contracts (dbt Mesh governance)
subcategory: Build-time contracts, platform constraint enforcement, versions and access
core_concepts: contract: enforced: true guarantees column names and data types at build time (preflight check + DDL); Constraint categories: definable+enforced, definable+not enforced (metadata), not definable; On most warehouse adapters only not_null is enforced; PK/FK/UNIQUE are metadata; Postgres enforces all; Contracts recommended for public models relied on downstream; Supported on table and incremental (and view for names/types); not Python, materialized view, ephemeral; Breaking changes (remove column, change type, remove constraint, delete contracted model) raise errors
engineering_principles: 'It's better to define a set of upfront guarantees that define the shape of your model. We call this set of guarantees a contract.' dbt runs 'a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined' and includes names, types and constraints in the DDL. 'When enforced, your contract must include every column's name and data_type.' Enforced constraints mean 'The model won't build if it violates the constraint'; unenforced ones exist 'for metadata purposes only'. Recommended for 'public models that are being relied on downstream'. 'A model's contract defines the shape of the returned dataset... the model does not build' if violated. Label: RECOMMENDED for public models; enforcement MANDATORY where platform supports it.
practical_examples: YAML: models: - name: dim_customers config: contract: enforced: true; columns: customer_id data_type: int constraints: [type: not_null]; customer_name data_type: string. Per-adapter tabs (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Postgres, Redshift, Spark, Fabric, Athena) showing which of not_null/primary_key/foreign_key/unique/check are enforced.
why_it_matters: Shows how the transformation layer compensates for warehouses that do not enforce keys: contracts enforce schema shape and NOT NULL at build time, while PK/FK remain metadata — the same enforced/informational split documented by Databricks and Snowflake. Versions and access extend this into API-style schema evolution.
authority_rationale: Official tool documentation from dbt Labs; enforcement ultimately depends on the underlying platform.
notes: Initial guesses https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/model-contracts and /model-versions returned HTTP 404; live pages are under /docs/mesh/govern/. Adapter tabs could not be attributed from the fetched text; platform docs (LAKE-02, LAKE-09) are authoritative. Related verified pages: 'Model versions' (Sep 10, 2026) — a shared model 'is operating like an API'; version only for breaking changes; files <model>_v<v>.sql; ref('dim_customers', v=2); unpinned ref resolves to latest; deprecation_date gives 'a known boundary on the cost of that migration'; cadence 'once or twice a year'. 'Model access' (Jul 20, 2026) — private/protected (default)/public; recommend new models private; public for 'a stable & mature interface'; access does not grant database privileges.

title: Add snapshots to your DAG (dbt snapshots, SCD Type 2)
core_concepts: Snapshots implement type-2 SCD over mutable source tables; Meta-fields dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to, dbt_scd_id, dbt_updated_at, dbt_is_deleted; Strategies: timestamp (recommended) and check (explicit column list); unique_key must be truly unique; hard_deletes ignore / invalidate / new_record; YAML-defined snapshots (v1.9), dbt_valid_to_current, environment-aware target_schema; Run hourly-to-daily; cannot be rebuilt; keep in a separate schema
engineering_principles: 'dbt provides a mechanism, snapshots, which records changes to a mutable table over time' and they 'implement type-2 Slowly Changing Dimensions over mutable source tables'. 'The unique key is used by dbt to match rows up, so it's extremely important to make sure this key is actually unique!' Timestamp strategy recommended because it 'handles column additions and deletions more efficiently than the check strategy'; 'It is better to explicitly enumerate the columns that you want to check.' 'Snapshots are only useful if you run them frequently' (hourly to daily). 'Snapshots can't be rebuilt. Because of this, it's a good idea to put snapshots in a separate schema so end users know they're special.' Clean data via an ephemeral model before snapshotting. Label: RECOMMENDED.
practical_examples: snapshots: - name: orders_snapshot relation: source('jaffle_shop','orders') config: schema: snapshots unique_key: id strategy: timestamp updated_at: updated_at dbt_valid_to_current: "to_date('9999-12-31')"; orders row moving from pending to shipped producing two versioned rows; hard_deletes: new_record adding dbt_is_deleted rows.
why_it_matters: Defines the canonical SCD2 column set and operational rules for history tables in cloud warehouses, filling the gap left by Snowflake Dynamic Tables (current-state only) and complementing Databricks APPLY CHANGES INTO; informs how a schema framework specifies validity intervals, surrogate SCD ids and delete handling.
authority_rationale: Official tool documentation from dbt Labs.
notes: Contrast verified: Snowflake decision guide — 'Dynamic tables represent the current state of the data, not a historical record'; Databricks blog (Nov 7, 2022) — 'One can easily perform SCD type 1 or SCD type 2 using Delta Live Tables using APPLY CHANGES INTO'.

title: Add data tests to your DAG (dbt data tests, with unit tests, sources and exposures)
subcategory: Generic and singular data tests; unit tests; source freshness; exposures
core_concepts: Data tests are assertions returning failing records; zero rows = pass; Singular tests (one-off SQL) vs generic tests (parameterized test blocks) — generic should be the bulk; Built-ins: unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships; Every model should test a unique + not_null primary key; test source assumptions; severity, warn_if, error_if thresholds; store_failures to dbt_test__audit; Unit tests (v1.8+) validate SQL logic on static fixtures before materialization, run in dev/CI
engineering_principles: 'Data tests are assertions you make about your models and other resources in your dbt project'; 'Data tests return a set of failing records'; generic tests 'should make up the bulk of your dbt data testing suite'; 'Out of the box, dbt ships with four generic data tests already defined: unique, not_null, accepted_values, and relationships'; 'We recommend that every model has a data test on a primary key, that is, a column that is unique and not_null'; 'We also recommend that you test any assumptions on your source data.' Unit tests 'allow you to validate your SQL modeling logic on a small set of static inputs before you materialize your full model'; 'dbt Labs strongly recommends only running unit tests in development or CI environments'. Label: RECOMMENDED (PK tests effectively MANDATORY in dbt practice as the substitute for unenforced keys).
practical_examples: YAML: order_id data_tests: [unique, not_null]; status accepted_values arguments values ['placed','shipped','completed','returned']; customer_id relationships arguments to: ref('customers') field: id; singular test tests/assert_total_payment_amount_is_positive.sql with HAVING total_amount < 0; unit test test_is_valid_email_address with given/expect fixture rows; dbt build order: unit tests -> materialize -> data tests.
why_it_matters: On platforms where PK/FK/UNIQUE are informational, dbt's unique/not_null/relationships tests are the primary mechanism for verifying entity and referential integrity after load; the recommendation that every model has a tested primary key is the operational counterpart of Kimball's surrogate-key discipline.
authority_rationale: Official tool documentation from dbt Labs.
notes: Related verified pages: 'Unit tests' (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/unit-tests, Sep 14, 2026); 'Add sources to your DAG' (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/sources, Sep 16, 2026) — sources 'name and describe the data loaded into your warehouse by your Extract and Load tools', source() creates lineage dependency, freshness via loaded_at_field + warn_after/error_after as 'a critical component of defining Service Level Agreements (SLAs)'; 'Add Exposures to your DAG' (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/exposures, Nov 3, 2026) — exposures 'define and describe a downstream use of your dbt project, such as in a dashboard, application, or data science pipeline', required name/type/owner, depends_on, maturity, dbt run -s +exposure:<name>. | Also catalogued as DQ-02 in catalog_15_data_quality_lineage.json

title: Apache Kafka 4.3 Documentation - Design (ordering, delivery semantics, log compaction, replication)
subcategory: Kafka core design: partitions, keys, exactly-once, compaction
core_concepts: topic = set of totally ordered partitions; semantic partitioning by record key (hash to partition); at-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once delivery definitions; idempotent producer (producer ID + sequence numbers, since 0.11.0.0); transactions across partitions and read_committed isolation; log compaction retains last value per key; null-payload tombstones; delete.retention.ms; acks, in-sync replicas, min.insync.replicas; consumer stores offset with output for end-to-end exactly-once
engineering_principles: Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so entities needing ordered updates must share a key (MANDATORY). Compaction guarantees at least the last known value per key, preserves order and never changes offsets; deletes are keyed messages with null payload kept for delete.retention.ms (default 24h). Exactly-once inside Kafka relies on idempotent producers plus transactions plus read_committed consumers; for external sinks the docs recommend storing the consumer offset in the same place as the output because many systems lack two-phase commit (RECOMMENDED).
practical_examples: Compacted topics used as changelog/state tables keyed by entity ID; tombstone emitted to delete a key; acks=all with min.insync.replicas for durable writes; Kafka Streams exactly-once processing.
why_it_matters: Forces every event schema to carry a stable entity key (the Kafka record key) and makes 'delete' a first-class schema concept (tombstone). Retention and compaction settings bound the reprocessing window that schema compatibility must cover. End-to-end exactly-once pushes an offset/idempotency column into sink table design.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Kafka project documentation (versioned 4.3 design page).
notes: The canonical https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/ URL is a JavaScript redirect and returned no body; the versioned 4.3 design page was used instead. Topic-level defaults (cleanup.policy=delete, retention.ms=7 days, delete.retention.ms=1 day, min.insync.replicas=1, message.timestamp.type=CreateTime) were taken from the 4.2 topic-config reference at https://kafka.apache.org/42/configuration/topic-configs/ (also fetched). The KafkaProducer 1.1 Javadoc URL returned by search (idempotence 'within a single session') was not opened.

title: Schema Evolution and Compatibility for Schema Registry on Confluent Platform
subcategory: Schema registry compatibility modes and per-format evolution rules
core_concepts: BACKWARD (default), BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FORWARD, FORWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL, FULL_TRANSITIVE, NONE; transitive modifier checks against all previously registered schemas, otherwise only the latest; mode-dependent upgrade order (consumers first under BACKWARD, producers first under FORWARD); Avro: new fields need defaults; null must be first union branch with default null; Protobuf: BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE best practice; adding message types not forward compatible; JSON Schema: LENIENT vs STRICT compatibilityPolicy; open vs closed content model (additionalProperties); Kafka Streams supports only BACKWARD and FULL variants
engineering_principles: Default compatibility is BACKWARD, not transitive (stated explicitly). Allowed changes depend on how fields were originally defined: only optional/defaulted fields can be added or removed compatibly (MANDATORY to declare removable fields optional from the start). Under BACKWARD 'upgrade all consumers before you start producing new events'; under FORWARD upgrade producers first; FULL allows independent upgrades (MANDATORY ordering). Protobuf best practice is BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE (RECOMMENDED). JSON Schema closed content model forbids adding/removing required fields under STRICT (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL design choice).
practical_examples: Avro optional field declared as ["null", T] with default null; Kafka Streams apps upgraded before upstream producers; choosing additionalProperties true vs false for JSON Schema subjects.
why_it_matters: Defines, at the field-declaration level, which schema changes are legal for shared event streams, and dictates deployment order of producers/consumers. A schema framework must record the compatibility mode per subject and enforce nullable-with-default for any field that may change.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation for the de facto standard Kafka schema registry.
notes: Second half of the page (format-specific rules for primitives, enums, arrays, unions) could not be read in extractable form; checkmark tables for required-field changes lost column alignment and should be verified on the live page. | Also catalogued as DQ-10 in catalog_15_data_quality_lineage.json

title: Confluent Event Streaming Patterns: Data Contract pattern (with catalog and Schema Evolution pattern)
subcategory: Data contracts, schema evolution strategies, idempotency patterns
core_concepts: Data Contract = shared schema enabling loosely coupled producers and consumers; central schema repository (Schema Registry); use established schema frameworks: Avro, Protocol Buffers, JSON Schema; Schema Evolution pattern: evolve in place vs dual schema upgrades (versioned streams payments-v1/v2); catalog patterns: Idempotent Writer/Reader, Compacted Event Stream, Schema Validator, Dead Letter Stream, Event Envelope, Correlation Identifier, Event-Time Processing, Schema-on-Read
engineering_principles: 'The Data Contract pattern allows these different applications to cooperate while remaining loosely coupled.' Compatible changes evolve in place; breaking changes require a new versioned stream where 'clients must only write to and read from the Event Stream that corresponds to the schema that they can process' (MANDATORY decision rule). 'Follow Schema Compatibility rules to determine which schema changes are compatible and which are breaking changes.' Use an established schema framework rather than custom support (RECOMMENDED).
practical_examples: Avro purchase record (item, amount, customer ID) registered in Schema Registry; payments-v1 and payments-v2 streams written in parallel during a breaking migration until consumers move.
why_it_matters: Provides the escape hatch (stream versioning) that compatibility modes cannot express, and defines the contract as the schema itself; a framework needs a stream/table versioning convention and a dedup identifier field for idempotent writers/readers.
authority_rationale: Confluent-authored official pattern catalog; treat as vendor guidance (4) if a neutral standard is required.
notes: Catalog index https://developer.confluent.io/patterns/ and Schema Evolution pattern https://developer.confluent.io/patterns/event-stream/schema-evolution/ were also fetched. The catalog page did not list patterns literally named Change Data Capture, Transactional Outbox or Event Sourcing. The Data Contract page defines the contract as schema only (no SLA/quality/ownership), which conflicts in scope with ODCS (PIPE-20).

title: Single Message Transforms for Confluent Platform (Kafka Connect SMT reference)
subcategory: Kafka Connect single message transforms and schema handling
core_concepts: SMTs modify individual records in flight inside Connect (no separate stream processor); applied after source connectors / before sink connectors; schema-aware (Struct) vs schemaless (Map) behaviour; transforms: Cast, ExtractField, Flatten, HoistField, InsertField, MaskField, ReplaceField, SetSchemaMetadata, TimestampConverter, ValueToKey, RegexRouter, TimestampRouter, TombstoneHandler, EventRouter, Filter with Predicates
engineering_principles: SMTs eliminate 'the need for a separate stream-processing application' for per-record shaping. Most transforms behave differently with a schema present (Struct) than without (Map), so schema presence changes connector behaviour. Transforms exist to rename/flatten/cast fields and to synthesise keys (ValueToKey) and schema metadata (SetSchemaMetadata) (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL).
practical_examples: Flatten nested CDC payloads into flat sink tables; ValueToKey to derive a record key from value fields; SetSchemaMetadata to rename/version the schema; EventRouter for Debezium outbox tables; MaskField for PII.
why_it_matters: Shows that nesting, key choice and schema names can be altered at the connector boundary; a framework should fix the canonical flattening and require keys at production time rather than relying on connector-side fixes.
authority_rationale: Official Confluent documentation for Kafka Connect transforms (mirrors Apache Kafka Connect transforms with Confluent additions).
notes: Page gives no explicit SMT-vs-stream-processor guidance and does not call SMTs stateless. The Apache Kafka Connect page itself was not fetched.

title: Debezium Outbox Event Router (transactional outbox pattern)
core_concepts: outbox pattern for reliable inter-service data exchange; outbox table columns: id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type, payload; topic routing from aggregatetype (outbox.event.<aggregatetype>); aggregateid as Kafka key for per-aggregate ordering; DELETE on outbox rows filtered; UPDATE not allowed; id usable for consumer deduplication
engineering_principles: 'The outbox pattern is a way to safely and reliably exchange data between multiple (micro) services.' The outbox row is written in the same transaction as the business change; the SMT routes by aggregatetype and keys by aggregateid, which 'is important for maintaining correct order in Kafka partitions' (MANDATORY shape when using the SMT). Outbox rows are insert-only: 'updates to records in an outbox table are not allowed' and deletes are filtered, so rows can be purged immediately.
practical_examples: customers aggregatetype routed to outbox.event.customers; payload stored as JSON; route.tombstone.on.empty.payload=false default; table.op.invalid.behavior=warn default.
why_it_matters: Prescribes a concrete OLTP table schema (the outbox) that bridges transactional writes and event streams, with an explicit event ID for idempotent consumers and an aggregate ID for ordering.
authority_rationale: Official Debezium reference documentation.
notes: Page does not use the phrase 'dual write' and does not state an at-least-once guarantee; it refers to an external blog for rationale.

title: Debezium connector for PostgreSQL (log-based CDC semantics) and Debezium Features
subcategory: Log-based CDC: event envelope, keys, tombstones, delivery guarantees, schema changes
core_concepts: logical decoding / WAL / pgoutput; consistent initial snapshot (op=r); change event envelope: before, after, op (c/u/d/r/t/m), source, ts_ms; REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT/FULL/NOTHING controls before-images; tables without primary key emit only create events; delete event followed by tombstone (tombstones.on.delete=true); exactly-once in normal operation, at-least-once under failure; schema.refresh.mode columns_diff; logical decoding does not carry DDL
engineering_principles: Log-based CDC 'Ensures that all data changes are captured', 'Can capture deletes', and 'Requires no changes to your data model, such as a "Last Updated" column' (Features page). Captured tables need a primary key (MANDATORY: otherwise only create events). REPLICA IDENTITY FULL is required for full before-images (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL). Deletes are a delete event plus a null-value tombstone to support compaction (RECOMMENDED to keep enabled). 'Debezium, like Kafka, provides at least once delivery of change events' under faults and 'Consumers should always anticipate some duplicate events' (MANDATORY idempotent sinks). 'Never drop a replication slot on the primary server or you will lose data.'
practical_examples: Snapshot rows emitted with op=r; update event under REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT carries only PK columns in before; skipped.operations default t (truncates skipped); topic naming <topic.prefix>.<schema>.<table>.
why_it_matters: Turns OLTP schema decisions (primary keys, replica identity, DDL coordination) into hard requirements for downstream streams, and prescribes the CDC envelope (op/before/after/source) that landing tables must be able to store; also mandates idempotent, duplicate-tolerant sinks.
authority_rationale: Official Debezium reference documentation.
notes: Companion Features page https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/features.html was also fetched (source of the 'no Last Updated column' and 'polling or dual writes' statements). Page is ~322k characters; fetched in three ranges. column.include.list text and provide.transaction.metadata ordering details were not captured. | Also catalogued as DQ-24 in catalog_15_data_quality_lineage.json

title: Spark SQL Guide - JSON Files (schema inference options and malformed-record handling)
subcategory: Schema inference pitfalls and explicit schemas
core_concepts: automatic JSON schema inference; samplingRatio (default 1.0), primitivesAsString, prefersDecimal, inferTimestamp (default false), dropFieldIfAllNull; mode PERMISSIVE (default) / DROPMALFORMED / FAILFAST; columnNameOfCorruptRecord (_corrupt_record) implicitly added during inference
engineering_principles: Inference defaults silently shape types: timestamps stay strings unless inferTimestamp=true, floats become doubles unless prefersDecimal=true, and PERMISSIVE mode 'sets malformed fields to null' while putting the raw string into the corrupt-record column only if a user-defined schema declares it (RECOMMENDED: declare schema including _corrupt_record; FAILFAST where correctness matters).
practical_examples: spark.read.schema(explicit_schema).json(path) with a StringType _corrupt_record column; samplingRatio<1 for faster but partial inference.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates why landing/bronze table schemas should be declared rather than inferred: inferred types (string timestamps, double money) and silently nulled bad records propagate into warehouse models.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Spark documentation.
notes: The page does not itself recommend an explicit schema; the explicit-schema requirement is stated on the Structured Streaming page (PIPE-08) for streaming file sources.

title: Structured Streaming Programming Guide - APIs on DataFrames and Datasets (output modes, watermarks, joins, fault tolerance)
core_concepts: Result Table model; Append / Complete / Update output modes; event-time tumbling, sliding, session windows; withWatermark late-data threshold; one-directional guarantee; conditions for watermark state cleanup; stream-stream joins: outer/semi joins require watermark plus time constraints; schema inference disabled for streaming file sources by default (spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference); replayable sources; sink guarantees (file exactly-once, Kafka/foreach at-least-once, foreachBatch batchId dedup)
engineering_principles: 'Structured Streaming from file based sources requires you to specify the schema... This restriction ensures a consistent schema will be used for the streaming query, even in the case of failures' (MANDATORY default). Watermark: 'the guarantee is strict only in one direction. Data delayed by more than 2 hours is not guaranteed to be dropped; it may or may not get aggregated.' State cleanup requires Append/Update mode and withWatermark on the same event-time column before aggregation (MANDATORY preconditions). 'By default, foreachBatch provides only at-least-once write guarantees. However, you can use the batchId provided to the function as way to deduplicate the output and get an exactly-once guarantee' (MANDATORY for exactly-once DB sinks). Files must be atomically placed (move) in file sources.
practical_examples: words.withWatermark('timestamp','10 minutes').groupBy(window(...)).count(); foreachBatch upsert keyed by batchId; outer stream-stream join with watermarks on both sides and a time-range condition.
why_it_matters: Requires an explicit event-time column in streaming schemas, dictates upsert keys of (entity/window, batchId) for idempotent sinks, and warns that late corrections can still arrive after the watermark, so aggregate tables should carry a processing-time updated_at for reconciliation.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Spark documentation.
notes: Checkpoint-recovery section was beyond the fetched range; the page never uses the phrase 'idempotent sink', the batchId deduplication text is the closest equivalent.

title: Apache Iceberg Table Spec
subcategory: Format specification: schema evolution, partition transforms, snapshots/isolation, format versions
core_concepts: schema evolution by type promotion, add, delete, rename, reorder; columns selected by field id; rename keeps field ID; type promotion: int->long, float->double, decimal precision widening; v3: date->timestamp, timestamp_ns; partition transforms identity, bucket[N], truncate[W], year, month, day, hour, void; partition spec evolution with unique spec IDs; partition field IDs stable; atomic metadata swap => serializable isolation; optimistic writers; snapshot reads; format v1 (immutable files), v2 (row-level deletes), v3 (deletion vectors, row lineage, new types), v4 in development
engineering_principles: 'Columns in Iceberg data files are selected by field id' and 'Renaming an existing field must change the name, but not the field ID' (MANDATORY mechanism). 'An atomic swap of one table metadata file for another provides the basis for serializable isolation'; 'Reads will be isolated from concurrent writes and always use a committed snapshot of a table's data.' Hidden partitioning 'simplifies queries because users don't have to supply both logical predicates and partition predicates.' 'When evolving a spec, changes should not cause partition field IDs to change.'
practical_examples: day(event_ts) partition transform; bucket[16] on customer_id; widening a decimal column's precision without rewriting data; v2 tables with position/equality deletes.
why_it_matters: Gives the formal, format-level definition of which schema changes are safe (ID-based tracking makes rename/drop/reorder safe) and makes partitioning a derived, hidden property of a real column rather than a user-maintained schema column.
authority_rationale: Normative specification published by the Apache Iceberg project.
notes: Page is ~352k characters; the schema evolution, partitioning, snapshot/isolation and version sections were read from the 100k-200k range. Snapshot/time-travel detail beyond isolation statements was not captured.

title: Apache Iceberg Docs - Evolution (schema, partition and sort-order evolution) and Partitioning (hidden partitioning)
subcategory: Schema evolution correctness guarantees; hidden partitioning vs Hive
core_concepts: Add / Drop / Rename / Update (widen) / Reorder as metadata-only changes; four correctness guarantees (no cross-column side effects); new columns get new IDs so existing data is never reused; name-tracked formats can un-delete a column if a name is reused; partition evolution without rewriting data; per-spec split planning; sort order evolution; hidden partitioning; problems with Hive partitioning
engineering_principles: 'Iceberg schema updates are metadata changes, so no data files need to be rewritten.' Guarantees: 'Added columns never read existing values from another column'; 'Dropping a column or field does not change the values in any other column'; 'Updating a column or field does not change values in any other column'; reordering does not change values (MANDATORY properties). 'Formats that track columns by name can inadvertently un-delete a column if a name is reused' (framework rule: never reuse dropped names). Partitioning page: 'Hive can't validate partition values -- it is up to the writer to produce the correct value'; 'Using the wrong format, 2018-12-01 instead of 20181201, produces silently incorrect results'; 'Most importantly, queries no longer depend on a table's physical layout' (RECOMMENDED: derive partitions from real timestamp columns).
practical_examples: ALTER TABLE ... to evolve partition spec from month(ts) to day(ts) while old files stay in place; replaceSortOrder; dropping and re-adding a column with a new ID.
why_it_matters: Establishes the strongest schema-evolution safety model among lakehouse formats and argues against synthetic partition columns (dt/event_date) in table schemas; both directly shape lakehouse schema standards.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Iceberg project documentation.
notes: Companion page https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/partitioning/ was also fetched (source of the Hive-partitioning critique quotes). Both pages required an offset fetch past ~100k characters of navigation.

title: Delta Lake - Table batch reads and writes (schema validation, schema evolution, column mapping, time travel)
organization_author: Delta Lake project (Linux Foundation) / Databricks contributors
subcategory: Schema enforcement and evolution; versioning and retention
publication_date: n.d. (features labelled up to Delta Lake 4.3.0)
core_concepts: schema validation on write: extra columns, type mismatches and case-only name differences rejected; missing columns set to null; mergeSchema / autoMerge / WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION add columns automatically (structs only, not arrays/maps); NullType handling; rename/drop without rewrite require column mapping (experimental); otherwise overwriteSchema rewrite; time travel VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF; delta.logRetentionDuration 30 days; delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration 7 days; VACUUM
engineering_principles: Schema-on-write by default: 'If there are columns in the DataFrame not present in the table, an exception is raised'; 'DataFrame column data types must match'; 'DataFrame column names cannot differ only by case' (MANDATORY default). Automatic evolution is opt-in and additive: 'Columns present in the source data but missing from the table are automatically added'; 'Adding nested columns is supported only for structs' (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL). Rename/drop need column mapping and dropping 'does not delete the underlying data for the column in files'; otherwise 'You can change a column's type or name or drop a column by rewriting the table.' 'To time travel to a previous version, you must retain both the log and the data files for that version' (RECOMMENDED: align retention with audit/reprocessing needs).
practical_examples: df.write.option('mergeSchema','true'); INSERT ... WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION (4.3+); SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 12; VACUUM with 7-day default deleted-file retention.
why_it_matters: Delta's strict default enforcement protects warehouse schemas from drift but makes rename/drop costly unless column mapping is enabled; retention defaults bound time travel used for backfill/audit. Conflicts with Iceberg (rename/drop free) and Hudi (rename/drop only via schema-on-read).
authority_rationale: Official Delta Lake project documentation.
notes: Column mapping mode setting value and the dedicated type-widening page were not fetched (linked only).

title: Apache Hudi - Schema Evolution
subcategory: Schema evolution on write vs schema on read; allowed operations and type promotion
core_concepts: backward-compatible schema evolution on write (default); experimental schema-on-read (hoodie.schema.on.read.enable) - irreversible; allowed: add nullable column at end (root or struct), add complex field with default, type promotion; disallowed: non-nullable adds, type demotion, add plus reorder; hoodie.write.set.null.for.missing.columns required or pipeline fails; type promotion matrix int->long->float->double->string; string<->bytes; ALTER TABLE ADD/ALTER/DROP/RENAME COLUMN only under schema-on-read
engineering_principles: 'Hudi supports backwards-compatible schema evolution scenarios out of the box' (RECOMMENDED path). Schema on read is 'experimental support for allowing backward incompatible schema evolution scenarios' and 'If schema on read is enabled, it cannot be disabled again' (OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL, one-way). Write mode rejects adding a non-nullable column, demoting a type, and adding a nullable column combined with reordering (MANDATORY constraints); missing incoming columns need hoodie.write.set.null.for.missing.columns 'otherwise the pipeline will fail'.
practical_examples: Adding a nullable column at the end of a COW/MOR table; promoting int to long; enabling schema-on-read to run ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN; hive.metastore.disallow.incompatible.col.type.changes=false for Hive metastore type changes.
why_it_matters: Hudi's write-mode rules are the most restrictive of the three formats; a portable lakehouse schema standard must limit itself to nullable end-of-struct additions and numeric widening unless it commits to a single format.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Hudi project documentation.
notes: The promotion matrix was reconstructed from flattened page text and should be verified on the live page; the ALTER COLUMN source-to-target matrix could not be reproduced reliably.

title: Apache Airflow - Best Practices
subcategory: DAG and task design: idempotency, atomicity, data intervals, top-level code, XCom
core_concepts: tasks as database transactions; same outcome on every re-run; UPSERT instead of INSERT; never read latest data; partition by data_interval_start; datetime.now() must not drive task logic; no DB/network/heavy computation at DAG top level; XCom for small messages; remote storage for large data; care when deleting tasks; unit tests; staging environment; metadata DB backup before upgrades; dependency isolation via virtualenv/external python/Docker/Kubernetes operators; watcher pattern; trigger rules rely on direct upstream only
engineering_principles: 'You should treat tasks in Airflow equivalent to transactions in a database'; 'the tasks should produce the same outcome on every re-run' (MANDATORY idempotency). 'Replace it with UPSERT' for inserts that would duplicate on retry (MANDATORY). 'Never read the latest available data in a task' - read the partition for data_interval_start (MANDATORY). datetime.now() 'should never be used inside a task, especially to do the critical computation' (MANDATORY). 'you should not run any database access, heavy computations and networking operations' at top level (MANDATORY). 'a good way of passing larger data between tasks is to use a remote storage such as S3/HDFS' (RECOMMENDED). 'Be careful when deleting a task from a Dag' (RECOMMENDED).
practical_examples: UPSERT into target table keyed by business key; templated {{ data_interval_start }} partition filters; moving expensive imports inside task functions; PythonVirtualenvOperator for conflicting dependencies.
why_it_matters: Translates orchestration guarantees into table-schema requirements: a declared merge/business key for UPSERT, and an interval/partition column so each run writes exactly one interval and backfills are repeatable.
authority_rationale: Official Apache Airflow project documentation.
notes: The page does not literally use the words 'idempotent' or 'atomic'; the transaction analogy and re-run statements are its wording. There is no 'Deleting a DAG' section. | Also catalogued as DQ-23 in catalog_15_data_quality_lineage.json

title: Dagster Docs - Assets (software-defined assets) and Asset checks
core_concepts: asset = object in persistent storage (table, file, ML model); asset definitions as declarative, code-as-source-of-truth descriptions; materialization = run function and persist results; asset definitions know their dependencies (vs ops in graphs); asset checks: single-property tests (nulls, schema match, freshness); blocking=True stops downstream materialization on failure
engineering_principles: 'An asset is an object in persistent storage, such as a table, file, or persisted machine learning model.' Asset definitions 'enable a declarative approach to data management'; 'Materializing an asset is the act of running its function and saving the results to persistent storage' (RECOMMENDED framing: the table is the first-class object). Asset checks: 'Each asset check should test only a single asset property to keep tests uncomplicated, reusable, and easy to track over time'; by default a failed check does not stop the run, blocking=True prevents downstream materialization (RECOMMENDED: schema conformance as a blocking check).
practical_examples: @asset functions producing tables; @asset_check verifying a column has no nulls or the table matches a declared schema; scheduling checks separately with alert sensors.
why_it_matters: Reframes orchestration around the data asset (table) with attached schema/quality checks, implying schema definitions should be machine-readable so materialized tables can be validated and downstream loads blocked on drift.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a widely used but vendor-backed orchestrator (per brief scale: reputable tool docs = 3).
notes: Asset checks page https://dagster.io/docs/guides/test/asset-checks was also fetched. Original docs.dagster.io URL 308-redirects to dagster.io/docs. The assets page does not compare against task-based orchestrators and does not detail lineage or freshness policies. Prefect was not researched.

title: Questioning the Lambda Architecture
organization_author: Jay Kreps (co-creator of Apache Kafka), O'Reilly Radar
core_concepts: Lambda: batch layer + speed layer, logic implemented twice; critique: maintaining identical results in two distributed systems is unfixable; Kappa: retain full log in Kafka, replay via second stream job into new output table, swap; reprocess only when code changes
engineering_principles: Lambda requires you to 'implement your transformation logic twice'; 'maintaining code that needs to produce the same result in two complex distributed systems' is painful and 'I don't think this problem is fixable.' Kappa: keep log retention long enough for the reprocessing window, 'start a second instance of your stream processing job' from the log start, 'direct this output data to a new output table', then 'switch the application to read from the new table' and delete the old one (RECOMMENDED pattern; retention length OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL).
practical_examples: Kafka topic with multi-day retention; parallel v2 stream job writing to a new serving table; consumer cutover and old-table deletion.
why_it_matters: Kappa requires serving-layer tables to be versionable/swappable and ties required stream retention to the reprocessing window; it argues against maintaining two schemas (batch and speed) for the same metric.
authority_rationale: Foundational, widely cited practitioner essay by Kafka's co-creator on a major publisher platform; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Nathan Marz's original Lambda Architecture source was not fetched; Lambda is described here via Kreps' summary.

title: The world beyond batch: Streaming 101 (companion to the book Streaming Systems)
subcategory: Batch vs streaming; event time vs processing time; windowing
core_concepts: streaming = execution engine for infinite data; unbounded vs bounded data; well-designed streaming systems are a strict superset of batch; event time vs processing time; skew; processing-time windows vs event-time windows (gold standard); Lambda architecture critique; preview of what/where/when/how axes
engineering_principles: 'I would argue that well-designed streaming systems actually provide a strict superset of batch functionality.' Event time is 'the time at which events actually occurred', processing time 'the time at which events are observed in the system'; skew is 'essentially the latency introduced by the processing pipeline.' Event-time windowing is 'the gold standard of windowing' (RECOMMENDED), processing-time windows break unless data 'arrive in event time order'. Lambda's dual pipelines are 'a bit unsavory' and maintaining them 'is a hassle'.
practical_examples: Session and fixed windows computed in event time with buffering for late data; comparing processing-time vs event-time window results under skew.
why_it_matters: Grounds the requirement that streaming and lakehouse schemas carry a true event-time column separate from ingestion/processing time, and reframes batch as a special case of streaming for architecture decisions.
authority_rationale: Widely cited essay by the Dataflow/Beam lead at Google; book Streaming Systems (Akidau, Chernyak, Lax; O'Reilly, July 2018, ISBN 9781491983874 per retailer listings) expands it.
notes: Book publisher page https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/streaming-systems/9781491983867/ returned HTTP 403 and streamingbook.net refused connection; book metadata (July 2018, 349 pages, expanded from Streaming 101/102) comes from WebSearch result listings only. Streaming 102 was not fetched.

title: The Dataflow Model: A Practical Approach to Balancing Correctness, Latency, and Cost in Massive-Scale, Unbounded, Out-of-Order Data Processing
organization_author: Tyler Akidau, Robert Bradshaw, Craig Chambers, Slava Chernyak, Rafael J. Fernandez-Moctezuma, Reuven Lax, Sam McVeety, Daniel Mills, Frances Perry, Eric Schmidt, Sam Whittle (Google); Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment vol. 8, pp. 1792-1803
subcategory: Unified batch/streaming model: windowing, triggers, watermarks, accumulation
core_concepts: never assume completeness of unbounded data; what / where (event time) / when (processing time) / how (refinements) decomposition; logical model separated from execution engine (batch, micro-batch, streaming); unaligned event-time windows (sessions); triggers; watermarks as heuristic lower bounds on event time; refinement modes: discarding, accumulating, accumulating and retracting; design principles: never rely on completeness, be flexible, add value per engine, clarity, robust analysis in context; Lambda experience: users stopped trusting weakly consistent results
engineering_principles: 'We as a field must stop trying to groom unbounded datasets into finite pools of information that eventually become complete.' Pipelines decompose into 'What results are being computed. Where in event time they are being computed. When in processing time they are materialized. How earlier results relate to later refinements.' The model 'Separates the logical notion of data processing from the underlying physical implementation, allowing the choice of batch, micro-batch, or streaming engine to become one of simply correctness, latency, and cost.' Principles (Section 3.2): 'Never rely on any notion of completeness.'; 'Be flexible...'; 'Encourage clarity of implementation.'; 'Support robust analysis of data in the context in which they occurred.' Watermark is 'a lower bound (often heuristically established) on event times that have been processed' (MANDATORY design stance for streaming schemas: carry event time; expect retractions).
practical_examples: Video-session analytics with session windows and retractions; MillWheel customer who ran weakly consistent streaming with nightly MapReduce truth and found 'customers stopped trusting the weakly consistent results over time', then rebuilt around strong consistency; FlumeJava/MillWheel/Cloud Dataflow implementations.
why_it_matters: Supplies the theoretical basis for event-time columns, late-data handling and refinement semantics in sink schemas (append vs upsert vs retraction rows), and the strongest documented argument against dual batch/speed tables for the same metric.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed foundational paper in PVLDB; authors are the Google Dataflow/Beam team.

title: Understanding ELT: Extract, Load, Transform

title: Kimball Dimensional Modeling Techniques (consolidated 'official' techniques, drawn from The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd Edition)

engineering_principles: Grain must be declared before dimensions/facts and is a binding contract; different grains must not be mixed in one fact table.
