title: Is Kimball dimensional modeling still relevant in a modern data warehouse? (dbt Community Discourse thread)
core_concepts: conformed dimensions still needed; grain discipline; outdated 'databases are slow and expensive' assumption; one wide table per analysis; single big table scaling limits; hybrid normalized layer + flat tables; BI tools rely on fact/dimension concepts; Data Vault and Anchor Modeling alternatives
engineering_principles: Defenders: conformed dimensions prevent 'inconsistent results'; 'if facts share a grain, then widen your table' but mismatched grains cause 'gaps and duplicates'; logic should not live in the BI layer. Critics: 'Databases are slow and expensive' is outdated, warehouses are 'over engineered', formal modeling 'largely been a theatrical exercise'. Wide-table views: build one wide table per analysis requirement; counter: a single big table 'hits a wall at scale' and lacks a trainable pattern; hybrid proposal of normalized engineering layer plus flat tables for ~80% of use cases.
practical_examples: Customer list reused across every slice; wide table per analysis; Data Vault 2.0 with Kimball on top; practitioner reports of DV implementations being 'a mess'.
why_it_matters: Documents the actual arguments of the 'Kimball is dead?' debate at practitioner level and shows that the consensus retains grain and conformance while relaxing performance-motivated rules.
authority_rationale: Community forum posts by named but mostly unverified practitioners; useful for the shape of the debate, not as a normative source.
notes: Opening post is by 'claire' (2019-01-30), not Tristan Handy. The Coalesce 2020 talk by Dave Fowler (Chartio, 2020-12-12, 'Kimball in the context of the modern data warehouse: what's worth keeping, and what's not') and the Brooklyn Data counter-talk ('Babies and bathwater') could not be opened (404/redirect) and are known only from search summaries.

title: Building a Kimball dimensional model with dbt
organization_author: dbt Labs Developer Blog / Jonathan Neo (Canva), edited by Kenny Ning, reviewed by Paul Hallaste and Josh Devlin
subcategory: Kimball in the modern data stack
core_concepts: dimensional modeling relevance; business process identification; fact and dimension tables; star vs snowflake; hashed surrogate keys via dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key; conformed dimensions; One Big Table for BI tools without relationships
engineering_principles: 'While the relevance of dimensional modeling has been debated by data practitioners, it is still one of the most widely adopted data modeling technique for analytics.' Fact tables 'represent a business process in the real world'; dimensions hold 'contextual or descriptive information'. Denormalize to a star to reduce consumer joins. Surrogate keys 'provide consumers... an easy-to-use key to join' and are generated by hashing (md5/hash) with dbt_utils. Build an OBT joining fact to all dimensions only when the BI tool lacks a semantic layer with relationships.
practical_examples: AdventureWorks sales process: fct_sales at order-detail grain with dim_product, dim_address, dim_customer, dim_credit_card, dim_order_status, dim_date; generate_surrogate_key(['productid']) in both dimension and fact; incremental materialization suggested for billion-row facts.
why_it_matters: Shows the dominant modern-data-stack tool's official stance: Kimball retained, surrogate keys implemented as hashes, OBT as a derived consumption artifact.
authority_rationale: Official dbt Labs developer blog (tool vendor), guest-authored and editorially reviewed.
notes: Does not cover SCD/dbt snapshots.

title: Star schema vs. OBT (benchmark on Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery)
subcategory: One Big Table / wide denormalized tables
core_concepts: One Big Table; star schema; query performance benchmark; storage amplification; hybrid: star upstream, wide table downstream
engineering_principles: TPC-DS-derived test (store_sales plus 4 dimensions, BI-style aggregates, caching off): OBT faster than star by 25-30% on Redshift (10-45% on multi-node, 9 of 10 queries), ~25% on Snowflake (mixed; star won 3 queries), 49% average on BigQuery with star showing 'much higher variance'. Storage: Redshift disk 'from a bit over 30 gigabytes to over 90' (store_sales ~29.8 GB vs OBT ~60.3 GB). Recommendation: star for 'easier ELT code organization, easier navigation for analysts, or lower disk use'; OBT for small teams/single-subject speed; hybrid builds the star then re-joins into a wide table for end users.
practical_examples: Redshift dc2.large single-node ran out of disk when joining all dimensions into the OBT.
why_it_matters: Only measured OBT-vs-star evidence found; quantifies the speed gain and the storage cost that make OBT CONTEXTUAL rather than a default.
authority_rationale: Major data-tooling vendor engineering blog with disclosed methodology; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Author notes dbt could not set column compression on Redshift, so storage figures are likely worst-case. | Also catalogued as BENCH-09 in catalog_23_benchmarks.json

title: The Rise of the Data Engineer ('Data modeling is changing' section)
organization_author: Maxime Beauchemin (creator of Apache Airflow and Apache Superset), published on freeCodeCamp
core_concepts: star schema less relevant; further denormalization; natural keys in fact tables; surrogate keys as a maintenance burden; dimension snapshots instead of complex SCD; conformance as a tradeoff
engineering_principles: Star schema approaches 'are less relevant than they once were' because storage/compute are cheap and engineering time is scarce; 'further denormalization' and natural keys reduce joins; 'maintaining surrogate keys in dimensions can be tricky, and it makes fact tables less readable'; snapshotting full dimension copies each ETL cycle is 'a simple generic approach that requires little engineering effort' while complex SCD techniques 'are not intuitive and reduce accessibility'; conformance 'is still extremely important' but is now a tradeoff aligned gradually.
practical_examples: Full dimension snapshots per ETL cycle as the SCD alternative; data engineers as 'librarians' cataloging metadata.
why_it_matters: The most-cited practitioner origin of the 'Kimball is less relevant' position; identifies exactly which Kimball rules (surrogates, SCD machinery, star-for-performance) cloud teams relax.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner essay; influential but not an official body or refereed work.
notes: Companion essay 'Functional Data Engineering - a modern paradigm for batch data processing' (Medium, 2018-01-08; pure/idempotent tasks, immutable partitions, partition snapshots instead of SCD2) returned HTTP 403 at https://maximebeauchemin.medium.com/functional-data-engineering-a-modern-paradigm-for-batch-data-processing-2327ec32c42a and is NOT verified; its content is known only from search summaries. Data Council talk page returned by search but not opened: https://www.datacouncil.ai/functional-data-engineering-a-set-of-best-practices

title: Activity Schema Specification v2.0
core_concepts: single activity stream table; required columns activity_id, ts, customer, activity, feature_json; optional anonymous_customer_id, revenue_impact, link; immutable activities; one entity per stream; temporal self-joins (First Ever, Last Before, First After, Aggregate In Between); no foreign-key joins
engineering_principles: 'An activity should never change'; 'A single entity cannot be identified with an email in one activity and a phone number in another'; 'All joins are self-joins to the activity_stream table, and they only use the entity and timestamp columns'; the model 'does not require any foreign key joins'; each activity keeps a consistent feature_json structure and stores only data it is authoritative for; entity tables are 'similar to dimension tables in a star schema'; 'Unlike dimensional modeling, activities should only store metadata that they are authoritative for.'
practical_examples: <entity>_stream naming; cohort activity defining result rows with appended relationships that never add or drop rows.
why_it_matters: A documented alternative to star schemas for single-entity behavioral analytics; its explicit rules let a framework scope it to event-sequence workloads and exclude multi-entity financial data.
authority_rationale: Published open specification with a named author, but originated and promoted by one vendor (Narrator) with limited independent adoption evidence.
notes: Project site https://www.activityschema.com/ (fetched) describes 'modeling all data in the warehouse as a single time series table' with 'no joins between models' and credits Ahmed Elsamadisi.

title: The Analytics Setup Guidebook - Data Modeling Layer & Concepts (and book index)
organization_author: Holistics / Huy Nguyen, Ha Pham, Cedric Chin
subcategory: Kimball in the modern ELT stack
core_concepts: data modeling layer; ELT - transform inside the warehouse; models as SQL SELECT statements; persisted models for performance; Kimball / Inmon / Data Vault as classical approaches
engineering_principles: Data modeling is a layer mapping raw data to business terms with transformations run 'within the data warehouse, as per the ELT paradigm'; models are SQL SELECT statements over tables or other models; persisting models (equivalent to materialized views) is justified 'for performance reasons'; readers experienced in 'Kimball, Inmon or Data Vault-style data modeling' can skim because the approach is 'contemporary'.
practical_examples: Turning homestay.listings into a star schema via a modeling-layer tool.
why_it_matters: Represents the vendor-authored 'modern data stack' view that modeling moves into the warehouse as a SQL layer, within which Kimball structures remain a target rather than a mandate.
authority_rationale: Free vendor guidebook by Holistics staff; widely read but commercial and not refereed.
notes: Book index http://www.holistics.io/books/setup-analytics/ (fetched) lists chapter 3 sections 'Kimball's Dimensional Data Modeling' and 'How has data modeling evolved in modern cloud era?' but those section URLs could not be resolved (404), so Holistics' specific verdict on surrogate keys/SCD is not verified here.

title: Domain-Driven Design Reference: Definitions and Pattern Summaries
subcategory: Strategic and tactical patterns (bounded context, aggregate, entity, value object, ubiquitous language, context map, domain events)
publication_date: 2015-03 (PDF; copyright 2015, CC BY 4.0; summarizes the 2003/2004 book plus later additions)
core_concepts: Bounded context defined as 'a description of a boundary (typically a subsystem, or the work of a particular team) within which a particular model is defined and applicable'; Boundaries set 'in terms of team organization, usage within specific parts of the application, and physical manifestations such as code bases and database schemas'; Aggregate: 'Use the same aggregate boundaries to govern transactions and distribution. Within an aggregate boundary, apply consistency rules synchronously. Across boundaries, handle updates asynchronously.'; Entities distinguished by identity; value objects immutable with no identity; Ubiquitous language: 'a change in the language is a change to the model'; rename code to match; Context map relationship patterns: Partnership, Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Conformist, Anticorruption Layer, Open-host Service, Published Language, Separate Ways, Big Ball of Mud; Domain events 'are ordinarily immutable', carry occurrence timestamp, entity identities, and often a recording timestamp and actor
engineering_principles: MANDATORY (Evans' wording): one model per explicitly bounded context with explicit schema/codebase boundaries; aggregates are the unit of transaction and distribution (synchronous consistency inside, asynchronous across); external references only to the aggregate root; value objects immutable; names in code follow the ubiquitous language. OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: Shared Kernel permits a small shared subset of 'the database design' governed jointly ('Keep this kernel small'). Repositories only for aggregate roots.
practical_examples: Shared Kernel: 'include ... the subset of code or of the database design associated with that part of the model ... shouldn't be changed without consultation with the other team.' Context Map: 'Name each bounded context, and make the names part of the ubiquitous language.' Domain event identity derived from timestamp+entity ids so duplicates 'can be recognized as the same.'
why_it_matters: Primary source for the rule that a bounded context has a schema boundary, that aggregate boundaries scope transactions and locking, that cross-aggregate references are by identity, and that table/column names should be ubiquitous-language terms. The context-map patterns are the decision table for when schemas may be shared (Shared Kernel) versus integrated via contracts (Open-host Service + Published Language).
authority_rationale: Written by the originator of DDD as the official pattern summary of the foundational book; freely licensed; the canonical definitions.
notes: Landing page https://www.domainlanguage.com/ddd/reference/ also fetched (no date shown; footer 2026). PDF text extracted locally with pdftotext; quotes verbatim from the PDF. Evans' 2003 Addison-Wesley book itself was not fetched.

title: Martin Fowler bliki: BoundedContext (with DDD_Aggregate and UbiquitousLanguage)
subcategory: Bounded context, aggregate, ubiquitous language explainers
core_concepts: 'DDD deals with large models by dividing them into different Bounded Contexts and being explicit about their interrelationships'; Citing Evans: 'total unification of the domain model for a large system will not be feasible or cost-effective'; Boundaries driven mainly by 'human culture'; example of a boundary inside one codebase: 'the separation between in-memory and relational database models in a single application'; Aggregate: 'a cluster of domain objects that can be treated as a single unit'; 'Transactions should not cross aggregate boundaries'; 'Aggregates are the basic element of transfer of data storage - you request to load or save whole aggregates'; Ubiquitous language: 'software doesn't cope well with ambiguity'; developers 'should watch for ambiguity or inconsistency that will trip up design'
engineering_principles: MANDATORY (as stated): transactions should not cross aggregate boundaries; load/save whole aggregates. RECOMMENDED: depict context relationships 'using a context map' (Vernon's book Ch. 3 cited as best source). Multiple models are the norm; do not force one canonical model.
practical_examples: In-memory vs relational model split as a bounded-context boundary within one application; aggregate root as the sole entry point for external references.
why_it_matters: Widely cited secondary explanation that confirms aggregates are the persistence and transaction unit (implying table groups that save together) and that a context boundary can be logical inside one codebase (relevant to modular-monolith schemas).
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner and author (PoEAA), long-standing reference site; secondary to Evans but highly influential.
notes: Companion pages fetched: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DDD_Aggregate.html (2013-04-23) and https://martinfowler.com/bliki/UbiquitousLanguage.html (2006-10-31). Fowler's aggregate entry does not mention reference-by-identity; that rule is from Vernon (ARCH-03).

title: Effective Aggregate Design, Parts I-III
subcategory: Aggregate design rules; transactional vs eventual consistency
publication_date: 2011-10-01 (library page); Part I PDF metadata 2011-09-29; Part II PDF metadata 2011-11-25
core_concepts: 'aggregate is synonymous with transactional consistency boundary'; Rule: Model True Invariants In Consistency Boundaries; Rule: Design Small Aggregates; Rule: Reference Other Aggregates By Identity ('not by holding a direct object reference'); Rule: Use Eventual Consistency Outside the Boundary (quoting Evans DDD p128: 'Any rule that spans AGGREGATES will not be expected to be up-to-date at all times'); 'a properly designed bounded context modifies only one aggregate instance per transaction in all cases' ... 'it is a rule of thumb and should be the goal in most cases'; Reasons To Break the Rules: User Interface Convenience; Lack of Technical Mechanisms; Global Transactions; (query performance)
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (strong default, explicitly a 'rule of thumb'): one aggregate instance modified per transaction; small aggregates; reference other aggregates by identity; eventual consistency via domain events for cross-aggregate rules; ask domain experts whether delay is tolerable; use retries and compensation on failure. CONTEXTUAL exceptions enumerated (batch creation of full aggregates, no messaging infrastructure, mandated 2PC, user-aggregate affinity).
practical_examples: Scrum-management domain (Product, BacklogItem, Release, Sprint) with TenantId; large-cluster Product aggregate replaced by small aggregates created via factory methods; BacklogItemCommitted domain event lets Sprint create CommittedBacklogItem asynchronously; application service resolves cross-aggregate lookups via repositories; CQRS suggested when identity-only references make view assembly expensive.
why_it_matters: The most detailed primary treatment of why aggregate tables must be transaction-scoped, why foreign keys to other aggregates should be identifiers not owned rows, and when multi-aggregate transactions are acceptable. Content became chapter 10 of 'Implementing Domain-Driven Design' (2013).
authority_rationale: Author of 'Implementing DDD'; essays reviewed by Eric Evans and Paul Rayner (per acknowledgments); hosted on the DDD Community library.
notes: PDFs fetched and text-extracted locally: https://www.dddcommunity.org/wp-content/uploads/files/pdf_articles/Vernon_2011_1.pdf and https://www.dddcommunity.org/wp-content/uploads/files/pdf_articles/Vernon_2011_2.pdf. Part III not fetched. 'Implementing DDD' (2013) book text not fetched.

title: Data sovereignty per microservice (.NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications)
subcategory: Bounded context to database mapping; polyglot persistence; eventual consistency
core_concepts: 'each microservice must own its domain data and logic'; 'Each BC must have its own model and database; likewise, each microservice owns its related data'; 'Each DDD Bounded Context correlates to one business microservice (one or several services)'; The BC pattern 'doesn't specify whether the Bounded Context is a distributed service or if it's simply a logical boundary ... within a monolithic-deployment application'; Monolith benefits: 'ACID transactions and the SQL language, both working across all the tables'; 'you must use eventual consistency when a business process spans multiple microservices ... you can't create integrity constraints or use distributed transactions between separate databases'; Same identity, different names across contexts: User (profile BC) vs Buyer (ordering BC); Polyglot persistence (SQL + NoSQL mix)
engineering_principles: MANDATORY for microservices: private data per service, accessed only via API or messaging. RECOMMENDED: start with one service per bounded context but 'you don't have to constrain your design to it'. Warns that a shared centralized DB yields 'huge tables that serve many different subsystems'.
practical_examples: CRM, purchasing and customer-support subsystems each holding their own customer attributes under separate bounded contexts; eShopOnContainers reference app.
why_it_matters: Vendor guidance that states the strong 'own database per bounded context' rule while acknowledging the bounded context can be a logical boundary in a monolith; directly addresses the shared-database-vs-separation decision for ERP-like systems.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft documentation (published architecture eBook).
notes: Cites Richardson's Database per Service, Fowler's BoundedContext and PolyglotPersistence, and Brandolini's context mapping article.

title: Pattern: Database per service (with Pattern: Shared database)
subcategory: Data ownership and physical separation options
core_concepts: 'Keep each microservice's persistent data private to that service and accessible only via its API'; Three options: Private-tables-per-service, Schema-per-service, Database-server-per-service; 'Private-tables-per-service and schema-per-service have the lowest overhead'; Enforce with 'a separate database user per service with access grants'; Drawbacks: 'Distributed transactions are best avoided because of the CAP theorem'; cross-database joins hard; multiple DB technologies complex; Shared Database: 'Each service freely accesses data owned by other services using local ACID transactions'; benefits 'familiar and straightforward ACID transactions', 'simpler to operate'; drawbacks development-time and runtime coupling
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: database-per-service with the lowest-overhead option (private tables or schema) as default; server-per-service only for throughput/storage-type needs. OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: shared database retains ACID simplicity at the cost of coupling. Use Saga for cross-service transactions and API Composition or CQRS for cross-service queries.
practical_examples: Per-service DB users with grants as the enforcement barrier; Saga/API Composition/CQRS named as the compensating patterns.
why_it_matters: Gives the practical ladder (tables -> schema -> server) for mapping bounded contexts onto physical storage in an ERP/SaaS, and the honest trade-off list for keeping a shared database.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner (author of 'Microservices Patterns'); widely referenced pattern catalog, but a personal site with no dates and commercial offerings.
notes: Companion page fetched: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/shared-database.html (n.d.). CONFLICT within the site: the Shared Database page is tagged 'pattern' and not labelled an anti-pattern, while the Database-per-Service page lists it as the 'Shared Database anti-pattern'.

title: Pattern: Saga (with Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumer)
core_concepts: Saga: 'a reliably coordinated sequence of local transactions'; choreography (domain events) vs orchestration (central orchestrator); Saga drawbacks: no automatic rollback (compensating transactions); 'lack of isolation (the I in ACID)' requiring 'countermeasures'; Transactional Outbox: store messages in an outbox table 'as part of the transaction that updates the business entities'; a message relay (transaction log tailing or polling publisher) publishes them; 'Messages are guaranteed to be sent if and only if the database transaction commits'; At-least-once: 'The Message relay might publish a message more than once' -> consumers must be idempotent; Idempotent Consumer: PROCESSED_MESSAGE table with primary key (subscriberId, messageID) inserted in the same transaction; duplicate insert fails and the transaction is rolled back
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: sagas for business transactions spanning services (2PC excluded). MANDATORY when publishing events from a DB-backed service: outbox (or event sourcing) to avoid dual-write loss; MANDATORY with at-least-once delivery: idempotent consumers via processed-message tracking.
practical_examples: Order/Customer credit-limit saga: Order Service creates PENDING order and emits Order Created; Customer Service reserves credit; Order approved/rejected. Outbox as a table for relational DBs or a record property for NoSQL. PROCESSED_MESSAGE(subscriberId, messageID) dedup table.
why_it_matters: Defines three concrete schema artifacts every context database needs when it participates in cross-context workflows: saga state (pending statuses/compensations), an outbox table, and a processed-messages table.
authority_rationale: Widely cited practitioner catalog; no dates; commercial framework (Eventuate) promoted alongside.
notes: Companion pages fetched: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html and https://microservices.io/patterns/communication-style/idempotent-consumer.html (both n.d.). The Saga page does not use the term 'semantic lock'; the outbox page gives no explicit OUTBOX column list.

title: Pattern: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (with Event Sourcing and API Composition)
core_concepts: CQRS: 'Define a view database, which is a read-only replica that is designed specifically to support that query', kept current by subscribing to domain events; CQRS drawbacks: 'Increased complexity', 'Potential code duplication', 'Replication lag/eventually consistent views'; 'Necessary in an event sourced architecture'; Event Sourcing: 'persists the state of a business entity ... as a sequence of state-changing events'; 'The event store also behaves like a message broker'; 'The event store is difficult to query'; 'a different and unfamiliar style of programming'; API Composition: an API Composer 'performs an in-memory join'; 'Some queries would result in inefficient, in-memory joins of large datasets'
engineering_principles: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: API Composition for simple cross-service queries; CQRS view databases when joins are large or event-sourced data must be queried; event sourcing when reliable event publication and audit are required, accepting eventual consistency.
practical_examples: View database typically a NoSQL/document store with a query-tuned schema; event store with periodic snapshots to limit replay.
why_it_matters: Establishes that denormalized read schemas are a legitimate, separately-owned schema class derived from domain events, and that event stores need CQRS projections because they are not directly queryable.
authority_rationale: Widely cited practitioner catalog; secondary to Fowler/Young/Microsoft on event sourcing.
notes: Companion pages fetched: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/event-sourcing.html and https://microservices.io/patterns/data/api-composition.html (both n.d.). CONFLICT with ARCH-10 (Microsoft): Richardson says the event store 'behaves like a message broker'; Microsoft warns not to confuse an event store with a message broker such as Kafka.

title: What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?
subcategory: Taxonomy: event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing, CQRS
core_concepts: Event Notification: 'the source system doesn't really care much about the response'; low coupling; 'It can be hard to see such a flow as it's not explicit in any program text'; Event-Carried State Transfer: recipients keep copies; 'lots of data schlepped around and lots of copies'; receiver complexity; Event Sourcing: 'The event store becomes the principal source of truth, and the system state is purely derived from it'; replay issues with external systems and schema change; 'There's no need for event processing to be asynchronous'; CQRS: 'Strictly CQRS isn't really about events'; 'many of my colleagues are deeply wary of using CQRS, finding it often misused'; 'all these patterns are good in the right place and bad when put on the wrong terrain'
engineering_principles: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL for all four; choose by coupling, resilience and complexity needs; CQRS only when a single model for reads and writes 'gets too complicated'.
practical_examples: Customer address change propagated as a notification vs as carried state; event store replay for audit and historic states.
why_it_matters: Disambiguates which 'event-driven' choice drives schema duplication (state transfer creates replicated columns in consumers), which creates an append-only store (event sourcing), and which creates dual read/write schemas (CQRS).
authority_rationale: Recognized author; frequently cited taxonomy article.
notes: The article does not use the phrase 'eventual consistency'; it discusses the duplication and asynchrony costs instead.

title: Event Sourcing (Development of Further Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture)
subcategory: Event sourcing pattern: log as record, snapshots, replay, reversal, versioning, external gateways
core_concepts: 'Capture all changes to an application state as a sequence of events'; 'The official system of record can either be the event logs or the current application state'; Snapshots: 'New snapshots can be made at any time in parallel without bringing down the running application'; Temporal query: 'We can determine the application state at any point in time'; Reversal: 'Reversal is the most straightforward when the event is cast in the form of a difference'; Code changes: new features, bug fixes ('make the fix and reprocess the events'), temporal logic via date-bound strategy objects; avoid bi-temporal unless needed; External systems wrapped in replay-aware gateways; record external query responses
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED when adopting event sourcing: snapshots for rebuild performance; design events as differences where reversal is needed; isolate external interactions behind gateways; keep temporal rules in the domain model.
practical_examples: Ship tracking example; PaymentGateway.send guarded by replay mode; storing prior values when events are not expressed as deltas.
why_it_matters: Original pattern description; its nuance that the system of record may be the log or the current state differs from later 'event store is the single source of truth' framings and matters for how an ERP treats ledger vs current-balance tables.
authority_rationale: Original pattern write-up by a recognized author; pre-dates most other literature.
notes: CONFLICT/nuance with ARCH-08 and ARCH-10 on whether the event log must be the single source of truth.

title: Event Sourcing pattern (with CQRS pattern) - Azure Architecture Center
subcategory: Event store design, versioning, idempotency, snapshots, pitfalls; CQRS read/write model separation
core_concepts: 'Event sourcing is a complex pattern that introduces significant trade-offs ... For most systems and most parts of a system, traditional data management is sufficient'; Per-entity eventstreams; 'event stores partition naturally by entity ID'; purpose-built store vs 'relational or document database with an append-only table'; 'Don't confuse an event store with an eventstream message broker' (Kafka lacks per-entity stream queries and optimistic concurrency); Versioning: 'you should never update the event data'; strategies: tolerant deserialization, event versioning, upcasting, in-place migration ('last resort'); Event ordering via timestamp and incremental identifier; store rejects duplicate entity-id+event-id; optimistic concurrency per stream; 'Snapshots are an optimization, not a replacement for the eventstream'; Idempotency: delivery 'typically at least once'; 'Track the last processed event sequence number for each consumer'; PII: keep personal data outside the store by identifier or use crypto-shredding; CQRS: separate models in a single store (foundational) or in different stores; 'Optimized data schemas'; use Transactional Outbox and idempotent read-model consumers; 'The event store is the write model and the single source of truth'
engineering_principles: MANDATORY if event sourcing is adopted: immutable append-only events, compensating events for corrections, per-stream optimistic concurrency, idempotent handlers. RECOMMENDED: intent-revealing events ('two seats were reserved' not 'remaining seats changed to 42'), snapshots every N events, separate PII store. OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: adopt selectively ('payment ledger or order-processing pipeline'), not for CRUD, MVPs, reference/lookup data, or teams without event-driven experience. CQRS without a second database is the foundational level.
practical_examples: Conference seat-reservation SeatAvailability entity rebuilt by replay; given-when-then testing; hotel booking command 'Book hotel room' vs 'Set ReservationStatus to Reserved'; C# ProductsDao read model and RateProduct command handler.
why_it_matters: Most complete, current vendor-neutral-in-substance checklist of event-store schema requirements and pitfalls (ordering, versioning, idempotency, GDPR), plus explicit guidance on when CQRS/ES are inappropriate for ERP-style reference data.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft Azure Architecture Center documentation, recently updated (2026).
notes: Companion page fetched: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs (ms.date 2025-02-20, updated 2026-10-11). CONFLICT with ARCH-07 on event store vs message broker; nuance vs ARCH-08 (Fowler: event processing need not be asynchronous) since Microsoft's reference workflow uses a queue.

title: CloudEvents - Version 1.0.3-wip core specification (and cloudevents.io)
organization_author: Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) CloudEvents project
publication_date: main branch 1.0.3-wip (n.d.); v1.0.2 released 2022-02-05; CNCF Graduated 2024-01-25
core_concepts: REQUIRED attributes: id, source, specversion, type; 'Producers MUST ensure that source + id is unique for each distinct event'; type SHOULD be prefixed with a reverse-DNS name (e.g. com.github.pull_request.opened); OPTIONAL: datacontenttype (RFC 2046), dataschema (URI; 'Incompatible changes to the schema SHOULD be reflected by a different URI'), subject, time (RFC 3339); Attribute names lowercase ASCII letters/digits, SHOULD NOT exceed 20 characters; 'data' reserved; extension attributes allowed; 'This specification does not place any restriction on the type of this information' (data payload); JSON event format MUST be supported; bindings/formats include HTTP, WebSocket, Protobuf batching; adopted by Amazon EventBridge and Azure Event Grid
engineering_principles: MANDATORY for conformance: the four required attributes and the source+id uniqueness rule. RECOMMENDED: dataschema URI per schema version, reverse-DNS type names, RFC 3339 time.
practical_examples: Event type naming 'com.github.pull_request.opened'; JSON format with datacontenttype defaulting to application/json.
why_it_matters: Provides the de facto standard envelope columns for an event/outbox table (id, source, type, time, subject, dataschema, datacontenttype) and the idempotency key (source+id) consumers should dedupe on.
authority_rationale: CNCF Graduated project specification maintained by a standards-body foundation.
notes: Landing page https://cloudevents.io/ also fetched (version/graduation facts). The GitHub page is the work-in-progress 1.0.3 text; released v1.0.2 wording may differ slightly.

title: AsyncAPI Specification v3.0.0
subcategory: Message-driven API contract specification (channels, operations, messages, payload schemas)
core_concepts: 'The AsyncAPI Specification is a project used to describe message-driven APIs in a machine-readable format'; protocol-agnostic (AMQP, MQTT, Kafka, WebSockets); 'A channel is an addressable component, made available by the server, for the organization of messages'; Operation action is send or receive; optional reply for request/reply; Message Object: headers ('MUST NOT define the protocol headers'), payload, correlationId, contentType, traits; Multi Format Schema Object with schemaFormat; default AsyncAPI Schema Object (JSON Schema based); required JSON Schema Draft 07; recommended Avro 1.9.0, OpenAPI 3.0.0 Schema, RAML 1.0, Protobuf 2/3; 'Custom values are allowed but their implementation is OPTIONAL'
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: describe every event channel and message with an explicit payload schema in a declared schemaFormat; separate application headers from protocol headers; carry correlationId for tracing.
practical_examples: Kafka topic as a channel with Avro payload; request/reply via operation reply object.
why_it_matters: The contract layer for event/output-port schemas: it fixes how a producer publishes the schema of each message so consumers and data products can validate against it (complements CloudEvents' envelope and ODCS's dataset-level contract).
authority_rationale: Official specification of an open standards initiative under the Linux Foundation.
notes: Page is ~112k characters; the final ~12k were not read. Stability status not labelled on the page.

title: Versioning of Events in Event Sourced Systems (report of Greg Young's DDD eXchange 2017 talk)
core_concepts: 'Updating an existing event can cause large problems and Young strongly argues against this'; 'A general rule when versioning events is that adding things does not cause a versioning conflict'; Weak schema (map by name, defaults for missing) with two rules: no renaming, no change of semantic meaning; 'an old version of the software is able to read a new event'; Strong type-based schemas 'generally recommends against'; only work 'if you can take the system down and upgrade it'; A new version is valid only 'if it can be converted from an older version of the same event. Otherwise, it is a new event'; Upcasting so 'an event handler only needs to know how to deal with the latest version'; Stream transformation at release ('The old stream can afterwards be deleted'); 'the real challenge comes when a system can't be taken down'
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: never mutate stored events. RECOMMENDED: additive, weak-schema evolution; upcasters; copy-transform streams during release windows; design for two software versions running concurrently.
practical_examples: Adding a property with a default value, compared to adding a non-nullable database column; transform/join/split of streams during release.
why_it_matters: Primary-author guidance (via a reputable report) on how event schemas evolve without breaking the immutable store, which governs how event payload columns and version fields are designed.
authority_rationale: Reputable technology news outlet reporting the originator of CQRS/event sourcing; secondary to Young's own book, which could not be read beyond its table of contents.
notes: Young's book 'Versioning in an Event Sourced System' at https://leanpub.com/esversioning/read was fetched but only the chapter list was readable (Why can't I update an event?, Basic Type Based Versioning, Weak Schema, Negotiation, Copy and Replace, Cheating, Internal vs External Models, Versioning Process Managers); no date shown.

title: How to Move Beyond a Monolithic Data Lake to a Distributed Data Mesh
subcategory: Founding article: failure modes of centralized platforms; domain data as a product
core_concepts: Three failure modes: 'Centralized and monolithic', 'Coupled pipeline decomposition' ('decomposed orthogonally to the axis of change'), 'Siloed and hyper-specialized ownership'; 'We have moved away from domain oriented data ownership to a centralized domain agnostic data ownership'; Source-aligned domain datasets ('represent the facts and reality of the business') vs consumer-aligned datasets; 'The architectural quantum in a domain oriented data platform, is a domain and not the pipeline stage'; Data product qualities: Discoverable, Addressable, Trustworthy and truthful, Self-describing, Interoperable, Secure; Domain-agnostic self-serve platform: 'To not include any domain specific concepts or business logic, keeping it domain agnostic'; Roles: data product owner, embedded data engineers
engineering_principles: MANDATORY (by Dehghani's definition of a data product): the six usability qualities with SLOs and a global addressing convention. RECOMMENDED: domains 'host and serve their domain datasets in an easily consumable way'; pipelines become internal implementation details of the domain.
practical_examples: Media-streaming domains (podcasts, artists, listeners) serving source-aligned datasets; central catalog with lineage; shared global identifiers for entities such as artists.
why_it_matters: Origin of the rule that analytical schemas are owned by the producing domain, that source-aligned products mirror operational facts rather than warehouse-wide canonical models, and that interoperability is achieved via global identifiers rather than a single enterprise schema.
authority_rationale: Originating author of the paradigm, published on a major practitioner site; not peer-reviewed.

title: Data Mesh Principles and Logical Architecture (with the 2022 O'Reilly book record)
subcategory: Four principles; data product quantum; federated computational governance
core_concepts: Four principles: domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and architecture; data as a product ('Analytical data provided by the domains must be treated as a product'); self-serve data infrastructure as a platform; federated computational governance ('automated execution of decisions by the platform'); Data product as architectural quantum: 'the smallest unit of architecture that can be independently deployed with high functional cohesion', bundling code, data and metadata, and infrastructure; Polyglot serving: data 'as events, batch files, relational tables, graphs, etc.' with the same semantics; Local vs global policy: 'the domain data model is a concern that should be localized to a domain'; 'how to identify a podcast listener is a global concern'; Governance as 'maintaining an equilibrium between centralization and decentralization'
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: domain-local data models; global standards for cross-domain identifiers and interoperability enforced computationally by the platform. RECOMMENDED: serve the same data product through multiple polyglot forms; include policy-enforcing code and metadata inside the product.
practical_examples: Podcast-listener identity as a global policy; data product components (pipelines, access APIs, metadata, access-control code, infrastructure).
why_it_matters: Defines where analytical schema authority sits (domain-local) and what must be globally standardized (identifiers, classifications), which is the governance split a schema framework must encode.
authority_rationale: Originating author; canonical article; the 2022 O'Reilly book is a recognized text.
notes: The 2020 article does not use the term 'output ports'. Book record verified via Google Books https://books.google.com.pk/books?vid=ISBN9781492092391&redir_esc=y : 'Data Mesh: Delivering Data-Driven Value at Scale', O'Reilly, 2022, ISBN 9781492092391, 345 pages, chapters shown include 'What Is Data Mesh?', 'Principle of Data as a Product', 'Principle of the Self-Serve Data Platform'; retailer listings in search results give 2022-03-22. The O'Reilly product page https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/data-mesh/9781492092384/ returned HTTP 403 (not verified).

title: Thoughtworks Technology Radar: Data mesh (with Data product thinking)
publication_date: 2019-11 (Assess) to 2022-03-29 (Trial, last update); Data product thinking 2023-09 (Trial) and 2025-04 (Adopt)
core_concepts: Ring history: Assess (Nov 2019, May 2020) -> Trial (Oct 2020, Oct 2021, Mar 2022); never Adopt; no longer on current Radar; Adoption requires 'investment in a self-serve platform, long-term domain ownership of data products, and incentives'; 'a large gap in open-source and commercial tooling'; organizational restructuring: separate platform team, data product owner per domain; 'implementations face high integration costs, and adoption is still limited to parts of large organizations'; 'technology vendors may distract organizations from the harder social aspects'; Data product thinking moved to Adopt (Apr 2025) 'whether or not an organization uses data mesh or a lakehouse'; products publish 'quality and SLI metrics such as freshness, completeness, and consistency'
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (Adopt): data product thinking with published quality/SLI metrics, catalog metadata, use-case-driven design, lifecycle retirement. OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL (Trial, stalled): full data mesh, suited to organizations 'with many domains and diverse data-driven use cases'.
practical_examples: Tools named: Soda Core, Great Expectations (quality), Monte Carlo (observability), DataHub, Collibra, Atlan, Informatica (catalogs); 'data product quanta' bundling code, data and policy.
why_it_matters: Independent-ish signal from the paradigm's originating consultancy that the ownership/product half of data mesh is mainstream while full federated architecture remains costly; frames which mesh rules a schema framework should make mandatory (product contracts) vs optional (physical decentralization).
authority_rationale: Major consultancy's long-running, widely followed assessment; conflict of interest noted (Thoughtworks originated data mesh).

title: Architecture and functions in a data mesh (Build a data mesh on Google Cloud, part 1)
subcategory: Cloud reference architecture: data products, domains, roles, governance, interfaces
core_concepts: 'A data product is a logical container or grouping of one or more related data resources'; 'A data resource is a physical asset in a storage system which holds structured data'; Products can be 'a table, view, structured file, topic, or stream', e.g. 'a BigQuery view over a BigQuery table'; reference implementation uses BigQuery authorized views and Pub/Sub topics; Roles: producer teams (product owner, tech lead, product support 'accountable for maintaining product Service Level Agreement (SLA)', domain SME, data owner), consumer teams, central governance team, central data platform team, optional COE; 'limiting autonomy risks creating a bottleneck at the central data platform team'; 'Promoting autonomy of data producers doesn't equate to creating an ungoverned technology landscape'; Governance embedded in platform; stewards codify policies; governance engineers automate checks; Platforms 'are never finished'; fund as ongoing products; pilot with funded use cases and a ready consumer
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: expose products via views/topics not raw tables; central metadata standards for all products; SLA ownership per product; coexistence plan with existing platforms. Reference Terraform 'not intended for production use'.
practical_examples: Authorized BigQuery views as output interfaces; Pub/Sub streams; Knowledge Catalog for discovery.
why_it_matters: Concrete mapping of 'output port' to physical schema objects (authorized view, topic) and of governance roles to who may change a product's schema.
authority_rationale: Official Google Cloud architecture documentation (vendor, but reference architecture rather than marketing).
notes: Original URL https://cloud.google.com/architecture/data-mesh redirected (301) to docs.cloud.google.com. Analytics Hub and Dataplex were not mentioned in the fetched content; data contracts not explicitly discussed.

title: Strategies for building a data mesh-based enterprise solution on AWS (AWS Prescriptive Guidance)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (Dhrubajyoti Mukherjee, Adjoa Taylor, Siva Venkat)
subcategory: Strategy framework, scoping, teams, implementation options
core_concepts: Central lake 'doesn't scale'; 'the data team can't process all requests in time, and it becomes a bottleneck'; Four principles: Domain ownership, Data as a product, Self-service data platform, Federated governance; Data Mesh Strategy Framework phases: Discover, Align, Launch, Scale, Evolve; 'we recommend aligning your strategy with the business value delivered by your organization' rather than tools first; Boundary: 'Ideally, you want to have one data mesh solution that encompasses your entire organization ... consider building a data mesh solution for each commercial brand or each geographic region'; one-way vs two-way door decisions; Launch activities: identify data domains, define domain tenancies, define business and technical metadata of data products, build access-management workflow, data quality and lineage tooling; Implementation options: Amazon DataZone, data.all, AWS Lake Formation
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: scope the mesh to org structure; MVP with lighthouse use cases; define product metadata and access workflows before scaling; treat the platform as never finished.
practical_examples: Central governance account plus member accounts pattern (hands-on DataZone pattern referenced in search results); per-brand or per-region meshes for large enterprises.

authority_rationale: Official AWS Prescriptive Guidance documentation.
notes: Companion page fetched: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-data-mesh/data-mesh-strategy-framework.html. Other pages (teams-interactions, roles-responsibilities, aws-offerings) were returned by WebSearch but not fetched.

title: How JPMorgan Chase built a data mesh architecture to drive significant value to enhance their enterprise data platform
organization_author: Anu Jain, Graham Person, Paul Conroy (JPMorgan Chase) and Nivas Shankar (AWS), AWS Big Data Blog
subcategory: Financial-services case study: product-aligned lakes, share-in-place, mesh catalog
core_concepts: 'Data products are groups of related data from the systems that support our business operations'; Each product has its own physically separated, product-specific data lake, 'catalogued and schematized', managed by data product owners making risk-based decisions; 'Enforces those decisions by sharing data, rather than copying it' (Glue Data Catalog, Lake Formation, Athena); Column-, record- and value-level access control; tokenization enforced in place ('no untokenized copies exist outside the lake'); Mesh catalog that 'doesn't hold any data' tracks which lakes share with which consumers for audit/lineage; Share-not-copy 'reduces storage costs and discrepancies'
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: one governed lake per data product; consumers read in place via catalog grants; lineage captured at the sharing layer; sensitive values tokenized at source.
practical_examples: Firm-wide reporting teams discovering and requesting lake data via the enterprise catalog instead of extracting and joining from multiple systems.
why_it_matters: Large regulated financial institution demonstrating domain-owned analytical schemas with centrally enforced sharing, fine-grained access and lineage - the template for ERP/financial data-product schemas.
authority_rationale: First-party practitioner case study on a major vendor's engineering blog; co-authored by AWS so partially promotional.
notes: No dedicated lessons-learned section; outcomes stated qualitatively. Cross-account mechanics not described in the article.

title: Data Mesh in Practice: How Europe's Leading Online Platform for Fashion Goes Beyond the Data Lake
organization_author: Max Schultze (Zalando) and Arif Wider (ThoughtWorks Germany)
subcategory: Retail case study: ownership, BYOB storage, central governance
core_concepts: Central lake symptoms: 'Lack of ownership', 'Lack of quality', 'Central team becomes the bottleneck'; 'Bring Your Own Bucket (BYOB)': domain-owned storage over a shared metadata layer; Product standards: Discoverable, Addressable, Self-describing, Trustworthy, Interoperable, Secure; 'Decentralized ownership does not imply decentralized infrastructure!'; 'Decentral Ownership' with 'Central Governance'; Data quality as 'A Contract between Consumer and Producer'; producers opt in to storage; classify data usage; Treat data as a product, not a by-product
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: decentralize ownership while keeping common storage, metadata, processing and sharing layers; make quality an explicit producer-consumer contract.
practical_examples: Zalando's shift from a central lake to domain-owned buckets registered in a shared metadata layer; templated data product creation.
why_it_matters: Practitioner evidence that polyglot/decentralized infrastructure is optional while ownership and contracts are the essential schema-governance change; introduces 'contract' language for data quality.
authority_rationale: Conference deck by practitioners (Zalando, Thoughtworks) hosted on SlideShare; informal format, Thoughtworks co-authorship is an interested party.
notes: Event not named on the page; WebSearch results associate the talk with NDC Oslo 2020 and a Databricks-hosted upload. Related Thoughtworks webinar 'Lessons from the trenches in data mesh' was returned by search but not fetched. CONFLICT with ARCH-14/15 emphasis on polyglot domain infrastructure.

title: What Is a Data Fabric?
subcategory: Vendor definition; active metadata; fabric vs mesh
core_concepts: Data fabric 'designed to democratize data access across an organization'; 'It is not a piece of software, but rather a design approach'; Catalogs 'employ active metadata'; 'Federated active metadata ... uses semantic knowledge graphs and AI/ML technologies to continuously analyze metadata' vs 'passive metadata, which is static and manually curated'; ML automates governance enforcement and lineage tracking; Data mesh: 'a decentralized data architecture that organizes data by a specific business domain'; fabrics 'coexist with data meshes, and often enhance their functionality' (automating data product creation and global governance); Lakes/warehouses 'often lack proper metadata management'; data virtualization 'makes data accessible without physically moving it'
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED (vendor view): metadata-driven, AI-automated integration and governance layer over heterogeneous stores; position fabric as complementary tooling for a mesh.
practical_examples: Active-metadata catalogs auto-tagging, profiling and classifying data; virtualization layer instead of ETL.
why_it_matters: Clearest accessible articulation of fabric as technology/metadata automation versus mesh as organizational design; implies every schema must carry rich machine-readable metadata.
authority_rationale: VENDOR MARKETING/educational content from a company selling data-fabric products (IBM Cloud Pak for Data, watsonx.data); informative but not independent.
notes: The page does not itself use the words 'organizational' vs 'technological'; that framing is a summary. No publication date shown.

title: Gartner Report: Are Data Fabric and Data Mesh the Same or Different? (Starburst summary; with Informatica vendor definition and unverified Gartner glossary)
organization_author: Jess Iandiorio (Starburst), summarizing Gartner 'Quick Answer: Are Data Fabric and Data Mesh the Same or Different?' (Ehtisham Zaidi et al., 2021-11-01)
subcategory: Analyst definition (second-hand) and fabric-vs-mesh contrast; vendor framings
core_concepts: Gartner (as excerpted): 'A Data Mesh is a solution architecture for the specific goal of building business-focused data products'; Gartner (as excerpted): 'A Data Fabric is a technology utilization and implementation design capable of multiple outputs and applied uses'; Fabric 'begins initially with the accumulation of passive metadata, then progresses into an active metadata scenario'; Gartner view that the two 'benefit from one another'; Starburst: 'both can co-exist together'; Informatica (vendor): 'A data fabric is a set of services and architecture that deliver reliable capabilities across data environments'; 'Enterprise Knowledge Graph, part of the CLAIRE AI engine, puts data in context'; Gartner glossary wording reported by third parties: 'a design concept that serves as an integrated layer (fabric) of data and connecting processes'
engineering_principles: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: fabric as a metadata-automation design layered over whatever ownership model (mesh or central) is chosen; mesh as a solution architecture for data products. No schema-boundary rules are stated by these sources.

title: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)
subcategory: Data contract specification for data product output schemas
core_concepts: 'A data contract defines the agreement between a data producer and consumers'; 'This standard describes a structure for a data contract'; 'Its current version is v3.2.0'; Sections: Fundamentals, Schema, References, Data quality, Support & communication channels, Pricing, Team, Roles, Service-level agreement (SLA), Infrastructures & servers, Authoritative definitions, Tags, Custom & other properties; 'The contract should be platform agnostic' (YAML format)
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: publish each data product's output schema together with quality rules, SLA, servers/locations, team/roles and authoritative definitions in a machine-readable, platform-agnostic contract.
practical_examples: YAML contract documents with per-section examples; since v3.1.0 each section has its own documentation page.
why_it_matters: The most concrete open specification for what a data product's output port must declare; maps directly onto Dehghani's discoverable/addressable/self-describing/trustworthy/secure attributes and gives a schema framework a standard artifact for analytical sharing.
authority_rationale: Open standard under a Linux Foundation sub-foundation (LF AI & Data), community-governed; younger and less widely adopted than CNCF/LF API specs.

The README's LF AI & Data affiliation appears only in the BibTeX citation block. Neither page mentions data mesh or data products explicitly; the linkage to output ports is an inference. | Also catalogued as DQ-09 in catalog_15_data_quality_lineage.json

title: The Six Primary Dimensions For Data Quality Assessment (DAMA UK whitepaper, 'Defining Data Quality Dimensions')
publication_date: Original October 2013 (per academic citations); dama-uk.org page shows 4 Apr 2025; image filename references 2020

title: Meet the data quality dimensions (UK Government Data Quality Hub)
organization_author: UK Government Data Quality Hub (Office for National Statistics)
core_concepts: accuracy; completeness; uniqueness; consistency; timeliness; validity; fitness for purpose; critical data items
engineering_principles: Validity = expected format, type and range (valid is not necessarily accurate); completeness is about critical vs optional data; no single dimension is sufficient; measure regularly because data changes over time.

title: ISO/IEC 9075-1:2023 Information technology — Database languages SQL — Part 1: Framework (SQL/Framework)
core_concepts: SQL:2023; multi-part standard; Part 1 Framework; Part 2 Foundation; Part 9 SQL/MED; Part 16 SQL/PGQ; JSON data type T801; optional features identified by feature IDs
engineering_principles: Scope per ISO catalogue (search summary): defines the conceptual framework, terms and notation used by the other parts; 2023 edition adds terms/concepts to support new data types required by incremental parts. SQL:2023 parts named: Framework, Foundation, SQL/CLI, SQL/PSM, SQL/MED, SQL/OLB, SQL/Schemata, SQL/JRT, SQL/XML, SQL/PGQ (Part 16).
practical_examples: SQL:2023 new features: JSON type (T801), enhanced JSON (T802), SQL/PGQ graph queries over tables, GREATEST/LEAST (T054), ANY_VALUE (T626), underscores in numeric literals (T662), UNIQUE null treatment (F292).
why_it_matters: The only international standard for the database language itself; precise citations should use part number, edition year and feature ID (e.g., ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 feature T801).
authority_rationale: International standard; BSI is the UK national body mirror of the ISO catalogue entry.
notes: ISO page https://www.iso.org/standard/76583.html returned 403 (search-returned). Part list and feature IDs from Wikipedia SQL:2023 (fetched) citing Eisentraut's 4 Apr 2023 post (URL 404). Part 15 SQL/MDA not confirmed. Paywalled per part. RECOMMENDED where features are standardised.

title: Temporal features in SQL:2011 (SIGMOD Record 41(3), September 2012)
core_concepts: SQL:2011 published December 2011; application-time period tables (valid time); system-versioned tables (transaction time, SYSTEM_TIME); PERIOD FOR as table metadata, no period data type; closed-open periods; PRIMARY KEY ... WITHOUT OVERLAPS; UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF; FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF / FROM..TO / BETWEEN..AND; bitemporal tables
engineering_principles: Periods are defined as named metadata over a pair of conventional datetime columns because adding a PERIOD type would need support across JDBC/ODBC/.NET, ETL and replication; closed-open semantics with implied end>start constraint; system-period columns are GENERATED ALWAYS and set from the transaction timestamp so history cannot be tampered with; at most one application-time and one system-time period per table; default query returns current rows.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE Emp(... PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (Sys_start, Sys_end)) WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING; ALTER TABLE Emp ADD PRIMARY KEY (ENo, EPeriod WITHOUT OVERLAPS); UPDATE Emp FOR PORTION OF EPeriod FROM DATE '2011-02-03' TO DATE '2011-09-10' SET EDept = 4 WHERE ENo = 22217; SELECT ... FROM Emp FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF TIMESTAMP '2011-01-02 00:00:00'.
why_it_matters: Primary account by the standard's authors of how temporal/bitemporal tables are standardised in ISO/IEC 9075-2; directly governs audit-history and effective-dating schema patterns.
authority_rationale: Written by members of the ISO SQL committee and published in ACM SIGMOD Record; the closest open primary source to the paywalled standard.
notes: Text extracted from the fetched PDF with pypdf. Authors note commercial adoption had been slow (one implementation in 2012). RECOMMENDED pattern. | Also catalogued as TEN-18 in catalog_14_tenancy_audit_temporal.json | Also catalogued as LIT-57 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: What's New in SQL:2016 (modern-sql.com)
core_concepts: SQL:2016 released December 2016; SQL/JSON functions in Part 2 SQL/Foundation; JSON_OBJECT/JSON_ARRAY; JSON_EXISTS/JSON_VALUE/JSON_QUERY/JSON_TABLE; IS JSON predicate; SQL/JSON path language; MATCH_RECOGNIZE; polymorphic table functions; LISTAGG; DECFLOAT; ISO/IEC TR 19075-5/-6/-7
engineering_principles: SQL:2016 has no native JSON type; JSON is stored as strings and processed by functions; a JSON type arrived only in ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 (feature T801).
practical_examples: JSON_TABLE to shred JSON documents into relational rows; LISTAGG as ordered-set string aggregation.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that JSON column typing was vendor-specific until 2023, which affects schema portability decisions for semi-structured columns.
authority_rationale: Well-known SQL practitioner closely tracking the ISO standard; not a standards body.
notes: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL for JSON features.

title: ISO/IEC 11179-5:2015 Information technology — Metadata registries (MDR) — Part 5: Naming principles
core_concepts: naming conventions; concept; data element concept; conceptual domain; data element; value domain; principles and rules for developing naming conventions
engineering_principles: Scope per ISO catalogue: provides instruction for naming concepts, data element concepts, conceptual domains, data elements and value domains as defined in ISO/IEC 11179-3; describes naming in metadata registries; gives principles and rules for developing naming conventions and example conventions.
practical_examples: Secondary sources (Wikipedia 'Representation term', DDI Alliance guide, a US state naming standard) describe the associated object-class-term + property-term + representation-term (+ qualifier) convention, e.g., EmployeeAddressText; representation terms (class words) such as Amount, Code, Date, Identifier, Indicator, Name, Text.
why_it_matters: The only international standard directly about naming data elements; a schema framework should cite it as the authority for having a documented naming convention with class words, while presenting the concrete pattern as 'aligned with' rather than 'required by' the standard.
authority_rationale: International standard; IEC webstore shows the official abstract.
notes: 25 pages; webstore showed 'CHF 0.-' (likely display artefact; treat as paywalled). Draft 4th edition: https://www.iso.org/standard/92786.html (search-returned). Abstract does not mention object class/property/representation term. RECOMMENDED (convention), OPTIONAL (specific pattern).

engineering_principles: Defines the information a metadata registry should record as a conceptual data model (search summary of SCC/Genorma listings): Clause 6 core model with reusable basic types and classes; Clauses 7-11 identification, designation/definition, registration, classification, mapping.
practical_examples: Registries built on 11179: NCI caDSR, AIHW METeOR, USHIK, Aristotle Metadata Registry (Wikipedia, fetched).
why_it_matters: Reference model for the metadata/data-dictionary layer of a schema framework (how data elements, value domains and definitions are registered and versioned).
authority_rationale: International standard (ISO catalogue URL returned verbatim by search).

title: ISO/IEC 25012:2008 Software engineering — SQuaRE — Data quality model
core_concepts: 15 data quality characteristics; inherent vs system-dependent quality; accuracy; completeness; consistency; credibility; currentness; accessibility; compliance; confidentiality; traceability; availability
engineering_principles: Scope per ISO catalogue: general data quality model for data retained in a structured format within a computer system; usable to establish DQ requirements, define measures, and plan/perform evaluations (incl. compliance with legislation). Verified definitions (iso25000.com): accuracy = attributes correctly represent the true value (syntactic and semantic); completeness = values for all expected attributes and related entity instances; consistency = free from contradiction and coherent with other data.
practical_examples: Inherent characteristics map to schema constraints and provenance columns; system-dependent ones (availability, recoverability, portability) map to platform controls.
why_it_matters: The international DQ vocabulary against which DAMA/DAMA UK dimensions must be reconciled; cite as ISO/IEC 25012:2008 with 25024 for measures.
authority_rationale: International standard; IEC webstore shows official abstract.
notes: 13 pages, CHF 100. The full 15-item list with inherent/system-dependent mapping was not verifiable from an opened source (paywalled; secondary pages show it only as images). RECOMMENDED. Conflicts with DAMA UK six-dimension vocabulary.

title: ISO/IEC 25024:2015 Systems and software engineering — SQuaRE — Measurement of data quality
core_concepts: quality measures per 25012 characteristic; target entities across data life cycle; no rating ranges or grades; structured data in legacy systems, data warehouses, the web
engineering_principles: Scope per ISO catalogue: basic set of measures for each 25012 characteristic, target entities, guidance on applying measures and on defining organisation-specific measures; explicitly does not define value ranges for grading; excludes knowledge representation, data mining and statistical significance.
practical_examples: Reported annexes (search summary): quality measure elements, alphabetical list of measures, table of measures by characteristic and target entity.
why_it_matters: Gives a standards-based way to express DQ metrics (e.g., completeness ratio of a column) in a schema framework without inventing thresholds.
authority_rationale: International standard; official abstract on IEC webstore.
notes: 45 pages, CHF 181. ISO page https://www.iso.org/standard/35749.html search-returned. RECOMMENDED.

title: ISO 8000-61:2016 Data quality — Part 61: Data quality management: Process reference model
core_concepts: process reference model; purpose/outcomes/activities per process; implementation processes: planning, control, assurance, improvement; data-related support processes; resource provision processes; relationship between DQ management and data governance; process capability / maturity assessment
engineering_principles: Scope per ISO catalogue (search summary): specifies the processes required for data quality management, each defined by purpose, outcomes and activities; covers principles, process structure, lower-level processes, relationship to data governance and implementation requirements; used to assess process capability or organisational maturity.
practical_examples: Applies to structured data in databases and to less structured data (images, audio, video, documents); process groups: Implementation (plan/control/assurance/improvement), Data-Related Support (architecture, transfer, operations, security), Resource Provision (organisation, human resources).
why_it_matters: Standardised process vocabulary for the DQ operating model that sits around a schema (planning, control, assurance, improvement).
authority_rationale: International standard; DIN Media is the German national-body listing.
notes: 21 pages, EUR 154.60 PDF, ICS 25.040.40. DIN page shows no abstract; scope and structure from search summaries (iteh.es DNS failure; ANSI preview 403). OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.

notes: iso.org 403 on fetch; CHF 135; page count disputed between resellers (20 vs 30). OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL.
