engineering_principles: MySQL Repeatable Read transactions cannot safely read a value and then write it; use Serializable or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
practical_examples: Single-node histories with values changing inside one transaction; RDS Multi-AZ anomalies tied to replica commit ordering.
why_it_matters: Shows the default level of a widely used ERP backend needs explicit locking or version checks for read-modify-write.
authority_rationale: Widely recognized independent testing with published histories.
notes: Tested 8.0.34; re-check against 8.4 before relying on it for that release.

title: Jepsen: PostgreSQL 12.3
core_concepts: G2-item; snapshot isolation; serializability bug; strict vs broad ANSI reading
engineering_principles: Even a mature serializable implementation can have bugs, so guarantees should be tested and engines kept patched.
practical_examples: G2-item under serializable caused by conflict detection crediting the wrong transaction ID.
why_it_matters: Confirms Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation and sets a minimum patch expectation for SERIALIZABLE-based designs.
authority_rationale: Widely recognized independent testing; the defect was confirmed by a PostgreSQL developer.
notes: The report describes a patch scheduled for the 2020-08-13 minor release.

title: Jepsen: Consistency Models
core_concepts: strict serializable; linearizable; snapshot isolation; repeatable read; causal; sticky availability
engineering_principles: Snapshot isolation and repeatable read are incomparable; snapshot isolation, cursor stability, sequential and anything stronger are unavailable in asynchronous networks.
practical_examples: Implication map across multi-object and single-object models.
why_it_matters: Lets a framework state what a chosen model costs in availability.
authority_rationale: Widely used practitioner reference grounded in the formal literature.

title: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design: CAP is Only Part of the Story
core_concepts: PACELC; consistency-latency tradeoff; PA/EL; PC/EC; PA/EC; PC/EL
engineering_principles: CAP limits behavior only during failures; the latency-consistency tradeoff shapes normal operation.
practical_examples: Classifies Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as PA/EL; VoltDB/H-Store and Megastore as PC/EC; MongoDB as PA/EC; PNUTS as PC/EL.
why_it_matters: Separates system-of-record choices (PC/EC) from latency-favoring read replicas for analytics.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed magazine article by a leading database researcher that introduced PACELC.
notes: System classifications reflect 2012 defaults and are dated, notably MongoDB. The full PACELC sentence quoted in the notes should be checked against the PDF because extraction was reviewed in a truncated column. | Also catalogued as LIT-22 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed
organization_author: Eric Brewer (IEEE Computer; republished by InfoQ)
core_concepts: 2 of 3 fallacy; partition mode; partition recovery; compensation; CRDTs; ACID vs CAP consistency
engineering_principles: CAP prohibits only perfect availability and consistency during partitions; detect partitions, limit operations, then recover and compensate.
practical_examples: ATM preserving balance >= 0 by capping withdrawals during a partition and fixing violations afterward.
why_it_matters: Shows how to design bounded degraded-mode operations and post-partition audit trails.
authority_rationale: Written by the originator of the CAP conjecture and published by IEEE Computer.
notes: publication_date is the InfoQ republication date; the original appeared in IEEE Computer, February 2012.

title: A Critique of the CAP Theorem
core_concepts: CAP ambiguity; delay-sensitivity; network delay; availability definitions
engineering_principles: CAP's definitions are inconsistent and ambiguous; reason about how operation latency responds to network delay.
practical_examples: Delay-sensitivity framework for comparing consistency guarantees.
why_it_matters: Warns against selecting a database from a CP or AP label alone.
authority_rationale: Preprint by a recognized researcher; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper. | Also catalogued as LIT-23 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: Sagas
organization_author: Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem (ACM SIGMOD 1987)
core_concepts: long-lived transactions; saga; compensating transactions; interleaving; saga recovery
engineering_principles: A long-lived transaction can be a sequence of interleavable transactions that all complete or are amended by compensating transactions.
practical_examples: Airline reservation split into per-seat transactions; bank statements and insurance claims as long-lived transactions.
why_it_matters: Basis for saga state tables and the requirement that each step has a defined compensation.
authority_rationale: Foundational peer-reviewed paper.
notes: Cornell copy used because the ACM DL page returned HTTP 403. OCR quality is poor, so check quotes against the scan.

title: Pattern: Transactional outbox
core_concepts: outbox table; message relay; polling publisher; transaction log tailing; idempotent consumers
engineering_principles: Store messages in the same local transaction as business changes and relay them separately; consumers must tolerate duplicates.
practical_examples: Relay implemented by polling publisher or transaction log tailing.
why_it_matters: Requires an outbox table and consumer de-duplication in place of 2PC.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner pattern catalog by the author of Microservices Patterns.
notes: The page does not specify outbox columns.

title: Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres
core_concepts: idempotency_keys table; atomic phases; recovery points; foreign state mutations; completer; reaper
engineering_principles: Group local work into atomic phases between external calls, record a recovery point, and enforce one key per user with a unique index.
practical_examples: Table with user_id, idempotency_key, locked_at, request_params, response_code, response_body and recovery_point, using SERIALIZABLE phases that map conflicts to 409.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete table shape for safe API retries in financial and SaaS systems.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner with payments-API experience; not official Stripe documentation.
notes: The retention horizon is stated as about 24 hours in one place and about 72 hours in another. | Also catalogued as CASE-34 in catalog_17_case_studies.json

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
core_concepts: TrueTime; external consistency; commit wait; Paxos; two-phase commit; lock-free snapshot transactions
engineering_principles: Exposing clock uncertainty enables external consistency; the authors prefer that programmers handle overuse of transactions rather than code around their absence.
practical_examples: Commit wait until TT.after(s); two-phase commit run over Paxos groups.
why_it_matters: Counterweight to the claim that 2PC is never viable, relevant when choosing a geo-distributed system of record.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed systems paper from the system's builders.
notes: Detailed claims in the notes come from the linked PDF, which is the ACM TOCS 31(3) 2013 version rather than the OSDI text.

title: Evolutionary Database Design
core_concepts: migration scripts; transition phase; developer database instances; DBA collaboration; schema plus data in version control
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: represent every change as a small, version-controlled migration applied by a tool that tracks applied changes. RECOMMENDED: a private database per developer and at least daily integration. Small changes are easier to get right and errors are quicker to find.
practical_examples: Rename a table and keep a view under the old name during the transition phase; a CI server applies migrations to its own database copy and runs the full build.
why_it_matters: Sets the baseline lifecycle for schema change that the rest of the framework refines.
authority_rationale: Written by the originators of the practice and published on a widely recognized engineering site.
notes: Does not present stored procedures as a general encapsulation layer; recommends a clearly separated data access layer.

title: ParallelChange
core_concepts: expand; migrate; contract; backward-incompatible change; transition period
engineering_principles: MANDATORY for incompatible changes under continuous delivery: support old and new versions together, move clients incrementally, then remove the old version. The cost is maintaining two versions and needing discipline to finish.
practical_examples: Most database refactorings follow this pattern; the migrate phase is the transition between the original and new schema.
why_it_matters: Provides the single meta-pattern from which safe DDL sequences can be derived.
authority_rationale: Canonical definition of the pattern on a recognized engineering site.
notes: Credits Joshua Kerievsky with first documenting the technique in 2006.

title: Refactoring Databases: Evolutionary Database Design
organization_author: Scott W. Ambler and Pramod J. Sadalage (Addison-Wesley Professional)
core_concepts: database refactoring; transition period; structural refactorings; data quality refactorings; referential integrity refactorings; architectural refactorings; method refactorings; transformations
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: make small changes that improve design without changing semantics, and support old and new schemas in parallel so application teams can deploy on their own schedule.
practical_examples: Catalog chapters cover structural, data quality, referential integrity, architectural and method refactorings, plus transformations; the companion site is databaserefactoring.com.
why_it_matters: Gives the framework a named vocabulary of schema change types.
authority_rationale: Foundational book by originating authors in the Fowler Signature Series.
notes: Only the publisher page was read, not the book text. ISBN-13 978-0-321-29353-4. | Also catalogued as LIT-71 in catalog_16_literature.json

title: Migration Style Guide
core_concepts: regular migrations; post-deployment migrations; batched background migrations; lock retries; reversibility; time budgets
engineering_principles: MANDATORY at GitLab: no migration may require downtime. Time limits are 3 minutes for regular migrations, 10 minutes for post-deployment migrations and 20 minutes for concurrent index creation; single background migration queries stay under 1 second with cold caches.
practical_examples: with_lock_retries for high-traffic tables, disable_ddl_transaction! for concurrent indexes, add_concurrent_index, explicit index names, bigint for large counters and timezone-aware timestamps.
why_it_matters: Supplies concrete, enforceable budgets and helpers for a schema change policy.
authority_rationale: Internal engineering standard from a major organization operating a large PostgreSQL deployment.
notes: Rules are specific to GitLab's Rails and PostgreSQL stack. Examples reference milestones up to 18.10.

title: Avoiding downtime in migrations
core_concepts: ignore then drop column; concurrent column rename; concurrent type change; integer to bigint conversion; application-first NOT NULL
engineering_principles: MANDATORY at GitLab: spread incompatible changes over several releases so running code never sees a missing structure. Ignoring and dropping a column must not happen in the same release.
practical_examples: ignore_column then remove_column in a post-deployment migration then remove the rule; rename_column_concurrently; change_column_type_concurrently; drop each foreign key before dropping a table.
why_it_matters: Directly supplies safe sequences for the framework's dangerous-operations table.
authority_rationale: Major-organization engineering standard grounded in production operation.
notes: This page defers foreign key and NOT NULL details to separate guides. The NOT NULL guide is cited in the markdown notes.

title: Online migrations at scale
core_concepts: dual writing; backfill; read path change; write path change; production comparison with Scientist
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: migrate in four phases (dual write, change reads, change writes, remove old data), keeping both stores consistent at every step and verifying in production.
practical_examples: Migrated hundreds of millions of Subscriptions objects; backfilled offline from database snapshots with Hadoop and Scalding, then reran the job to confirm nothing was missed.
why_it_matters: Shows how to verify a large data migration without heavy production queries.
authority_rationale: Major-organization engineering blog describing a real production migration.
notes: The article gives no exact record count. | Also catalogued as CASE-22 in catalog_17_case_studies.json

title: Braintree PostgreSQL safe operations redux (gist blog.md)
core_concepts: lock queueing; lock_timeout; NOT VALID then VALIDATE; unique index then USING INDEX; one DDL per transaction; forward and backward compatibility
engineering_principles: MANDATORY at Braintree: hold exclusive locks for about 2 seconds at most, keep code and schema forward- and backward-compatible, and do not revert schema on rollback. A waiting lock queues all later queries on the table.
practical_examples: Add a CHECK constraint NOT VALID then validate instead of a direct NOT NULL; add foreign keys NOT VALID; retry lock acquisition after pausing and checking for long-running queries.
why_it_matters: Explains the lock mechanics behind most PostgreSQL migration incidents.
authority_rationale: Practitioner write-up of a high-volume payments operator's rules.
notes: The page has no formal title; title here is descriptive. Covers PostgreSQL 9.1 to 12, so check rules against current versions. The original 2014 post is at https://pgrs.net/2014/05/14/safe-operations-for-high-volume-postgresql/. The Medium/PayPal URL in the brief returned HTTP 403.

title: strong_migrations README
core_concepts: dangerous operations; safe alternatives; lock timeout; statement timeout; batched backfill
engineering_principles: MANDATORY per the README: set a short lock timeout for migrations. Other checks fail by default and offer an expand-and-contract or concurrent alternative; raw SQL cannot be verified by the tool.
practical_examples: lock_timeout of 10 seconds and statement_timeout of 1 hour; set timeouts with ALTER ROLE under PgBouncer transaction mode; add foreign keys with validate: false then validate separately.
why_it_matters: A ready-made list of operations an automated gate should flag across PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.
authority_rationale: Widely known tool documentation by a well-known practitioner.
notes: Page shows no release version; footer 2026.

title: ALTER TABLE (PostgreSQL 18 documentation)
core_concepts: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE; table rewrite; volatile defaults; NOT VALID; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT; SET NOT NULL scan skip
engineering_principles: Authoritative facts: non-volatile defaults need no rewrite, volatile defaults and most type changes rewrite the table and indexes, validation takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, and a valid CHECK constraint lets SET NOT NULL skip its scan.
practical_examples: ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT.
why_it_matters: Ground truth for classifying PostgreSQL operations as safe or dangerous, by engine version.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY behaviour is on a separate page cited in the markdown notes. Rewriting forms are not MVCC-safe.

title: Versioned migrations (Flyway documentation)
core_concepts: versioned migrations; flyway_schema_history; checksums; unique versions; roll forward
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: migrations apply in order exactly once, and an applied migration is not edited once it reaches a permanent downstream environment; add a new migration and roll forward.
practical_examples: File V001.002__NewTwitterColumn.sql; Flyway Desktop adds a timestamp by default to reduce version conflicts between team members.
why_it_matters: Defines the immutable, ordered migration history model.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a leading migration tool.
notes: Undo caveats (Teams edition; assumes the whole migration succeeded) are at https://documentation.red-gate.com/fd/undo-migrations-273973334.html. The page does not state what happens on a checksum mismatch.

title: Using Liquibase Rollback
core_concepts: rollback by tag; rollback-to-date; rollback-count; update-testing-rollback; future-rollback-sql
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: test rollback scripts like application code using a deploy, roll back, redeploy cycle. Structural changes combined with data migration are harder to roll back.
practical_examples: update-testing-rollback in CI; future-rollback-sql so auditors can confirm every change has a rollback.
why_it_matters: Represents the pro-rollback position in the down-migration controversy.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a leading migration tool.
notes: Some commands are Liquibase Secure only. Automatic rollback coverage is at https://docs.liquibase.com/workflows/liquibase-community/automatic-custom-rollbacks.html.

title: Auto Generating Migrations (Alembic documentation)
core_concepts: autogenerate; candidate migrations; rename blindness; named constraints; compare_type; compare_server_default
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: manually review and correct every candidate migration, since autogenerate is not intended to be perfect. Name constraints explicitly so they can be tracked.
practical_examples: Table and column renames appear as add and drop pairs and must be hand-edited into a rename.
why_it_matters: Evidence for requiring human review of ORM-generated DDL.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of the standard SQLAlchemy migration tool.
notes: CHECK constraint detection is name-based only and off by default.

title: Atlas migration lint analyzers
core_concepts: destructive changes; data-dependent changes; backward-incompatible changes; concurrent index policy; blocking changes; naming rules
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: analyze migration files in CI against coded rule families for destructive, data-dependent, incompatible, blocking and naming violations.
practical_examples: DS102 table dropped, MF104 nullable to non-nullable, BC102 column rename, PG101 missing CONCURRENTLY, NM101 to NM106 naming conventions.
why_it_matters: A rule taxonomy the framework's automated validator can adopt.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a reputable schema tool.
notes: Many PostgreSQL and MySQL analyzers require Atlas Pro. Declarative vs versioned concepts are at https://atlasgo.io/concepts/declarative-vs-versioned. | Also catalogued as THIN-19 in catalog_20_thin_areas.json

title: Introduction to DevOps Database Delivery
core_concepts: state-based deployment; migration-based deployment; hybrid approaches; data context of changes
engineering_principles: OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: neither approach is ideal. State-based deployment scripts do not understand the data context of a change, while migration-based scripts accumulate and must run in order.
practical_examples: A state-based table rename drops and recreates the table without preserving data unless extra scripts are written; a team may start state-based and move to migrations once the database stabilizes.
why_it_matters: Frames the main authoring trade-off for the framework.
authority_rationale: Vendor practitioner article; the vendor sells tools for both approaches.
notes: Replaces the Redgate approaches page, which now only states SQL Change Automation is retired from sale.

title: Database change management (DORA capability)
core_concepts: database changes in version control; migration tooling; DBA collaboration; zero-downtime techniques; production-like testing; delivery metrics
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: keep changes as scripts in version control, apply them with tooling and test them on a production-like, scrubbed data set. The stated goal is 100% of database changes through a fully automated process.
practical_examples: Measure the share of failed changes involving the database, added lead time, downtime cost and the automated share of changes.
why_it_matters: Links database practice to delivery performance and supplies metrics.
authority_rationale: Summary from a major research program; the page itself is guidance rather than a peer-reviewed paper.
notes: resource_type is the closest enum value; this is a capability summary. Accelerate (2018) was not opened.

title: Squawk Rules Overview
core_concepts: migration linter; blocking statements; type hygiene; NOT VALID enforcement; concurrent index enforcement
engineering_principles: RECOMMENDED: lint PostgreSQL migrations in CI for statements that could block reads or writes.
practical_examples: Rules include require-concurrent-index-creation, constraint-missing-not-valid, prefer-bigint-over-int, prefer-timestamptz, ban-drop-column and renaming-column.
why_it_matters: Low-cost automated gate for the dangerous operations list, plus type checks.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a specialist open-source linter.
notes: The overview page lists rule names only; descriptions are on individual rule pages not opened. | Also catalogued as THIN-17 in catalog_20_thin_areas.json

title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
core_concepts: MTD; RTO; RPO; business impact analysis; seven-step process; full, incremental and differential backups; alternate sites
engineering_principles: MANDATORY for federal systems and used here as the reference vocabulary: derive MTD, RTO and RPO from the BIA, keep RTO shorter than MTD, test backups regularly and store encryption keys separately from backups.
practical_examples: Offsite vendor criteria cover geographic area, accessibility, security, environment and cost; alternate sites are cold, warm, hot, mobile or mirrored.
why_it_matters: Provides the formal definitions for recovery objectives.
authority_rationale: Published by a national standards body.
notes: A US federal guideline; international_standard is the closest enum value. Text was extracted locally from the downloaded PDF. Landing page: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/34/r1/upd1/final.

title: Back up and Restore of SQL Server Databases
core_concepts: full, differential and log backups; recovery models; restore testing; backup checksums; separate storage; untrusted backup risk
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: testing is required; a backup strategy does not exist until backups are restored in every planned combination and checked for physical consistency. Store backups separately, encrypt them and use least privilege.
practical_examples: Restore to a test system and run DBCC CHECKDB; use BACKUP CHECKSUM and RESTORE VERIFYONLY; document procedures in a run book.
why_it_matters: Strongest vendor statement of the restore-testing rule.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Warns that restoring a .bak file from an untrusted source can compromise the instance.

title: Oracle Database 19c Backup and Recovery User's Guide: Introduction
core_concepts: RMAN; physical backups; logical backups; Flashback; fast recovery area; user error
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: physical backups are the foundation; logical backups supplement them but are not sufficient alone. RMAN is the preferred tool.
practical_examples: Use Oracle Flashback Table to return tables to an earlier time without taking the database offline; Flashback Database requires a fast recovery area.
why_it_matters: Clear vendor position in the logical versus physical backup debate.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Data Guard is covered on a separate page cited in the markdown notes.

title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS whitepaper)
core_concepts: backup and restore; pilot light; warm standby; multi-site active/active; replication versus backup; data plane failover
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: test backups and keep point-in-time backups alongside replication, since replication may not protect against corruption or malicious deletion. OPTIONAL/CONTEXTUAL: choose the tier by RTO, RPO and cost.
practical_examples: Copy backups across accounts and Regions with AWS Backup; schedule periodic automated restores; redeploy infrastructure with IaC.
why_it_matters: Gives the DR tier model and explicit support for the rule that replication is not backup.
authority_rationale: Official vendor whitepaper.
notes: RPO and RTO ranges per tier were in a figure and were not captured.

title: #StopRansomware Guide
core_concepts: offline encrypted backups; restore testing; golden images; immutable storage caveats
engineering_principles: MANDATORY: keep offline, encrypted backups of critical data and regularly test their availability and integrity, because many ransomware variants seek out and delete or encrypt accessible backups.
practical_examples: Maintain golden images and version-controlled IaC templates offline; restore from offline backups in order of critical services.
why_it_matters: Adds the attacker model that reachable backups are not safe backups.
authority_rationale: Joint guidance from US government security agencies.
notes: Does not mention the 3-2-1 rule or specify backup retention periods; 3-2-1 is sourced in the markdown notes from the CISA Data Backup Options PDF.

title: Platform Multitenant Architecture (Salesforce Architects)
core_concepts: metadata-driven kernel; MT_Objects / MT_Fields metadata tables; MT_Data with flex value columns; pivot tables for indexes, uniqueness, relationships; OrgID on every row; physical partitioning by OrgID; metadata caching
engineering_principles: Objects and fields are metadata rows, not physical tables; all tenant data lives in shared generic tables keyed by OrgID and partitioned by OrgID; indexes/uniqueness/relationships are implemented through pivot tables; this enables online schema change per tenant without affecting others.
practical_examples: MT_Data value columns storing all field types as strings; MT_Indexes / MT_Unique_Indexes / MT_Relationships pivot tables.
why_it_matters: Reference design for extreme pooled multi-tenancy with per-tenant customization, showing the cost (polymorphic storage, pivot indexes) of avoiding per-tenant schema.
authority_rationale: Official Salesforce architecture documentation.
notes: The legacy developer.salesforce.com/wiki/multi_tenant_architecture URL returned HTTP 403. | Also catalogued as CASE-41 in catalog_17_case_studies.json

title: Organizations and organizational hierarchies overview (Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations)
core_concepts: legal entity; company and DataAreaId; operating units; organizational hierarchies with purposes; shared master data (party, address book, products); establishments (10.0.48+); immutable storage on invoices
engineering_principles: A company is the only creatable legal entity type and is bound to a DataAreaId used as the data-security boundary (users see only their current company); hierarchies of legal entities serve tax/statutory reporting; shared master data cannot be overridden per organization; operating units cannot be deleted once in a hierarchy.
practical_examples: Cost center, business unit, value stream, department, retail channel operating-unit types; establishment hierarchy purpose for invoice registration IDs.
why_it_matters: Shows company_id as both posting boundary and security boundary, and master data as tenant-wide — the key ERP multi-company schema rule.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft product documentation.

title: Subsidiaries in OneWorld (NetSuite Help Center)
core_concepts: subsidiary tree rolling up to a root; each subsidiary a separate legal entity; country determines edition and tax nexus; transactions post to a single subsidiary except intercompany; elimination subsidiaries and elimination journal entries; 250-subsidiary limit
engineering_principles: Model companies as a hierarchy; every transaction posts to exactly one subsidiary unless intercompany; intercompany revenue/expenses must be eliminated at consolidation via dedicated elimination entities.
practical_examples: Intercompany sales/purchases, inventory transfers, cross-subsidiary fulfillment, advanced intercompany journal entries.
why_it_matters: Authoritative statement of posting-boundary and elimination-entity patterns for consolidated reporting.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle NetSuite documentation.

title: Odoo 18.0 Documentation: Companies
core_concepts: company as independent business entity; branches as subdivisions; shared products/contacts with optional company restriction; entity-scoped records; parent cannot become branch; reports for parent alone or with branches
engineering_principles: Independent subsidiaries are separate companies, not branches; records linked to an entity are visible only within it; master data shared by default but restrictable; structure must be planned up front because conversions are irreversible.
practical_examples: Quotations/invoices scoped to the active company or branch; user access limited to a branch.
why_it_matters: Open-source ERP confirmation of the company/branch split and shared-vs-scoped master data rule.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation, but user-guide level rather than architectural specification.
notes: Inter-company transaction and consolidation pages were not fetched.

title: PostgreSQL Wiki: Audit trigger 91plus
organization_author: PostgreSQL community wiki (Craig Ringer et al.)
core_concepts: audit.logged_actions table; hstore row_data and changed_fields; statement vs row level auditing; session user, transaction id, client address, application_name; excluded columns; limitations: no SELECT/DDL auditing, superuser tampering
engineering_principles: Capture change type, actor, timestamps (transaction/statement/clock), statement text and before/changed values in the same transaction; run the app as a non-superuser, non-owner role with minimal rights on the audit schema; use IS DISTINCT FROM in WHEN clauses; store timestamps with time zone.
practical_examples: SELECT audit.audit_table('target_table', audit_rows, audit_query_text, excluded_cols); changes by owners/superusers 'can be trivially tampered with'.
why_it_matters: The reference implementation of generic trigger-based auditing in PostgreSQL and its honest limitation list.
authority_rationale: Widely cited community reference, not official docs; last edited 2017.

title: Ledger overview (SQL Server 2022+ / Azure SQL)
core_concepts: updatable ledger tables (system-versioned + history); append-only ledger tables; ledger view; SHA-256 Merkle tree blocks / hash chain; database digests in immutable storage; ledger verification; protection against DBAs (detection, not prevention)
engineering_principles: Hash all modified rows per transaction into blocks chained to prior blocks; publish digests to tamper-proof storage (immutable blob, Confidential Ledger, WORM); verification recomputes hashes and reports inconsistencies; append-only tables block UPDATE/DELETE at the API; ledger cannot prevent file-level tampering but guarantees detection.
practical_examples: Updatable ledger table for system-of-record apps; append-only ledger table for SIEM; ledger database where every table is a ledger table.
why_it_matters: The main relational-database answer to cryptographic audit attestation after QLDB's retirement.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft documentation.

title: Hibernate Envers
core_concepts: @Audited; revisions per transaction; audit tables; revision entity with timestamp/custom attributes; AuditReader historical snapshots
engineering_principles: A revision identifies the full set of changes to audited entity fields in one transaction; audit tables are generated from mappings; history is queried as entity state at a revision or revisions in a date range.
practical_examples: @Audited fields on a Person entity; AuditReader queries for entity at revision.
why_it_matters: Representative ORM-level auditing that captures application context the database cannot see.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of a widely used ORM extension (7.4 latest stable).
notes: The user guide's Envers chapter (ValidityAuditStrategy REVEND details) was not reachable within fetched offsets.

title: AWS to Kill Amazon QLDB (end of support July 31, 2025)
core_concepts: QLDB end of support 2025-07-31; migration to Aurora PostgreSQL; pgAudit, S3 and Database Activity Streams as substitutes; no native immutable journal in Aurora PostgreSQL
engineering_principles: Per AWS's Dan Blaner (quoted): Aurora PostgreSQL does not keep a permanent, immutable record of changes; history must be generated as audit data and stored outside the database.
practical_examples: Two-phase migration (full load then ongoing replication) using S3, Step Functions, Glue and DMS.
why_it_matters: Establishes that QLDB is retired and that immutability in mainstream relational engines must be built (hash chain + external digest storage).
authority_rationale: Reputable technology news outlet quoting AWS staff; official AWS QLDB pages returned 404 / could not be fetched.
notes: Secondary source; the AWS developer-guide 'what-is' page is gone (HTTP 404) and the AWS blog fetch was rate-limited then redirected.

title: 21 CFR 11.10 Controls for closed systems (FDA electronic records; LII e-CFR mirror)
organization_author: U.S. FDA (regulation), Cornell Legal Information Institute (host)
core_concepts: secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails; record changes shall not obscure previously recorded information; audit trail retained as long as the record; protection of records for retrieval; limiting system access
engineering_principles: Audit trails must independently record date/time of operator entries and actions that create, modify or delete electronic records; prior values must remain visible; retention of the audit trail equals retention of the record; access limited to authorized individuals.
practical_examples: Applies to pharma/medical-device electronic records; drives history tables or system-versioning plus retention policies.
why_it_matters: The clearest statutory statement of what a mandatory audit trail must do, usable as a MANDATORY baseline for regulated systems.
authority_rationale: U.S. federal regulation text (hosted by LII; ecfr.gov fetch was rate-limited).

title: MariaDB Server: System-Versioned Tables
core_concepts: WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING; ROW_START/ROW_END pseudo-columns; FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF / BETWEEN / FROM TO / ALL; PARTITION BY SYSTEM_TIME; WITHOUT SYSTEM VERSIONING per column; DELETE HISTORY privilege; transaction-precise versioning; dump-history
engineering_principles: Store the history of all changes; partition history away from current data for performance and retention; exclude volatile columns from versioning; history removal is a privileged operation; TRUNCATE is blocked.
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE t (...) WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING PARTITION BY SYSTEM_TIME INTERVAL 1 MONTH; DELETE HISTORY FROM t BEFORE SYSTEM_TIME '...'.
why_it_matters: Shows retention-oriented extensions (history partitions, DELETE HISTORY) absent from the standard.
authority_rationale: Official MariaDB documentation.
notes: Old mariadb.com/kb URL redirected to the new docs structure.

title: Controlling the Validity and Visibility of Data in Oracle Database (Temporal Validity) and Using Oracle Flashback Technology
core_concepts: Temporal Validity (PERIOD FOR valid-time columns); DBMS_FLASHBACK_ARCHIVE.ENABLE_AT_VALID_TIME CURRENT/ALL/ASOF; AS OF PERIOD FOR queries; Flashback Time Travel / Flashback Data Archive with RETENTION; AS OF TIMESTAMP, VERSIONS BETWEEN; valid time vs transaction time
engineering_principles: Valid time is user-controlled and transaction time is system-managed; valid-time periods are two datetime columns declared via PERIOD FOR; Flashback Archive tracks transactional changes for the table's lifetime for compliance and audit with a retention period and supports digital shredding; Temporal Validity unsupported in CDB (12.2).
practical_examples: CREATE TABLE employees_temp (..., PERIOD FOR emp_track_time); CREATE FLASHBACK ARCHIVE DEFAULT fla1 TABLESPACE tbs1 QUOTA 10G RETENTION 5 YEAR; ALTER TABLE inventory FLASHBACK ARCHIVE.
why_it_matters: Oracle is the only fetched vendor offering both temporal dimensions natively, illustrating bitemporal capability and retention-bounded history.
authority_rationale: Official Oracle documentation (12.2 VLDB Guide; 19c Development Guide).
notes: Second page fetched: https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/adfns/flashback.html (Flashback Time Travel).

title: Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL
core_concepts: valid time vs transaction time; bitemporal tables; valid-time state tables; closed-closed vs closed-open periods; current / sequenced / nonsequenced statements; temporal keys and referential integrity; tracking logs; temporal partitioning and vacuuming
engineering_principles: Valid time captures the history of a changing reality and transaction time the sequence of table states; they are orthogonal; the preferred period representation is a closed-open pair of datetimes; sequenced queries are the most useful yet unsupported by SQL-92, so applications must implement them manually.
practical_examples: Bitemporal LOT table with FROM/TO (valid) and START/STOP (transaction) dates; chapters on modifying state tables and bitemporal tables.
why_it_matters: Foundational text behind SQL:2011's model; defines the vocabulary and the closed-open convention the framework should use.
authority_rationale: Recognized book by the originating researcher; free PDF hosted by the author's university.
notes: Copyright page reads 2000 (ISBN 1-55860-436-7); the book's own text anticipates a 1999 copyright date and it is commonly cited as 1999. PDF text extracted locally with pymupdf.

title: Kimball Group: Design Tip #152 Slowly Changing Dimension Types 0, 4, 5, 6 and 7; Type 2: Add New Row
core_concepts: SCD Type 0 retain original; Type 1 overwrite; Type 2 add row with effective/expiration dates and current indicator; Type 3 add column; Type 4 mini-dimension; Type 5/6/7 hybrids; surrogate keys
engineering_principles: Type 2 requires a new surrogate key per version and at least three extra columns (row effective date, row expiration date, current row indicator); Type 4 moves volatile attributes to a mini-dimension with its own surrogate key; Type 7 keeps dual foreign keys (durable key for current, surrogate for historical).
practical_examples: Fact table carrying both base-dimension and mini-dimension keys (Type 4/5); Type 6 row with current-value column overwritten as Type 1.
why_it_matters: The analytical-side equivalent of application-time state tables; SQL Server lists SCD maintenance as a temporal-table use case.
authority_rationale: Originating authors' site for the dimensional-modeling canon.
notes: Type 2 definition fetched from https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/type-2/ (n.d.).

title: Reference: Out of Order Changes and Effective Dating (Workday Administrator Guide)
core_concepts: effective date vs entry date; out-of-order (backdated) changes; later-effective edits overwrite backdated ones; future effective dates
engineering_principles: Changes are applied by effective date, not entry order; a backdated change applies only until the next already-existing effective-dated version, which overwrites it; users must re-enter later-effective versions to carry a change forward.
practical_examples: Salary plan edited 2000-01-01, 2021-12-01, then backdated to 2010-05-01: the 2010 change is superseded on 2021-12-01.
why_it_matters: Documents real ERP application-time semantics that differ from SQL:2011 FOR PORTION OF splitting; a framework must specify its merge rule.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.

title: Debezium Documentation: Features and FAQ
core_concepts: log-based CDC; captures all changes including deletes; no data model changes required; initial and incremental snapshots; at-least-once after crash; self-describing events and schema registry; source load
engineering_principles: Read committed row-level changes from the transaction log; avoid polling and 'last updated' columns; expect duplicates after connector crashes and design idempotent consumers; events carry schema so downstream can survive upstream schema change.
practical_examples: Kafka Connect source connectors; Debezium Server to Kinesis/Pub/Sub; embedded engine.
why_it_matters: Defines the CDC model and its schema prerequisites and delivery semantics.
authority_rationale: Official documentation of the leading open-source CDC platform (3.7).
notes: FAQ also fetched: https://debezium.io/documentation/faq/ (delivery semantics, schema evolution).

title: Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern
core_concepts: dual-write problem; outbox table in same transaction; CDC relays outbox rows; columns id/aggregatetype/aggregateid/type/payload; insert-then-delete; at-least-once delivery; consumer de-duplication
engineering_principles: Write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business change; let log-based CDC publish it; use aggregateid as message key for ordering and id for idempotent consumption; avoid XA.
practical_examples: Order service inserting OrderCreated into outbox; consumer message-log table of processed UUIDs.
why_it_matters: Prescribes the schema artefact (outbox table) that makes CDC-based eventing transactional.
authority_rationale: Engineering blog of the Debezium project lead at Red Hat.

title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: Logical Decoding Concepts and Publications (replica identity)
core_concepts: logical decoding from WAL; replication slots (crash-safe, retain WAL); output plugins; replica identity required for UPDATE/DELETE; primary key default; REPLICA IDENTITY FULL fallback; error on publisher without identity
engineering_principles: A published table needs a replica identity (PK by default) or UPDATE/DELETE fail; FULL is an inefficient fallback; slots emit each change once normally but may resend after crash; unused slots must be dropped to avoid WAL bloat and wraparound.
practical_examples: ALTER TABLE orders REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; wal_level = logical; one receiver per slot.
why_it_matters: Grounds the 'CDC requires primary keys' schema rule in the engine's own documentation.
authority_rationale: Official PostgreSQL manual.
notes: Also fetched https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding-explanation.html (slots, WAL retention caution).

title: Track Data Changes (Change Data Capture and Change Tracking) - SQL Server
core_concepts: change data capture (asynchronous, log-based, historical data); change tracking (synchronous, which rows changed); no schema changes required; built-in cleanup; commit-order based; critique of trigger/timestamp solutions
engineering_principles: Built-in tracking avoids custom triggers/timestamp columns that add schema changes and overhead and mis-order long-running transactions; CDC stores change history in change tables; Change Tracking stores only row identity and is cheaper.
practical_examples: sys.sp_cdc_enable_db / sys.sp_cdc_enable_table; KEEP_CDC on restore; Sync Services for ADO.NET with change tracking.
why_it_matters: Vendor confirmation that log-based CDC is preferred over trigger/timestamp polling and of the storage trade-off between history and change-only tracking.
authority_rationale: Official Microsoft documentation.

title: Soft Deletion Probably Isn't Worth It; Easy, alternative soft deletion: deleted_record_insert
subcategory: soft delete critique and deleted_record alternative
core_concepts: deleted_at costs: query filtering, broken foreign keys, hard pruning; undelete rarely used; GDPR retention pressure; deleted_record table with jsonb data; AFTER DELETE trigger deleted_record_insert(); simple time-based purge
engineering_principles: Prefer hard delete plus an archive of deleted rows as JSONB in a separate table (via CTE or generic trigger) over a deleted_at flag; keeps live queries clean, preserves FK integrity and makes regulatory purge a single DELETE; trade-off is harder restoration.
practical_examples: deleted_record(id, data jsonb, deleted_at, object_id, table_name, updated_at); DELETE FROM deleted_record WHERE deleted_at < now() - '1 year'::interval.
why_it_matters: The most-cited practitioner argument shaping modern soft-delete guidance; gives a concrete alternative schema.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner (ex-Heroku, ex-Stripe) personal blog.
notes: Follow-up fragment also fetched: https://brandur.org/fragments/deleted-record-insert (2022-12-28).

title: GitLab Development Documentation: Data deletion guidelines
subcategory: mark for deletion vs hard delete
core_concepts: mark for deletion (preferred); hard deletion; avoid direct DestroyService calls; MarkForDeletionService
engineering_principles: Mark aggregates (projects/groups) for deletion at a future date rather than hard deleting immediately, to minimize accidental data loss.
practical_examples: Projects::MarkForDeletionService.new(project, current_user).execute instead of Projects::DestroyService.
why_it_matters: Counterpoint to the anti-soft-delete position: aggregate-level deferred deletion as an organisational guideline.
authority_rationale: Official engineering handbook of a major open-source organisation.
notes: No column naming or retention-period guidance on the page.

title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: Sequence Manipulation Functions (gaps in sequences)
core_concepts: nextval values not reclaimed on abort; gaps from aborts, crashes, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT; setval non-transactional; sequences cannot provide gapless numbering
engineering_principles: Sequences trade gaplessness for concurrency; gapless legal numbering requires a different mechanism (e.g., a locked counter row assigned at posting time).
practical_examples: BEGIN; SELECT nextval('s'); ROLLBACK; -- value is consumed and never reused.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the 'PostgreSQL sequences are not gapless' requirement for invoice/document numbering.
authority_rationale: Official PostgreSQL manual.

title: GDPR Article 17 (Right to erasure) and Article 30 (Records of processing activities)
organization_author: European Union (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), hosted by gdpr-info.eu (Intersoft Consulting)
core_concepts: erasure without undue delay; exceptions: legal obligation, public interest, legal claims; records of processing; envisaged time limits for erasure; security measures description; 250-employee exemption
engineering_principles: Personal data must be erasable on request unless retention is legally required or needed for legal claims; controllers must document per data category the planned erasure time limits — implying a retention-basis attribute per record class.
practical_examples: Retention schedule table mapping data categories to legal basis and erasure deadline; erasure workflow with legal-obligation exceptions.
why_it_matters: Sets the erasure ceiling that must be reconciled with audit/ledger immutability and statutory retention floors.
authority_rationale: Verbatim regulation text on a widely used unofficial mirror; EUR-Lex official text not fetched.
notes: Art. 30 fetched at https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/.

title: Managing the lifecycle of objects (Amazon S3 Lifecycle)
core_concepts: transition actions to cheaper storage classes; expiration actions; regulatory compliance period expiry; rules apply to existing and new objects; bucket policy cannot block lifecycle actions
engineering_principles: Encode retention as declarative rules: hot for N days, infrequent access, archive (Glacier), then expire after the compliance period.
practical_examples: Transition to Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier Flexible Retrieval after one year, expire after retention period.
why_it_matters: Analytical/archive-side counterpart to partition-based retention for exported history, backups and audit logs.
authority_rationale: Official AWS documentation.

title: 18 U.S. Code 1520 - Destruction of corporate audit records (Sarbanes-Oxley s.802)
organization_author: U.S. Congress (Pub. L. 107-204), hosted by Cornell LII
core_concepts: 5-year retention of audit/review workpapers; SEC rulemaking on retention of relevant records
engineering_principles: Audit workpapers must be kept 5 years from the end of the fiscal period of the audit; related SEC rules extend retention (not verified here).
practical_examples: Retention class 'audit workpapers' with 5-year floor.
why_it_matters: Statutory retention floor commonly cited for financial systems; shows retention must be class-specific.
authority_rationale: U.S. statute text.
notes: The 7-year figure often quoted for SOX comes from SEC Rule 2-06, which was not fetched.

title: 45 CFR 164.316 - Policies and procedures and documentation requirements (HIPAA Security Rule)
organization_author: U.S. HHS (regulation), hosted by Cornell LII
core_concepts: 6-year documentation retention; written (electronic) policies and procedures; record of required actions and assessments
engineering_principles: Retain required documentation 6 years from creation or from when last in effect, whichever is later.
practical_examples: Retention class 'HIPAA security documentation' with 6-year floor.
why_it_matters: Healthcare retention floor to encode in retention schedules.
authority_rationale: U.S. federal regulation text.

title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 10.5.1 (audit log retention) - third-party transcription
organization_author: WithPCI (third party); underlying standard by PCI Security Standards Council
core_concepts: retain audit log history at least 12 months; most recent three months immediately available for analysis; testing procedures 10.5.1.a-c
engineering_principles: Audit logs need a 12-month retention floor with 3 months online/searchable; archive older logs with retrievability.
practical_examples: Tiered log storage: 3 months hot, remainder archived (e.g., S3 lifecycle to Glacier).
why_it_matters: Payment-card retention floor for audit logs.
authority_rationale: Third-party transcription; official PCI SSC document library not fetched (requires license acceptance).
notes: Verify wording against the official PCI DSS v4.0.1 document before relying on it.

title: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Article 226 - Content of invoices (sequential number)
organization_author: Council of the European Union; UK National Archives legislation.gov.uk (archived EU text)
core_concepts: date of issue; sequential number based on one or more series uniquely identifying the invoice; closed list of mandatory invoice details
engineering_principles: Invoice numbers must be sequential within one or more series and unique; implies per-series counters assigned at issue and never reused.
practical_examples: Series per company/year with sequential counter; corrective invoices referencing the original number (2025/516 amendment, effective 2030-07-01 per search summary).
why_it_matters: Legal basis for gapless/sequential document numbering in EU ERP schemas.
authority_rationale: Official legislation text (UK-archived version as amended by 2010/45/EU; no amendments applied after 2020-12-31).
notes: EUR-Lex consolidated text not fetched; UK copy is frozen at IP completion day.

title: Patterns for Accounting (Accounting Narrative)
core_concepts: Account; Accounting Entry; Accounting Transaction; Retroactive Event; Replacement / Reversal / Difference Adjustment; event sourcing link
engineering_principles: Balance is derived as the sum of entries; transactions link the entries of a transfer; corrections should be modelled as adjustments — reversal and difference adjustments preserve history while replacement deletes it.
practical_examples: Posting an opposite entry to cancel an incorrect transaction, then posting the correct one.
why_it_matters: Classic pattern language for ledger schemas and the taxonomy of correction strategies.
authority_rationale: Recognized author; page is an acknowledged first draft (2006).
notes: The suggested PDF (martinfowler.com/apsupp/accounting.pdf) was not fetched; the HTML narrative was used.

title: Modern Treasury Ledgers: Ledgers Guarantees and Guide to Ledger Objects
core_concepts: credits equal debits per currency per ledger; balance = sum of entries; transactions archived not deleted; posted entries immutable; idempotency keys; lock_version; atomic multi-entry writes; ledger isolation; Read Committed plus locking
engineering_principles: Enforce zero-sum per currency, forbid deletion (archive instead), make posted transactions immutable, support idempotent creation, version account balances so contributing entries are auditable, write all entries atomically, and lock for serial writes when a transaction depends on a balance.
practical_examples: Ledger transaction composed of at least two ledger entries, each updating one ledger account; account categories aggregate accounts.
why_it_matters: Explicit, product-grade list of ledger invariants suitable for direct translation into constraints and posting logic.
authority_rationale: Official product documentation of a widely used ledger API provider.
notes: Objects page also fetched: https://docs.moderntreasury.com/ledgers/docs/guide-to-ledger-objects.

title: Books: an immutable double-entry accounting database service
core_concepts: books / journal_entries / book_entries tables; journal entries must balance to 0; insert-only tables; corrections via new entries; per-book version counter and cached balances; shelves for multitenancy; Cloud Spanner
engineering_principles: Only the balance row is mutable; all entries are inserts; every journal entry nets to zero; mistakes are corrected with new entries, yielding an inherent audit log and consistency.
practical_examples: Payout splitting across books; namespaced secondary indexes by shelf ID.
why_it_matters: Concrete relational schema for an immutable ledger at scale, including tenancy scoping.
authority_rationale: Major-organisation engineering blog.
notes: Also catalogued as CASE-29 in catalog_17_case_studies.json

title: Ledger: Stripe's system for tracking and validating money movement
core_concepts: immutable auditable log; double-entry bookkeeping; accounts and events; clearing accounts net to zero; imbalance as detectable data-quality signal; replay to rebuild state; 5 billion events/day
engineering_principles: Transactions once published cannot be deleted or modified; corrections revert and reprocess; clearing accounts that should net to zero expose missing/late/incorrect transactions; completeness and timeliness tracked as DQ metrics.
practical_examples: charge.creation / charge.release events moving funds between typed accounts; 99.99% of dollar volume verified within four days.
why_it_matters: Shows how ledger invariants double as reconciliation/data-quality controls at scale.
authority_rationale: Major-organisation engineering blog.
notes: stripe.com URL redirected to stripe.dev. | Also catalogued as CASE-28 in catalog_17_case_studies.json

title: Accounting for Computer Scientists
core_concepts: accounts as nodes, transactions as edges; sum of all balances is zero; balance determined by flows; balancing the books as sanity check
engineering_principles: Model money movement as a directed graph; each transaction touches exactly two accounts with equal and opposite effect; balances are derived; partition sums must offset.
practical_examples: Edge labelled with amount from one account to another; checking that any node partition's balances sum to zero.
why_it_matters: Intuitive derivation of the zero-sum invariant that ledger schemas must enforce.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner/author personal blog.

title: ActiveRecord::Timestamp (Ruby on Rails 8.1 API)
core_concepts: created_at/created_on and updated_at/updated_on auto-managed; record_timestamps setting; UTC default
engineering_principles: Frameworks automatically populate creation/update timestamps when the conventional columns exist; store in UTC.
practical_examples: config.active_record.record_timestamps = false; config.active_record.default_timezone = :local.
why_it_matters: Evidence that created_at/updated_at are a framework-enforced convention (who prescribes audit columns).
authority_rationale: Official API documentation of a major web framework.
notes: django-simple-history docs (https://django-simple-history.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, 3.13.0 2026-07-22) also fetched as an ORM-level history example.

title: GX Core overview (Great Expectations 1.x)
core_concepts: Data Context; Data Source / Data Asset / Batch Definition; Expectation (verifiable assertion about data); Expectation Suite; Validation Definition; Checkpoint; Actions (alerting); Data Docs
engineering_principles: Describe data with declarative, verifiable Expectations grouped into Suites; bind a Suite to a Batch Definition via a Validation Definition; run Validation Definitions in production through Checkpoints that trigger Actions; publish results as human-readable Data Docs. Workflows are programmatically defined in Python even though Expectations themselves form a declarative language.
practical_examples: Component chain Data Context -> Data Source -> Data Asset -> Batch Definition -> Expectation Suite -> Validation Definition -> Checkpoint -> Actions/Data Docs; the page shows version 1.24.1 of the 1.x line.
why_it_matters: Gives a schema framework a vocabulary for post-load content assertions (as opposed to DDL shape constraints) and a production pattern (Checkpoint + Actions) for alerting on validation failure.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation of the tool.
notes: Page does not describe metric history or anomaly detection; GX appears in the OpenLineage integrations list (see DQ-18).

title: dbt: Model contracts
core_concepts: contract: enforced: true; Column name + data_type preflight check; Constraints not_null, primary_key, foreign_key, unique, check; Definable-and-enforced vs definable-not-enforced vs not-definable per platform; Breaking-change detection against prior project state; Major version bump on backwards-incompatible change
engineering_principles: A contract is a set of upfront guarantees about a model's shape; dbt verifies query columns match the YAML and emits names/types/constraints into DDL so the platform enforces them at build time. Most analytical platforms only enforce not_null; Postgres enforces all five. Removing a column, changing a data_type, or removing/modifying a constraint on a contracted model is a breaking change requiring a major version bump.
practical_examples: YAML: models: dim_customers with config.contract.enforced: true, columns customer_id int (constraints: not_null), customer_name string. Supported for table, incremental (on_schema_change append_new_columns or fail) and view (names/types only); not Python models, materialized views, ephemeral, sources, seeds, snapshots.
why_it_matters: Directly answers where structural constraints are actually enforced: the OLTP database (Postgres) enforces PK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK, analytical warehouses mostly do not, so DDL constraints must be the OLTP floor and warehouse tests must compensate downstream. Also supplies the breaking vs non-breaking classification for schema changes.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with last-updated date; the per-platform enforcement table is the authoritative statement for dbt adapters.
notes: The per-adapter table cells could not be attributed reliably from the fetched text except the explicit statements for Postgres (all five enforced) and Microsoft Fabric (only not_null checked).

title: Soda Core v4 (data quality and data contract verification engine)
core_concepts: YAML data contracts; Dataset checks: schema, row_count; Column checks: missing (percent threshold), invalid (valid_values); 50+ built-in checks; soda contract verify (local, pipeline, Soda Cloud/Runner); soda-{datasource} packages
engineering_principles: Author checks declaratively in a YAML contract per dataset and verify schema and data with a CLI/Python API wherever the pipeline runs; the same contract can be published to Soda Cloud and verified remotely.
practical_examples: Contract with dataset-level schema and row_count checks and column-level missing/invalid checks; packages for Athena, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB, Fabric, PostgreSQL, Redshift, Snowflake, Spark DataFrames, SQL Server, Synapse, Trino. Docs home (also fetched, https://docs.soda.io/) shows a reconciliation check row_count_diff comparing a Snowflake orders dataset to a MySQL source with must_be_less_than: 1.
why_it_matters: Shows a YAML-declarative alternative to dbt tests that can run at ingestion or in the warehouse and that includes source-to-target reconciliation checks as first-class syntax.
authority_rationale: Official project README (vendor-maintained open source); less detailed than full docs, and the docs home page lacked technical depth.
notes: README no longer uses the name SodaCL; legacy v3 packages soda-core-{datasource} are pinned to 3.5.x. License type not stated in fetched text.

title: Deequ - Unit Tests for Data (AWS Labs)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (awslabs); Schelter et al.
core_concepts: VerificationSuite and Check; Metrics computation driving assertions; Constraint suggestion; MetricsRepository (persisted metrics); Anomaly detection on metrics over time; Incremental metrics via algebraic states; Data profiling; PyDeequ
engineering_principles: Define unit tests for data as constraints over computed metrics (completeness, uniqueness, value sets, non-negativity, quantiles) and run them as Spark jobs; persist metrics so changes can be detected as anomalies; suggest constraints automatically for large datasets; compute metrics incrementally for growing/partitioned data.
practical_examples: Scala example over a five-row Item DataFrame checking size, completeness, uniqueness, allowed values, non-negativity, URL presence and median of numViews; reports productName 80% complete and only 40% of description values containing a URL. Deequ 2.x per-Spark-version artifacts (e.g., -spark-3.5); 2.1.0+ requires Java 11.
why_it_matters: Reference design for code-based, metrics-first validation at the Spark/ingestion layer and for storing quality metrics over time, which anomaly-based observability requires.
authority_rationale: Official AWS Labs project README backed by a peer-reviewed VLDB 2018 paper (Schelter et al., PVLDB 11(12), pp. 1781-1794).
notes: Apache-2.0 license.

title: Pandera documentation (0.35.0)
core_concepts: DataFrameSchema; DataFrameModel (dataclass/pydantic-style); Column and Check; Lazy validation with SCHEMA vs DATA error report; Decorators check_input/check_output/check_io/check_types; Backends: pandas, PySpark SQL, Polars, Ibis, PyArrow, DataFusion; Narwhals backend; Schema inference; Hypothesis data synthesis
engineering_principles: Validate dataframes at runtime against statically declared schemas inside the pipeline code (at function boundaries via decorators), collect all violations lazily, and reuse schemas to synthesise test data.
practical_examples: schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({'column1': pa.Column(int, pa.Check.ge(0)), 'column2': pa.Column(float, pa.Check.lt(10)), 'column3': pa.Column(str, [pa.Check.isin([*'abc']), pa.Check(lambda s: s.str.len() == 1)])}); equivalent class Schema(pa.DataFrameModel) with pa.Field(ge=0) and @pa.check methods. Import from pandera.pandas (top-level import warns since v0.24.0).
why_it_matters: Represents the in-process, pre-write validation point (before data reaches a database or lake), complementing DDL constraints and warehouse tests.
authority_rationale: Official project documentation of a widely used open-source tool.
notes: Schema inference supported only on the pandas backend; feature support varies by backend.

title: Elementary - dbt-native data observability (OSS repository)
core_concepts: Anomaly detection tests as native dbt tests; Automated freshness/volume/schema monitors; dbt artifacts uploader (run results, metadata); Lineage enriched with test results; Alerts to Slack and Microsoft Teams with owner tagging; Configuration as code in the dbt project
engineering_principles: Collect quality metrics via dbt tests, store dbt artifacts in the warehouse, detect anomalies in freshness/volume/column metrics, and route alerts to owners; use lineage with test results for impact and root-cause analysis.
practical_examples: OSS = Elementary dbt package + CLI that runs tests, detects anomalies and sends alerts; README attributes column-level lineage to Elementary Cloud; Cloud docs (https://docs.elementary-data.com/, also fetched) describe a metadata-only architecture ('We never access or process your raw data'), incidents and AI triage.
why_it_matters: Shows how observability can be implemented inside the warehouse-test layer with owner metadata driving alert routing, a requirement a schema framework must supply (owner per table).
authority_rationale: Official README of a reputable open-source tool; Apache-2.0; 2.4k stars; limited technical depth on the fetched pages.
notes: Anomaly-detection parameters (training period, sensitivity) were not retrievable from the fetched pages.

title: What is Data Observability? (Monte Carlo) [vendor]
core_concepts: Data observability definition; Five pillars: freshness, quality, volume, schema, lineage; Data downtime; Data reliability engineering borrowing from SRE
engineering_principles: Treat data health like application health: monitor freshness (how up to date tables are), quality (NULL %, unique %, accepted ranges), volume (completeness), schema (who changed what, when) and lineage (affected upstream/downstream assets); measure data downtime (periods when data is partial, erroneous, missing or inaccurate) as the consumer-facing reliability metric.
practical_examples: Pillar descriptions with example signals; data downtime proposed as an SLA-like metric analogous to a SaaS product being up or down.
why_it_matters: Supplies the most widely cited taxonomy of observability signals, but it is vendor-originated and has changed (the updated page uses 'quality' where earlier versions used 'distribution'), so it should be treated as a taxonomy rather than a standard.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner/vendor post; marketing context; the author claims to have coined the term in 2019.

title: Shifting Left: How Data Contracts Underpin People, Processes, and Technology [vendor blog]
organization_author: Confluent; Andrew Jones (author of 'Driving Data Quality with Data Contracts')
core_concepts: Shift left for data; Data contract as human- and machine-readable metadata document; Schema, SLAs, documentation, categorisation, versioning and change management in the contract; Ownership by the data product owner; Publishing the contract to Schema Registry and applying it to a topic; Data product definition
engineering_principles: Handle quality, structure and governance at the point of data creation rather than after problems spread; codify schema and SLAs in a contract owned by the producer, publish it to the registry that both operational and analytical consumers use, and let the registry enforce quality checks and migration rules. Downstream fixes are duplicated with slightly different logic and unmanaged upstream schema changes break every consumer.
practical_examples: Contract published to Confluent Schema Registry via a platform-team CD task, applied to a Kafka topic (streaming interface), exposed as tables via Tableflow for analytics, derived data products built with Flink.

title: Apache Iceberg: Branching and Tagging (Audit Branch / Write-Audit-Publish)
core_concepts: Branches and tags as named snapshot references with retention; write.wap.enabled table property; spark.wap.branch session config; Audit branch workflow; fast_forward procedure to publish; expireSnapshots removes expired branch references; Schema applies across all branches
engineering_principles: Write new data to an audit branch so the main table history is unaffected, validate the branch with data quality checks, then publish by fast-forwarding main to the branch head; retain branches/tags by age and snapshot count; writes to a branch are validated against the current table schema, while tag/snapshot queries use the schema in place at snapshot time.
practical_examples: Six-step audit-branch procedure: enable write.wap.enabled; create an audit branch with e.g. 7-day retention; set spark.wap.branch and run the write; validate; call fast_forward to move main; branch reference removed by expireSnapshots after retention. Historical tags with weekly/monthly/yearly retention; temporary 7-day test branches keeping the latest 2 snapshots.
why_it_matters: The current, vendor-neutral mechanism for the WAP promotion gate at the storage layer, enabling validation before consumers can see data without copying it.
authority_rationale: Official Apache project documentation (Java docs, version 1.12.0).

title: Whoops, the Numbers Are Wrong! Scaling Data Quality @ Netflix (Hadoop/DataWorks Summit 2017 slides)
core_concepts: Write-Audit-Publish ETL pattern (Prep, Write, Audit, Publish); Quinto data quality service with fail/warn rule behaviours; Metacat federated metastore storing extended table attributes (primary keys, lifecycle, audience, valid-thru); Row-count and null-count audits; Tiered coverage: not every table needs quality coverage
engineering_principles: Write the new partition to an audit table rather than production, evaluate metrics against configured rules (each rule maps metric + evaluation to fail-the-job or warn), and only then move the partition into the warehouse table; favour modular components over all-or-nothing frameworks; a query-based solution suffices for many use cases.
practical_examples: Row count must be >= 0 and >= prior value (fail on breach); null count compared with a normal distribution (warn), e.g., a jump from 21 to 17,240 nulls flagged; publish step sets a valid-thru timestamp in Metacat; Python libraries 'Jumpstarter' (Quinto) and 'WAP'.
why_it_matters: Primary-source origin of the WAP pattern later built into Iceberg; demonstrates audit metrics, severity tiers and catalog attributes a schema framework can mandate (PK declared in catalog, publish timestamp).
authority_rationale: Major-organisation conference talk by the practitioner who introduced the pattern; slides rather than a peer-reviewed paper.
notes: Related gating case studies: Intuit circuit breakers, Strata SF session 2019-03-27 by Sandeep Uttamchandani (https://conferences.oreilly.com/strata/strata-ca-2019/public/schedule/detail/73082.html, fetched and verified) - 'data availability in dashboards a function of the data quality', inspired by microservices circuit breakers; stage-gating mechanics exist only in a third-party slide copy (not verified). Airbnb 'How Airbnb Built Wall to prevent data bugs' (https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/how-airbnb-built-wall-to-prevent-data-bugs-ad1b081d6e8f) and 'Data Quality at Airbnb' (https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/data-quality-at-airbnb-870d03080469): URLs returned verbatim by WebSearch but fetch returned HTTP 403, so url_verified would be false; search snippets indicate Wall is a Python framework on Airflow with config-file checks that can be declared blocking or non-blocking, and Midas certification as a 'gold standard' promise; Part 2 byline suggests Jan 2021 rather than 2020.

title: Databricks: Manage data quality with pipeline expectations (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines)
core_concepts: Expectation = name + SQL boolean constraint + action; Warn (default; EXPECT / dp.expect); Drop (ON VIOLATION DROP ROW / dp.expect_or_drop); Fail (ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE / dp.expect_or_fail; transaction rolled back); expect_all / expect_all_or_drop / expect_all_or_fail; Data quality metrics in the pipeline event log
engineering_principles: Validate each record as it flows through the pipeline with declarative constraints; choose warn to keep rows and record metrics, drop to filter invalid rows, or fail to halt and roll back the update; constraints may not call custom Python, external services or subqueries on other tables; metrics are visible in the Data quality tab or event log.
practical_examples: @dp.expect('valid_timestamp', "timestamp > '2012-01-01'") and CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2012-01-01'). Companion patterns page (https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectation-patterns, updated 2026-10-26, also fetched): quarantine by computing is_quarantined = NOT(rule1 AND rule2) with @dp.expect_all(rules) and two filtered views (one table with a flag, not a separate physical table); row-count validation materialized view with CONSTRAINT no_rows_dropped EXPECT (a_count == b_count) and fail-on-violation; range validation using mean +/- 3 standard deviations over 30 days with expect_or_drop; caveat that expectations control data quality not orchestration, so blocking downstream work requires separate pipelines linked by a job.
why_it_matters: Official articulation of warn/drop/fail severity tiers, the quarantine pattern and source-to-target row-count reconciliation inside a pipeline, all of which a schema framework can prescribe generically.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with last-updated dates.
notes: Python examples use the dp namespace (not dlt). Expectations apply only to streaming tables, materialized views and temporary views; not supported with AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.

title: Kimball Design Tip #164: Have You Built Your Audit Dimension Yet?
core_concepts: Audit dimension attached to fact tables; Environment/version variables (ETL master version, currency-conversion version, allocation version); Data quality indicator flags (missing data, data supplied/estimated, unlikely value); Flags sourced from the error event fact table; Metadata elevated to ordinary data
engineering_principles: Attach an audit dimension to every fact table so business users can see which ETL configuration produced each row and whether quality screens raised warnings; populate version columns from a time-ranged version table and quality flags from the back-room error event schema; keep the design simple initially; flags are warnings, not diagnoses.
practical_examples: Two column groups (environment variables and quality flags); quotes: 'elevates metadata to the status of ordinary data', 'one of the most effective tools for managing data quality and data governance', 'keep it simple and not get too idealistic in the beginning'.
why_it_matters: Provides the dimensional-modelling counterpart to control tables: an audit FK on every fact row that ties quality and provenance to the schema itself, enabling reconciliation and compliance queries.
authority_rationale: Recognised author of the Kimball methodology publishing on the Kimball Group site; foundational practitioner guidance rather than a standard.
notes: Related Kimball Group technique pages also fetched and verified (n.d.): Error Event Schemas (https://www.kimballgroup.com/?p=19414) - data quality screens test data from source systems to the BI platform; error event fact table (one row per error) and error event detail fact table (one row per column per table involved), kept in the ETL back room; Audit Dimension technique page (https://www.kimballgroup.com/?p=19403) - audit attributes include versions of ETL code, useful for compliance and auditing; Late Arriving Facts (https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/late-arriving-fact/) - look up the dimension keys that were effective when the measurement event occurred. title: Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials: Account Reconciliation and Subledgers (Using General Ledger, 26A)
core_concepts: Subledger-to-General Ledger reconciliation; Prerequisite: transactions accounted and journals posted; Exception categories: incomplete accounting, amount mismatch, manual journals, non-subledger journals; Account Analysis report; Payables/Receivables to Ledger Reconciliation reports; Trial Balance; Control accounts restricted to subledger sources; Run after period close
engineering_principles: Compare open subledger balances with the corresponding GL account balance for each accounting period; when they differ, match each subledger transaction to its accounting entry to isolate the cause; designate payables/receivables accounts as control accounts that other sources cannot post to; run reconciliation only after the subledger periods are closed to new transactions; reconcile at ledger or primary balancing segment level; the accounting department owns the process.
practical_examples: Automatic flagging of transactions without complete accounting, amounts that do not tie to the accounting entry, manually entered journals to the account and journals not from the subledger; summary data reflects the extraction run time while detail is real time, so extraction should run after close to minimise discrepancies.
why_it_matters: Authoritative statement of what financial reconciliation requires (control accounts, period-close gating, categorised explained differences), which a schema framework should mandate for financial fact tables and ledgers.
authority_rationale: Official vendor product documentation for a widely used financial system.

title: reladiff - high-performance diffing of large datasets across databases (fork of data-diff)

engineering_principles: Validate replication or migration by comparing checksums of row segments across databases and downloading only mismatching segments, or by joining within one database; materialise diffs for audit.
practical_examples: Cross-database mode for source-to-target verification; same-database mode for before/after comparisons with extra table statistics; Python 3.8+; MIT license.
why_it_matters: Gives the row-level reconciliation technique (hash/segment comparison) that complements count and aggregate controls when exact source-to-target fidelity must be proven.

title: Databricks: Capture and view data lineage using Unity Catalog
core_concepts: Automatic runtime lineage for Spark DataFrame and Databricks SQL queries; Table-level lineage incl. notebooks, jobs, pipelines, dashboards, ML model versions, file paths; Column-level lineage; System tables system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage (rolling 395-day window); Catalog Explorer lineage retained indefinitely from 2024-09-01; External metadata objects for non-metastore assets

title: Data lineage in classic Microsoft Purview Data Catalog
