title: PostgreSQL 18: COMMENT - define or change the comment of an object
core_concepts: COMMENT ON TABLE / COLUMN / CONSTRAINT / VIEW / SCHEMA / DATABASE / DOMAIN / FUNCTION / POLICY / TRIGGER and others; One comment per object; new COMMENT replaces; NULL or empty string removes; Comments dropped with their object; Viewing via psql \d family and obj_description / col_description / shobj_description; Visibility: any user connected to the database can see all comments
engineering_principles: Store table and column descriptions in the database catalog alongside the DDL so documentation travels with the schema and can be harvested by catalogs; never place sensitive information in comments because they are visible to every connected user.
practical_examples: COMMENT ON TABLE my_schema.my_table IS 'Employee Information'; COMMENT ON COLUMN my_table.my_column IS 'Employee ID number'; COMMENT ON TABLE mytable IS NULL to remove.
why_it_matters: Establishes the OLTP mechanism for the design-time requirement that every table and column carries a description, which catalog ingestion (pull) can then surface.
authority_rationale: Official PostgreSQL documentation (PostgreSQL 18).

title: uuid benchmark war
organization_author: Ardent Performance Computing blog (byline not captured)

engineering_principles: Time-ordered keys narrowed the insert gap to bigint in this test; bigint stayed smallest.

title: A deeper look at old UUIDv4 vs new UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18
core_concepts: UUIDv7; UUIDv4; B-tree fragmentation; physical correlation
engineering_principles: Random keys lower leaf density and destroy physical correlation.
practical_examples: PostgreSQL 18; hardware not stated. 50M into empty table: v4 1,239,840 ms, v7 106,343 ms. Next 50M: v4 2,776,881 ms, v7 100,354 ms. Index at 100M: 3,956 MB vs 3,008 MB. 1M rows pgstatindex: density 71 vs 89.98, fragmentation 49.99 vs 0.
why_it_matters: Largest PostgreSQL 18 data size found, and exposes index internals.

title: Are MySQL UUID inserts really that slow?

engineering_principles: Under a tiny buffer pool, UUIDv1 matched INT while UUIDv4 fell away as the table grew.

why_it_matters: Only MySQL 8 sysbench run with published Lua scripts found.

title: A Performance Analysis for Efficient Schema Design in Cloud-Based Distributed Data Warehouses
organization_author: Fred E. R. Rabelo Ferreira and Robson do Nascimento Fidalgo, UFPE (ICEIS 2024)
subcategory: One Big Table vs star schema
core_concepts: SSB; fully denormalized schema; memory pressure
engineering_principles: Denormalization is not a guaranteed gain; the winner depends on the engine.
practical_examples: SSB SF10 (60M rows) and SF50 (300M rows), 3 nodes with 16 GB RAM each on AWS. Star faster than flat by 74 percent on Redshift and 63 percent on MariaDB Columnstore; flat 42 percent faster on Singlestore. SF50 volume: Redshift 12.7 GB fact vs 62.7 GB flat.
why_it_matters: Strongest independent, peer-reviewed evidence on this question and contradicts vendor-hosted results.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed conference, university authors, states a public script; engine versions not found.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Funding and conflict statement not located. Small clusters. The script location was not followed.

title: TiDB: A Raft-based HTAP Database
core_concepts: CH-benCHmark; Raft learner; TiFlash; freshness
engineering_principles: Separate row and column replicas limit interference, at the cost of some replication lag.
practical_examples: Six servers, 188 GB, two E5-2630 v4 each. AP clients degraded TP at most 10 percent; TP degraded AP at most 5 percent. At 100 warehouses, under 1000 ms lag: 98.64-99.58 percent with 2 AP clients, 84.82-87.17 percent with 32. MemSQL 7.0 TP throughput fell by more than 5x with more AP clients.
why_it_matters: Rigorous design, but a vendor reporting on its own system.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed in PVLDB; full vendor conflict.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. NOT independent: all authors from PingCAP, and the competitor comparison is authored by the vendor.

title: HyBench: A New Benchmark for HTAP Databases
organization_author: Chao Zhang, Guoliang Li, Tao Lv (Tsinghua University, China Software Testing Center)
core_concepts: HyBench; H-Score; F-Score; workload isolation
engineering_principles: Isolated architectures hold throughput and freshness better under concurrency; no architecture wins everywhere.
practical_examples: Four-node cluster, 40-core E5-2630, 128 GB, 1 TB SSD; SF1/10/100 (518 MB, 5.3 GB, 56 GB); PostgreSQL 14 streaming replication plus four anonymized commercial systems. SF1: PostgreSQL-SR H-Score 320, F-Score 24 ms; A4 QPS 676.29, XPS 45.49, F-Score 78 ms, H-Score 200. A4 ATS fell 7.99 to 1.08 at T-max with an F-Score of 19.6 s at (100,20).
why_it_matters: Best independent-leaning open benchmark for isolation and freshness, with public code.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed in PVLDB with public code; commercial systems anonymized.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Conflict: supported partly by Huawei and CCF-Huawei fund; thanks GaussDB, OceanBase, Dameng, Alibaba Cloud and Tencent Cloud teams. Commercial systems unnamed due to DeWitt clauses, so results cannot be mapped to products. Repository github.com/Rucchao/HyBench-2023 not opened.
